title: He sold 10% of Apple for $800. Was it a mistake?
seo_title: Ronald Wayne sold 10% of Apple for $800: was it a mistake?
summary: Ronald Wayne co-founded Apple, then gave up his 10% stake for $800 within two weeks. Hindsight says disaster. What he knew at the time says something else.
intro: On 1 April 1976, three men signed a three-page agreement that created the Apple Computer Company. Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak took 45% each. The third signature belonged to Ronald Wayne, who had written the document himself and took the remaining 10%.

On 12 April, an amendment removed him from the partnership. For giving up his 10%, he received $800. Half a century later, people still call it one of the worst business decisions ever made. Wayne, now in his nineties, sees it differently, and the reasons are worth understanding.

sections.h: Who is Ronald Wayne?
paras: Ronald G. Wayne was an engineer who worked at Atari, the video game company, where he got to know Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak. YourStory and SlashGear both report he was 41 when Apple was formed; Wayne himself has recalled being 40 while "these kids were in their 20s", as Cult of Mac quotes him.

That age gap shaped his role. He described himself to CNNMoney as wanting to be "the adult in the room". Jobs brought him in partly to help persuade Wozniak, and SlashGear reports that Wayne eased Wozniak's worries about the company owning his designs in a conversation at Wayne's home in Mountain View.

sections.h: What Ronald Wayne did at Apple
paras: In the company's first days Wayne made three lasting contributions. He drafted the partnership agreement that set out each founder's share and duties, assigning himself mechanical engineering and documentation, as CNNMoney and Cult of Mac describe.

He drew Apple's first logo: a detailed pen illustration of Isaac Newton sitting under a tree with an apple above him. It was later replaced by the simpler bitten-apple design by Rob Janoff, according to Cult of Mac. And he wrote the manual for the Apple I computer, as YourStory and SlashGear report.
His 10% was meant partly as a tie-breaker. With Jobs and Wozniak holding equal shares, Wayne's vote could settle disagreements between them.

sections.h: Why did Ronald Wayne sell his Apple stake for $800?
paras: The key detail is the legal form of the business. Apple in April 1976 was a general partnership, not a company with limited liability. In a general partnership each partner can be held personally responsible for all of the business's debts, not just a share matching their stake.

Then came Apple's first big order. A Bay Area computer store, The Byte Shop, placed a large order, and Jobs borrowed $15,000 to buy the parts, according to YourStory, SlashGear and The Washington Times. The store, YourStory notes, was rumoured to be slow to pay its bills.

Wayne's position was very different from his partners'. He owned a house, a car and savings. Jobs and Wozniak, still in their twenties, had far less that creditors could take. If the order went wrong and Apple could not repay its debts, the person with the most to lose personally was Wayne, even though he owned the smallest share.

So he withdrew. The amendment dated 12 April 1976 dissolved his share, as Business Standard reported when the documents were auctioned. He received $800, and later a further $1,500 to give up any future claim, according to Cult of Mac, SlashGear and The Washington Times, bringing the total to $2,300.

sections.h: What would Wayne's 10% of Apple be worth today?
paras: Estimates are everywhere and vary widely with Apple's share price; The Washington Times and SlashGear both put the figure at more than $400 billion in 2026. These are rough guesses that ignore how a 10% stake would have been diluted as Apple incorporated, raised money and issued new shares.

Even the papers he signed became valuable. In December 2011 the original partnership agreement and the amendment removing Wayne sold at Sotheby's in New York for about $1.59 million including fees, as Business Standard and KQED reported. KQED, citing Bloomberg, notes that Wayne himself had sold the documents years earlier for a few thousand dollars.

sections.h: Does Ronald Wayne regret leaving Apple?
paras: He has said consistently that he does not. "I've never regretted the move," he told CNNMoney in 2016. He has also joked that if he had stayed, he would probably have ended up "the richest man in the cemetery", a line reported by CNNMoney, Cult of Mac and The Washington Times.

In April 2026, at 91, he repeated the point in an emailed statement reported by The Washington Times: "My success has never been defined by money." He added that it had been defined by acting with clarity and sound judgment "given what I actually knew at the time". His advice to entrepreneurs was blunt: "Never assume your exposure ends at your percentage, because it doesn't."

sections.h: Judging a decision by what was known at the time
paras: Hindsight makes Wayne's choice look absurd. But in April 1976 nobody knew Apple would succeed. What was known was that a small partnership had borrowed money against an order from a customer with a shaky payment record, and that one partner had far more personal property at risk than the others.

Seen that way, Wayne made a reasonable call to protect his family's security. It turned out to be a costly one, but those are different things. A good decision can have a bad outcome, and the reverse is also true.

title: Do 70% of lottery winners really go broke?
seo_title: Do 70% of lottery winners go broke? The statistic checked
summary: It's one of the most-shared money stats online. The group it's credited to says its research doesn't back it. Here's what studies actually found.
intro: In January 2018, an American nonprofit did something unusual. It published a statement saying that a famous statistic, repeated for years in articles and videos under its name, was not backed by its research and could not be confirmed by the organisation.

The statistic was "70 percent of lottery winners go broke." You have probably heard it, often with a confident "within a few years" attached. We went looking for the study behind it. There isn't one. But there is real research on what happens to lottery winners, and it is more interesting than the myth.

sections.h: Where does the 70% lottery statistic come from?
paras: The figure is usually credited to the National Endowment for Financial Education (NEFE), a US nonprofit based in Denver. The Spanish fact-checking site Newtral found that media had been repeating it since at least 2001, sometimes with the extra claim that winners go broke within five years.

In its statement dated 12 January 2018, NEFE explained what it believes happened. In 2001 it brought together a think tank of experts from several fields to discuss sudden windfalls. One participant reportedly mentioned the figure during the discussion. NEFE says the remark was made independently, was never verified, and was later attributed to the organisation as if it were its own research.
So a passing comment in a meeting became a "study" through repetition. NEFE now says plainly that it cannot provide a statistic on windfalls and bankruptcy.

sections.h: What the Florida lottery study actually found
paras: The best-known real research comes from economists Scott Hankins, Mark Hoekstra and Paige Marta Skiba. They linked records of nearly 35,000 winners of Florida's Fantasy 5 lottery game, from April 1993 to November 2002, to bankruptcy filings. Their paper, The Ticket to Easy Street?, was published in The Review of Economics and Statistics in 2011.

They compared people who won $50,000 to $150,000 with people who won less than $10,000. Because winning is random, the small winners act as a fair comparison group. The bigger winners were less likely to file for bankruptcy right after their win. But three to five years later, they were about 50% more likely to file than the small winners.

In other words, for people who were already under financial strain, the money delayed bankruptcy rather than preventing it. The bigger winners did not, on average, use their prize to pay down debt or build up lasting assets. Skiba said winning "seemed to do little to help lottery winners ease their debt."

sections.h: What the Florida study does not show
paras: This is where the viral version goes wrong. Of the roughly 35,000 winners in the study, about 2,000 were linked to a bankruptcy within five years of winning, according to Vanderbilt University and to economist Tim Harford's summary in the Financial Times. That is fewer than 6%, nowhere near 70%.

The study also covered mid-sized prizes, not giant jackpots, and it measured bankruptcy filings, which is only one sign of money trouble. It shows that a windfall does not automatically fix existing money problems. It does not show that most winners end up ruined.

sections.h: Are lottery winners happier? The Swedish evidence
paras: Sweden has some of the best data on this question. Economists Erik Lindqvist, Robert Östling and David Cesarini surveyed Swedish lottery players between 5 and 22 years after a large win, and compared winners with similar people who did not win. Their study appeared in The Review of Economic Studies in 2020.

Large-prize winners reported higher overall life satisfaction that lasted more than a decade, with no clear sign of fading. The effects on day-to-day happiness and mental health were much smaller. The main driver was satisfaction with their finances: the money made people feel more secure, more than it made them feel cheerful.

A separate study from the University of Gothenburg, based on a survey of 420 Swedish winners, found that most kept working as before and preferred to save their winnings as security for the future. The researcher, Anna Hedenus, described the dramatic cases of winners who waste everything as exceptions.

sections.h: Why the myth keeps spreading
paras: A few vivid stories of winners who lost everything get retold again and again. They are memorable, and they fit a satisfying idea that easy money never lasts. The quieter majority, who keep working and put the money aside for security, rarely make headlines.

A round, confident number credited to a real organisation then makes the story feel scientific. That combination, a striking anecdote plus a precise-sounding statistic, is why so many money myths travel so far.

sections.h: How to check a viral statistic
paras: This story is a useful template. When you see a striking number, look for the original source, not the article that repeats it. Ask who measured it, how many people were studied, and over what period. If the trail ends in "studies show" with no study, treat the number as unproven.

The real research still carries a sensible message. Sudden money does not change the habits or pressures that were there before. If a windfall ever lands on you, taking time before any big decision is a reasonable first step.

title: Is the 10,000-hour rule true? What the research actually found
seo_title: 10,000-hour rule: is it true? What the research found
summary: The 10,000-hour rule says practice makes you world-class. The scientist behind the original study said it was oversimplified. Here is what the research shows.
intro: In a music academy in West Berlin in the early 1990s, a group of psychologists asked young violinists a simple question: how many hours have you practised alone, year by year, since you started? The answers would later travel around the world as a slogan: practise for 10,000 hours and you will be world-class at anything.
The man who led that study spent years saying the slogan was not what he found. The real story is more useful than the rule, because it tells you how to practise, not just how long.

sections.h: Where does the 10,000-hour rule come from?
paras: The number comes from a 1993 paper by the psychologist Anders Ericsson and his colleagues Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Römer, published in Psychological Review. They studied violin students at the Music Academy of West Berlin, split into groups rated best, good, and less accomplished, the last group being students training to become music teachers.
The best students had spent the most time in solitary practice. By the age of 20, the top violinists had averaged roughly 10,000 hours, though individuals varied widely around that figure.

The finding became famous in 2008, when Malcolm Gladwell's bestseller Outliers turned it into the 10,000-hour rule. In the book, Gladwell wrote that ten thousand hours is the magic number of greatness.

sections.h: What did Anders Ericsson say about the rule?
paras: Ericsson, who worked at Florida State University, wrote that Gladwell got several things wrong. In a 2016 piece adapted from his book Peak, written with the journalist Robert Pool, he said there was nothing special or magical about ten thousand hours.

His first point was that the number was arbitrary. Gladwell could just as easily have chosen another age. At 18, for example, the best Berlin students had averaged about 7,400 hours of solitary practice, and they were still students, a long way from mastering the violin.

His second point was that 10,000 was an average, not a line that every top performer had crossed. His third point mattered most: the study measured a particular kind of practice, which Ericsson called deliberate practice. Simply spending time on an activity was not the same thing.

He also noted that the study only included students already good enough to get into a top academy. It did not show that almost anyone could become an expert by putting in the hours. Ericsson did agree with Gladwell on one thing: becoming excellent in a competitive field takes a huge amount of effort over many years.

sections.h: What is deliberate practice?
paras: In Ericsson's description, deliberate practice means constantly pushing yourself just beyond what you can already do. It usually involves training designed by a teacher or expert, focuses on specific skills, and uses feedback to find and fix weaknesses.

This is why he argued that the Beatles' long nights playing in Hamburg, a story Gladwell used in Outliers, were not a clean example of the rule. Ericsson wrote that performing is not the same as practising, and that the band's real edge was songwriting, which those club shows did little to build.

Gladwell has also said the rule is often misread. In a 2014 online question-and-answer session, he wrote that practice is not a sufficient condition for success, and joked that he could play chess for 100 years and never become a grandmaster.

sections.h: How much does practice really explain?
paras: In 2014, Brooke Macnamara, David Hambrick and Frederick Oswald published a meta-analysis in Psychological Science that combined 88 studies of practice and performance. Overall, practice explained about 12% of the differences in how well people performed.

The share changed a lot by field. It was about 26% in games such as chess, about 21% in music, about 18% in sports, about 4% in education, and less than 1% in professions. Macnamara said deliberate practice was unquestionably important, but not nearly as important as its strongest supporters had claimed.

In 2019, Macnamara and Megha Maitra at Case Western Reserve University repeated the violin study with a new group of students. They did not find that the best violinists had practised more than the good ones; by age 20, both groups had logged similar amounts. Ericsson had previously criticised such reviews for mixing up total hours with true deliberate practice, so the debate among researchers continues.

sections.h: So is the 10,000-hour rule true?
paras: Not as a rule. Nobody has shown that 10,000 hours is a threshold, and the research suggests practice is one factor among several. Researchers have pointed to others worth studying, such as the age at which someone starts and abilities like working memory.

But the useful idea survives the myth. Both sides of the debate agree that practice matters, and the original study was really about the quality of practice, not just the quantity. An hour spent working on your weakest skill, with someone telling you what to fix, is worth more than an hour of repeating what already comes easily.

If you are learning a new skill at work or helping a child with music or maths, the takeaway is practical. Pick one specific weakness, practise it on purpose, get feedback quickly, and then move to the next one. Counting hours is easy. Making each hour count is the part that works.

title: He built 5,127 prototypes. Then the experts said no.
seo_title: James Dyson's 5,127 prototypes: why vacuum makers said no
summary: James Dyson built 5,127 prototypes of a bagless vacuum. The big manufacturers still turned it down, and their reason is the real lesson of the story.
intro: By the time James Dyson reached his 3,727th prototype, his wife was giving art lessons to bring in extra money. He had already built thousands of versions of the same machine, and he still had more than a thousand to go.

Dyson later wrote in Wired that by prototype 2,627 the family was "really counting our pennies." The machine he was trying to perfect was a vacuum cleaner without a bag. When it finally worked, the companies best placed to sell it did not want it.

sections.h: Who is James Dyson?
paras: James Dyson is a British engineer and designer who trained in furniture and interior design in London. Before vacuums, he was known for the Ballbarrow, a wheelbarrow that used a large ball instead of a wheel.

Dyson lost his father when he was nine, and he has said that experience left him with a sense that his future was down to him. He told Entrepreneur that almost every businessperson he spoke to said his vacuum idea was mad.

sections.h: How the bagless vacuum idea started
paras: The idea came from irritation. In the late 1970s Dyson's own vacuum kept clogging and losing suction, and he could not find a replacement bag. "I loathed changing the vacuum cleaner bag," he told Fortune. The bag, he realised, was the problem: as it clogged with dust, suction dropped.

His answer was to remove the bag entirely and use cyclone separation, spinning the air so fast that dust is thrown out and collected in a bin. Investors who had backed the Ballbarrow would not back this, so he went out on his own, working from a workshop at home.

sections.h: Why did Dyson make 5,127 prototypes?
paras: Dyson built 5,127 prototypes before he had a design that worked well enough, a figure confirmed by the European Patent Office, Fortune and his own Wired column. Accounts of how long this took range from about four to five years, starting around 1978-79. His first model was made from cardboard and tape.

He tested slowly and carefully. One of the golden rules of development, he said, is to change only one thing at a time between tests. That discipline is why the number is so high: each prototype answered a single question.

The cost was real. He has said that eventually he owed over a million dollars. In Fortune he recalled that bankruptcy did not frighten him because he could always make things, but losing the family home did. His wife, Deirdre, sold paintings and taught art, the family grew its own vegetables, and Encyclopedia.com's Gale profile notes he took a second mortgage on the house to fund the work.

sections.h: Why vacuum companies rejected Dyson's invention
paras: With a working design, Dyson went to the big manufacturers in Europe and the United States. Several showed early interest, then backed away. Some deals died with in-house lawyers; others simply did not want to change their product lines.

One reason comes up again and again. Replacement bags were a profitable sideline for the major brands. The European Patent Office notes that manufacturers reportedly feared disrupting the market and upsetting bag makers, and a 2001 profile in New Zealand's Management magazine reports that one maker turned him down because it earned too much from selling bags.

Looking back, Dyson told Fortune: "I wasted so much time and money trying to meet with those who are now my competitors." Several of the companies that had turned him down later began making cyclone-style machines of their own.
In other words, the experts were not only judging whether the idea was good. They were also judging what it would cost them if it was.

sections.h: How Japan kept the idea alive
paras: In 1986 Dyson licensed his design to Apex, a small Japanese company. It sold the machine as the G-Force for 250,000 yen, close to $2,000 at the time, and it became a niche, high-end product.

The royalties mattered more than the sales volume. They paid for further work on the cyclone design back in England. Meanwhile Dyson fought patent cases against companies that had started making similar machines, and in 1991 he settled one with Amway.

sections.h: The Dyson DC01 and what came next
paras: Banks and venture investors kept saying no. In 1993, after his local bank manager lobbied on his behalf, Lloyds Bank agreed to lend him about $1 million for tooling, according to Fortune. That year Dyson launched the DC01 under his own name in Britain, with a clear bin so customers could see the dirt.

It sold through catalogues and the department store John Lewis. Within about two years, by early 1995, it was Britain's best-selling vacuum cleaner. A machine the industry had rejected was now beating it on its home ground.

Dyson has always said the prototypes were the point, not a waste. "There are countless times an inventor can give up on an idea," he wrote in Wired, adding: "The process bore the fruit. I just kept at it." He has also said that having no money forced him to be creative, since he could not pay for salespeople or advertising and had to sell the machine himself.

title: She bet $5,000 on pantyhose. And kept her day job.
seo_title: Sara Blakely: Spanx from $5,000 savings, kept her day job
summary: Sara Blakely started Spanx with $5,000 of savings, no investors and her fax-machine sales job intact. Testing the idea before quitting was the bold move.
intro: In the late 1990s, a saleswoman in Atlanta wanted to wear a pair of cream-coloured trousers without visible lines underneath. She took a pair of pantyhose, cut off the feet with scissors, and wore them under the trousers. It worked better than anything she could find in a shop.
That small fix became Spanx. What most people remember is the billion-dollar ending. The more useful part of Sara Blakely's story is what she did not do at the start: she did not quit her job.

sections.h: Who is Sara Blakely?
paras: Sara Blakely grew up in Clearwater, Florida, and studied communication at Florida State University. She had hoped to become a lawyer, but she did poorly on the LSAT, the US law school admission test, twice.

She then worked briefly at Walt Disney World before taking a sales job with the office supply company Danka. She spent about seven years selling fax machines door to door and rose to become a national sales trainer.

sections.h: What selling fax machines taught her
paras: It was hard, unglamorous work. Blakely has told CNBC that most doors were slammed in her face, that she had her business card ripped up at least once a week, and that police escorted her out of buildings a few times.

That experience turned out to be useful. Seven years of cold calls taught her how to handle rejection and how to sell face to face, two skills she would need when nobody in the hosiery business took her seriously.

sections.h: How Spanx started with $5,000
paras: After the pantyhose experiment, Blakely saw a product: shapewear without feet, so it could be worn with sandals or open shoes. She put about $5,000 of her own savings into developing it. She never took money from an outside investor. She later told Fortune: "I started it with five grand from selling fax machines."

She did much of the early work herself. She researched hosiery patents and wrote her own patent application. When hosiery mills turned her down by phone, she drove to North Carolina to pitch them in person. A few weeks later, a manufacturer in Charlotte called back and agreed to make the product.

Her biggest early sale came from a meeting with a buyer at the department store Neiman Marcus in Dallas. To show how well the product worked, Blakely took the buyer to the ladies' room and demonstrated it on herself. Neiman Marcus agreed to stock Spanx.

sections.h: Why Sara Blakely kept her day job
paras: For about two years, Blakely kept working at Danka during the day and built Spanx in the evenings and early mornings. Her salary paid her bills while she tested whether the idea could stand on its own.

That meant she was not under pressure to sell at any price or to give away part of the company to raise money. Spanx was officially founded in 2000, and for its first 21 years Blakely funded it herself. "I never had a single investor in Spanx other than me," she told Fortune.

She also kept the idea mostly to herself at first. She told Fortune that ideas are most vulnerable in the moment you have them, and that if she had heard people's doubts that early, she would probably still be selling fax machines.

sections.h: The Oprah moment and growth of Spanx
paras: The turning point came in November 2000, when Oprah Winfrey named Spanx one of her Favorite Things, a list known for boosting sales of the products on it. Blakely left Danka around this time. Accounts differ slightly on the timing: Inc., citing Forbes, says she quit two weeks before the show, while other reports say she resigned after Oprah picked the product.

Spanx was still tiny. Blakely told Entrepreneur she had no employees and was working from her apartment when Oprah's team called, so she asked friends and neighbours to help with the orders. "They came over, we sat in a circle on my floor, and that was my staff meeting," she recalled.

In March 2012, Forbes put Blakely on the cover of its billionaires issue and named her, at 41, the world's youngest self-made female billionaire. In October 2021, the investment firm Blackstone bought a majority stake in Spanx at a valuation of $1.2 billion. Blakely kept a significant stake and became executive chairwoman.

To celebrate the deal, she gave every Spanx employee two first-class plane tickets to anywhere in the world and $10,000 to spend on the trip. "I really want every employee to celebrate this moment in their own way," she wrote on Instagram.

sections.h: What Sara Blakely's story teaches about starting up
paras: The story is often told as a bold leap. The real lesson is careful testing. Blakely did not bet her rent on a hunch. She put in money she could afford to lose, kept her income, and used her own sales skills to prove there were real buyers before she walked away from her job.

Quitting too early can force bad decisions, because a founder who needs money next month may accept the wrong deal or give up too soon. Keeping a salary bought Blakely time. By the time she resigned, Spanx had a manufacturer, a major store and national attention.

title: They could've bought Netflix for $50 million. Saying no made sense.
seo_title: Netflix's $50 million offer to Blockbuster: why it said no
summary: In 2000 Netflix offered itself to Blockbuster for $50 million. With what Blockbuster knew then, saying no looked sensible. Here's what changed after.
intro: In early 2000, two founders of a small, money-losing DVD-by-mail company walked into Blockbuster's headquarters in Dallas. Reed Hastings later recalled whispering to his co-founder Marc Randolph on the way in that Blockbuster was a thousand times their size.

Their pitch: Blockbuster buys Netflix, and Netflix runs Blockbuster's online rental business. When CEO John Antioco asked for a price, they said $50 million. He said no. Two decades later the small company had become a global giant and the big one was a single store in Oregon. The easy story is that Blockbuster was foolish. The true story is more useful.

sections.h: What happened at the Netflix-Blockbuster meeting in 2000?
paras: Netflix was founded in 1997 by Hastings and Randolph. By 2000 it rented DVDs by post, was not profitable, and the dot-com boom was starting to crack. In his book, Hastings describes the plan they offered: Blockbuster would buy Netflix and Netflix would build and run Blockbuster.com.

The $50 million price did not land well. In his 2019 book That Will Never Work, Randolph wrote that Antioco told them the dot-com hysteria was "completely overblown." Former Netflix CFO Barry McCarthy said in a 2008 interview that Blockbuster "laughed us out of their office." Randolph has used almost the same words, saying Blockbuster "laughed us out of the room."

Antioco remembers it differently. In a 2022 LinkedIn post, reported by Next TV, he said there were no serious conversations about buying Netflix at the time. He accepted that Netflix executives had visited to discuss a deal and, when talks stalled, made an off-the-cuff offer to sell, but said nobody, Netflix included, thought the company was worth anything close to that price.

sections.h: Why saying no looked sensible at the time
paras: Look at the two companies side by side in 2000. Blockbuster had close to 9,000 stores and about $6 billion in annual revenue, according to both CNBC and Hastings's own account. Netflix was a startup that, by Hastings's recollection, expected to lose about $57 million that year.

Paying $50 million for a business losing more than that every year, just as internet stocks were crashing, was not an obvious bargain. Many careful executives would have passed, especially with a profitable store chain to protect and shareholders watching every dollar. The decision only looks absurd because we know the ending.

sections.h: How Blockbuster almost beat Netflix
paras: Here is the part most retellings leave out: Blockbuster did fight back. It launched Blockbuster Online in 2004, and within a few years its plan called Total Access let customers return mailed discs at a local store and walk out with a new film. Netflix could not match that, because it had no stores.

It worked. Randolph told CNBC that many people do not realise "how close Blockbuster came to actually winning," and said that Blockbuster was hurting Netflix badly. A Motley Fool account based on Gina Keating's book Netflixed says Blockbuster Online's membership roughly doubled in six weeks after Total Access launched. Hastings told Keating in 2009: "If it hadn't been for their debt, they could have killed us."

sections.h: Why did Blockbuster fail in the end?
paras: Total Access was expensive. Both CNBC and the Motley Fool report that Blockbuster lost about $2 every time a customer swapped a disc in store. The company was also carrying about $1 billion of debt after its 2004 spin-off from Viacom, and activist investor Carl Icahn was pushing hard on costs.

In 2007, after clashes with Icahn and the board, including over his bonus, Antioco agreed to step down. His successor, former 7-Eleven chief James Keyes, raised Total Access prices and shifted focus back to the stores. On 23 September 2010 Blockbuster filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, with CNN reporting nearly $1 billion of debt at the time.
So the 2000 meeting was not where Blockbuster lost. It lost in the years after, through leadership changes, pricing choices and a balance sheet that could not carry a long fight.

sections.h: Where Netflix and Blockbuster are today
paras: Netflix started streaming in 2007 and kept going. In its filings for 2024 it reported roughly 302 million paid memberships worldwide, and trade reports put the figure at 301.6 million at the end of that year.
Blockbuster is down to a single store, in Bend, Oregon. Randolph has said the company that once had 9,000 stores is down to one.

sections.h: What the Netflix offer really teaches
paras: The lesson is not that Blockbuster's leaders were stupid. With what they knew in 2000, passing was defensible. The real mistake was judging Netflix mainly by its size and losses that day, instead of asking where it was heading if customers kept liking it.

Hastings himself has been generous about the rival. He told Marketplace that Blockbuster "had us beat hands down" on brand, power and resources, and credited Netflix's survival to a culture that "valued people over process" and put innovation ahead of efficiency. In other words, the small company's edge was not money. It was how quickly it could change its mind.

Randolph put the idea simply: if you are unwilling to disrupt yourself, someone else will be willing to do it for you. Blockbuster eventually built a strong answer to Netflix. It just could not afford to keep it running.

lesson: Don't judge an idea only by its size today. Judge where it's heading, and whether you can afford to follow it there.

faq: Did Blockbuster really have the chance to buy Netflix?

Yes, according to Netflix's founders. In 2000 Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph offered to sell Netflix to Blockbuster for $50 million and were turned down. Former Blockbuster CEO John Antioco has said the offer was off-the-cuff and that no serious talks took place.
Why did Blockbuster say no to buying Netflix?

Blockbuster had about 9,000 stores and roughly $6 billion in revenue, while Netflix was a loss-making DVD-by-mail startup that expected to lose about $57 million that year. With the dot-com bubble bursting, $50 million looked like a poor deal.
Did Blockbuster try to compete with Netflix?
Yes. It launched Blockbuster Online in 2004 and later Total Access, which let customers return mailed discs in stores. Netflix's founders have said this came close to beating them.
When did Blockbuster go bankrupt?

Blockbuster filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 23 September 2010, carrying close to $1 billion of debt. Reed Hastings later said that without its debt, Blockbuster could have killed Netflix.
Is there still a Blockbuster store?
Yes. One store remains open in Bend, Oregon, in the United States.
Did John Antioco regret turning down Netflix?

We found no public statement in which Antioco says he regrets it. In a 2022 interview reported by Next TV, he disputed the popular version of the story: he said Netflix made an off-the-cuff offer to sell during talks about a different deal, that there were no serious negotiations, and that nobody thought Netflix was worth anything close to that price.

title: Decca said no to the Beatles. Then it signed the Rolling Stones.
seo_title: Decca rejected the Beatles in 1962: what happened next
summary: On 1 January 1962 Decca auditioned the Beatles and turned them down. A year later the same executive signed the Rolling Stones. Here is the full story.
intro: On New Year's Day 1962, four young men from Liverpool set up their gear in a studio in London after a long drive south through the snow. Over about an hour they played 15 songs, hoping a major record label would give them a contract.

The label said no. The band was the Beatles, and the label was Decca. The rejection became one of the most famous mistakes in business history. What is told far less often is what the man blamed for it did next.

sections.h: What happened at the Beatles' Decca audition?
paras: The audition took place on 1 January 1962 at Decca's studios in London. The line-up was John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and their drummer at the time, Pete Best. Their manager, Brian Epstein, a Liverpool record shop owner, had been working hard to get them a deal.

The session was supervised by Mike Smith, a young Decca talent scout who had seen the band at their home venue, the Cavern Club in Liverpool. His boss was Dick Rowe, Decca's head of A&R, the department that finds and signs new artists.
The Beatles recorded 15 songs, a mix of cover versions and a few of their own. Epstein was told the band would hear back within weeks.

sections.h: Why did Decca reject the Beatles?
paras: Another group auditioned at Decca the same day: Brian Poole and the Tremeloes. Decca chose them. Accounts of the decision say the Tremeloes were based near London, which made them cheaper and easier to work with than a band from Liverpool, more than 200 miles away.

Seen from 1962, that was not a foolish choice. The Beatles had no hit records and no national profile. The recording itself was not their best work either; George Martin, the producer who later signed them, admitted he might also have turned the group down on the strength of that Decca tape.

sections.h: Who said 'guitar groups are on the way out'?
paras: The most famous line in the story comes from Brian Epstein's 1964 autobiography, A Cellarful of Noise. Epstein wrote that at a lunch meeting, Rowe told him: "Not to mince words, Mr. Epstein, we don't like your boys' sound. Groups of four guitarists are on the way out." Over the years it has been shortened in retelling to "guitar groups are on the way out."

Rowe denied saying it, and kept denying it until his death in 1986. The music writer Johnny Rogan later described Epstein's account as unfair to Rowe. We only have Epstein's version of that lunch, written about two years after it happened, so it is fairest to treat the exact words as his memory rather than a verified quote.

sections.h: How the Beatles found a deal after Decca
paras: Epstein did not give up. He had the Decca recordings transferred to discs at the HMV record shop on Oxford Street in London, so they would be easier to play to other labels. An engineer there liked what he heard and put Epstein in touch with a music publisher, who in turn contacted the office of George Martin, head of the Parlophone label at EMI.

Epstein met Martin on 13 February 1962. Martin heard enough potential to offer the band a recording session, which took place at EMI's studios on 6 June 1962. Parlophone signed them, and Love Me Do became their first single. The rest became music history.

sections.h: Did Decca sign the Rolling Stones?
paras: Yes, and this is the part of the story most people skip. In 1963, George Harrison recommended a band to Dick Rowe. The Beatles had seen them playing rhythm and blues at a club in Richmond, near London. They were called the Rolling Stones.

Rowe went to see them at the Crawdaddy Club in Richmond, and Decca quickly signed them. Reports differ on the exact date of the deal, from late April to May 1963, but they agree it happened within days of Rowe's visit. The Stones' first single, a cover of Chuck Berry's Come On, followed that summer.

Rowe went on to sign or work with many other successful acts at Decca, including Tom Jones, the Moody Blues, the Animals and the Small Faces. Andrew Loog Oldham, the Stones' early manager, later said Rowe should be remembered not as the man who turned down the Beatles, but as the man who signed the Rolling Stones.

sections.h: What the Decca story teaches about bad decisions
paras: Decca's choice looks absurd only because we know how the story ended. With what Rowe and Smith knew in January 1962, choosing a nearby band over an unknown group from far away was a reasonable business call that turned out badly.

What Rowe did next is the useful part. When a Beatle told him about another band, he did not get defensive. He went to see them for himself, and he moved fast. A single miss did not make him more cautious. It made him pay closer attention.

Most of us will make a call that looks wrong later, whether it is a job we turned down or an idea we dismissed. The question that matters is not who to blame. It is what we will look for differently next time, and whether we will act quickly when that chance arrives.

Where is the next chance that looks like the one I missed, and am I watching for it?

title: His game flopped. Its chat tool sold for $27.7 billion.
seo_title: Slack's origin story: how a failed game became $27.7B
summary: Stewart Butterfield's game Glitch shut down in 2012. The chat tool his team built while making it became Slack, which Salesforce bought for $27.7 billion.
intro: On 14 November 2012, a small studio in Vancouver told its players that their online game, Glitch, would close in a few weeks. It had "not attracted an audience large enough to sustain itself," the team wrote. Many of its developers would soon be looking for new jobs.

On that same day, according to a chat screenshot he later shared, co-founder Stewart Butterfield told colleagues he had come up with "a better code name" for a different project: the in-house chat tool the team had built to make the game. The new name was Slack.

sections.h: Who is Stewart Butterfield?
paras: Stewart Butterfield is an entrepreneur, long based in Vancouver, best known for co-founding two very different internet companies, Flickr and Slack. Both started as something else.
After leaving Flickr in 2008, he founded a new company, Tiny Speck, to build an online game. The game was Glitch.

sections.h: What was the game Glitch?
paras: Glitch was a quirky multiplayer game with a highly stylised, hand-drawn look that ran in a web browser. Its creators included Keita Takahashi, the designer of Katamari Damacy, and its makers said it pushed the limits of what a browser game could do. PCWorld called it "a surprisingly rewarding game."
It went live in September 2011, though PCWorld noted it only briefly left its invitation-only beta. IEEE Spectrum reported that it cost about $17 million to develop.

The trouble was timing and reach. Glitch was built on Adobe Flash, which iPhones and iPads did not support, just as people were moving their play to phones. In its closing notice, Tiny Speck pointed to the decline of Flash and the shift to mobile, and admitted the game was unlikely ever to find a big enough audience.

sections.h: Why did Glitch shut down?
paras: Tiny Speck announced the closure on 14 November 2012, and the game world went dark on 9 December 2012. Players were offered refunds, or the option to donate their money to charity or to a fund for the departing staff. The Glitch website and forums stayed open until the end of 2012, according to IEEE Spectrum.

The team was candid. They had hoped to build something many people would pay for, they wrote, but "only managed to create a crazy, beautiful game." Butterfield said on Twitter that the company was not closing, only the game.

sections.h: How Slack started from a failed game
paras: While building Glitch, the team had made its own internal communication tool, a chat system organised into channels with a searchable record of what was said. TechCrunch later described Slack as that internal channel turned into a public product.

After Glitch closed, Butterfield bet the remaining investment money on that tool. A history written by early Slack employees says he funded the pivot from what was left of Tiny Speck's funding, and that every dollar went into the new product.

The tool had been known internally by the codename "linefeed," Business Insider reported. Butterfield has said the new name is an acronym for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge"; some reports give "Communication" in place of "Conversation." Slack opened as a preview in August 2013, and launched publicly on 12 February 2014. Within its first year, active users grew from about 15,000 to more than half a million, according to that same early-staff history.

sections.h: How Slack grew to a $27.7 billion deal
paras: Slack spread quickly through workplaces. By the end of January 2019 it had more than 10 million daily active users and about $400.6 million in annual revenue, as both CNBC and TechCrunch reported.

Slack went public through a direct listing on the New York Stock Exchange on 20 June 2019, under the ticker WORK. Its shares opened at $38.50, well above the $26 reference price. A direct listing meant Slack sold existing shares to the public rather than raising new money through a traditional IPO.

On 1 December 2020, Salesforce agreed to buy Slack for $27.7 billion in cash and stock, the largest acquisition in its history. The deal closed in July 2021, and Butterfield stayed on to lead Slack inside Salesforce. Salesforce chief executive Marc Benioff called the deal "a match made in heaven," UPI reported. When it closed, Butterfield said the two companies were "uniquely positioned to lead this historic shift to a digital-first world."

sections.h: Flickr: the same story, the first time
paras: Remarkably, it was the second time this had happened to Butterfield. In the early 2000s he and Caterina Fake ran a company called Ludicorp, which was building an online game called Game Neverending. They added a photo-sharing feature for players, and it became more popular than the game.

That feature became Flickr, which launched quietly at a technology conference in San Diego in early 2004. Game Neverending was shut down in November 2004 because, as The Guardian's Jack Schofield reported, the company did not have the resources to develop both, and Yahoo bought Flickr in 2005. Twice, the side tool turned out to be the real business, and twice Butterfield was willing to let go of the original plan.

lesson: The tool you built to solve your own problem might be worth more than the project it was built for. When a plan fails, look at what you made along the way.
check_title: Before you write off a project that didn't work, ask:
check: What did we build for ourselves that others might need too?
Am I attached to the original plan, or to solving a real problem?

title: He started over at 65. On $105 a month.
seo_title: Colonel Sanders started over at 65: the KFC story
summary: A new highway emptied Harland Sanders's Kentucky cafe. At 65, living on $105 a month, he took his chicken recipe on the road and built KFC.
intro: In the mid-1950s, Harland Sanders was 65 years old and had just sold the roadside restaurant he had run for a quarter of a century. A new highway route was taking the traffic away from his corner of Corbin, Kentucky, and he auctioned the business at a considerable loss.

His regular income was now a Social Security cheque of $105 a month. Most people would have called that retirement. Sanders got in his car and started driving, taking his chicken recipe to anyone who would let him cook it.

sections.h: Who was Harland Sanders?
paras: Harland David Sanders was born on 9 September 1890 near Henryville, Indiana. He left school after the seventh grade and spent his early decades moving between a long list of jobs before he settled in Kentucky.

Around 1930 he began running a service station in North Corbin, on the busy US 25 highway, and started cooking for travellers in a small dining room there. Encyclopaedia Britannica dates the opening of Sanders' Cafe to 1929; a roadside historical marker in Corbin says he arrived in 1930 and bought a small restaurant in 1932. Either way, it grew into a full restaurant and motel.
In 1935 the Governor of Kentucky, Ruby Laffoon, made him an honorary Kentucky colonel. The title was a civic honour, not a military rank, but he used it for the rest of his life.

sections.h: How the recipe and the first franchise came about
paras: By about 1940 Sanders had settled on the method that made his name: chicken seasoned with a secret blend of 11 herbs and spices and cooked in a pressure cooker. Britannica and the University of New Hampshire's profile of him both describe the recipe this way.
The chicken was popular, but for years it was simply the best-known dish at one roadside restaurant. Sanders's living still depended on the cars that passed his door.

In 1952 Sanders licensed his recipe to Pete Harman, who ran a restaurant in Salt Lake City, Utah. Harman became the first Kentucky Fried Chicken franchisee. The arrangement was simple: Sanders supplied the seasoning and the method, and he was paid a royalty of five cents for every chicken sold.
At the time it was a side income. The cafe in Corbin was still the main business, which is why what happened next hit so hard.

sections.h: Why Sanders had to sell his cafe at 65
paras: In the mid-1950s a new highway route was planned and built that bypassed Corbin, and customer numbers at the cafe fell sharply. Sources differ on the exact year and road: the Corbin marker says plans for a federal highway were announced in 1956, while the Scribner Encyclopedia of American Lives describes a US 25 bypass in 1955. Most accounts link the loss of traffic to the arrival of Interstate 75.

Sanders sold the business. The Scribner encyclopedia and the accountancy magazine AAT Comment both record that, at 65, he was left with a Social Security income of $105 a month. The Corbin marker gives his age at the sale as 66, so reports vary by a year.
He did not start a new restaurant. He decided to sell the one thing that had survived the bypass: his recipe.

sections.h: How he built KFC on the road
paras: Sanders drove from town to town, cooking his chicken for restaurant owners and their staff and offering them the right to sell it. If they liked it, they could sign up and pay him his five cents a chicken. Progress was slow at first. According to both Britannica and the University of New Hampshire, he signed only five restaurants in his first two years.

Then it snowballed. Within a couple of years, AAT Comment reports, would-be franchisees were coming to him instead of the other way round, and Sanders himself, with his colonel title, became the product's best advertisement.
By 1964 more than 600 restaurants in the United States and Canada were selling Kentucky Fried Chicken. Britannica estimates Sanders was earning about $300,000 a year from the business by then.

sections.h: Selling KFC for $2 million, and what came after
paras: In 1964, in his seventies, Sanders sold most of the company to John Y. Brown Jr. of Kentucky and Jack Massey of Tennessee. The price was $2 million, plus a lifetime salary of $40,000 a year and a role as the face of the brand.

Under the new owners the chain grew quickly. By the time they sold it to the drinks company Heublein, it had about 3,500 outlets. Britannica and Restaurant Business date that sale to 1971; the Scribner encyclopedia gives 1972.
Sanders remained the company's ambassador, travelling and appearing in its advertising for the rest of his life. He died on 16 December 1980 in Kentucky, aged 90.

sections.h: What the bypass could not take away
paras: Looking back, the highway did not destroy Sanders's business so much as reveal what it really was. The building, the location and the passing traffic were gone. What remained was a recipe people liked, a method he could teach, and two decades of experience feeding strangers.

The franchise model also suited his situation. He did not need money to build new restaurants; other owners already had kitchens and customers. His job was to show them the product and keep the quality consistent, which was something he had been doing every day in Corbin.

More than 600 KFC outlets; he sells the company for $2 million

lesson: Losing the plan you built is not the same as losing what you are good at. Sanders's cafe was gone, but his recipe and his skill at selling it were not, and those turned out to be the real business.

check: What am I great at that other people would pay for?
Who could I sell it to this month, not someday?
faq: How old was Colonel Sanders when he started KFC?

He licensed his recipe to his first franchisee, Pete Harman, in 1952, when he was 61 or 62. He turned franchising into his full-time work in the mid-1950s at about 65, after a highway bypass forced him to sell his Corbin, Kentucky cafe.
How much was Colonel Sanders's Social Security check?
After selling his cafe at a loss, Sanders had a Social Security income of $105 a month, according to the Scribner Encyclopedia of American Lives and AAT Comment.
How much did Colonel Sanders sell KFC for?

In 1964, with more than 600 outlets, he sold the company to investors led by John Y. Brown Jr. and Jack Massey for $2 million, plus a lifetime salary of $40,000 a year to stay on as the brand's ambassador.
Was Colonel Sanders a real colonel?
No. 'Kentucky colonel' is an honorary title given by the state's governor. Sanders received it in 1935 from Governor Ruby Laffoon and used it for the rest of his life.
How did Colonel Sanders earn money from franchising?
He charged restaurants a royalty of five cents for every chicken they sold using his seasoning and method, rather than a large upfront fee.
Who founded KFC?

Harland Sanders, known as Colonel Sanders, founded Kentucky Fried Chicken. He developed his fried chicken at his roadside cafe in Corbin, Kentucky, and in 1952 licensed the recipe to Pete Harman in Salt Lake City, Utah, who became the first Kentucky Fried Chicken franchisee.
Where was the first KFC restaurant?

The first Kentucky Fried Chicken franchise was Pete Harman's restaurant in Salt Lake City, Utah, in 1952. Sanders's own cafe in North Corbin, Kentucky, where he first served the chicken, is marked as the birthplace of Kentucky Fried Chicken.
When was Colonel Sanders born, and when did he die?
Harland David Sanders was born on 9 September 1890 near Henryville, Indiana. He died on 16 December 1980 in Kentucky, aged 90.
Who owns KFC today?
KFC is owned by Yum! Brands. Sanders sold the company in 1964 to investors led by John Y. Brown Jr. and Jack Massey, and it has changed hands several times since.
What was Colonel Sanders's net worth?

There is no reliable published figure for his net worth. What is documented is that he was earning about $300,000 a year from franchising by the early 1960s, and that in 1964 he sold the company for $2 million plus a lifetime salary of $40,000 a year.

title: He quit Wall Street to sell books online. His boss had one line for him.
seo_title: Jeff Bezos quit Wall Street: the regret test behind Amazon
summary: In 1994 Jeff Bezos had a senior job at a New York hedge fund. His boss said his idea suited someone without a good job. Here is how he decided to go.
intro: In 1994 Jeff Bezos walked through Central Park with his boss, David Shaw, and explained why he wanted to leave a well-paid job on Wall Street to sell books on the internet. Shaw listened carefully. Then, as Bezos later told Princeton graduates, he said: "That sounds like a really good idea, but it would be an even better idea for someone who didn't already have a good job."

It was a fair point, and Bezos took it seriously. The way he finally made up his mind has since become one of the most quoted decision-making tools in business: picture yourself at 80 and ask which choice you would regret.

sections.h: Who was Jeff Bezos before Amazon?
paras: Bezos was born in January 1964 in Albuquerque, New Mexico. He studied electrical engineering and computer science at Princeton, graduating in 1986, and worked at a few firms before joining D. E. Shaw & Co. in New York in 1990.

D. E. Shaw was an investment firm that used computers and mathematical models to trade. Bezos rose quickly and became a senior vice president, which Britannica says made him reportedly the firm's youngest. He met his future wife, MacKenzie, at the firm, where she worked as a research associate.

Part of his job was to look for new business opportunities on the young internet. According to HistoryLink, the Washington state history encyclopedia, he and David Shaw had even discussed the idea of an online "everything store".

sections.h: The 2,300% statistic that started it
paras: In the spring of 1994, Bezos came across a figure that stopped him. In his own words to Princeton's class of 2010: "I came across the fact that Web usage was growing at 2,300 percent per year." At the time very few people had ever bought anything online.

He started listing products that could be sold on the web and settled on books. There were millions of titles in print, far more than any physical shop or mail-order catalogue could hold, but a website could list them all. Books were also easy to describe, and in the early days Amazon simply ordered each book from a distributor after a customer bought it.

sections.h: What his boss told him
paras: When Bezos told Shaw he planned to leave and start an online bookstore, Shaw did not dismiss the idea. He took him on that long walk in Central Park and gave his honest view: good idea, but a better one for someone who did not already have a good job.

HistoryLink adds that Shaw asked him to think it over, and pointed out that D. E. Shaw itself might one day compete in the same space. Bezos was leaving a senior role, a reliable salary and, since he was going in the middle of the year, his annual bonus.

sections.h: What is the regret minimization framework?
paras: Bezos explained his thinking years later in an interview with the Academy of Achievement, and Business Insider has quoted the same words. "I wanted to project myself forward to age 80 and say, 'OK, I'm looking back on my life. I want to minimize the number of regrets I have.'"

He went on: "I knew that if I failed, I wouldn't regret that. But I knew the one thing I might regret is not ever having tried." He joked that only a nerd would call this a "regret minimization framework", but the name stuck.

The useful part of the test is that it changes the question. Instead of asking "What if this fails?", which tends to favour staying put, it asks which choice you will be glad you made over a whole lifetime. For Bezos, failing at something he believed in felt bearable. Never trying did not.
In the same Princeton speech he summed it up simply: "I took the less safe path to follow my passion, and I'm proud of that choice."

sections.h: From a Bellevue garage to Amazon.com
paras: In 1994 Jeff and MacKenzie Bezos headed west to Seattle, a city HistoryLink says he chose partly for its pool of software engineers. Business Insider, citing Wired, reports that MacKenzie drove while Jeff typed the business plan on his computer. Accounts differ on exactly where the drive began.

On 5 July 1994 he incorporated the company in Washington state as Cadabra Inc., a name he soon changed to Amazon. The couple rented a house in Bellevue, near Seattle, and the garage became the first office. Amazon says the first desks were made by buying wooden doors from Home Depot and attaching legs, because doors were cheaper than desks.

Amazon.com opened to the public on 16 July 1995, offering more than a million titles. Its first sale was Douglas Hofstadter's book Fluid Concepts and Creative Analogies. Amazon's own press release from October 1995 says that in the first four weeks it shipped books to customers in all 50 US states and more than 45 other countries. The company went public in 1997.

sections.h: Why this decision still matters
paras: It is easy to look back and say leaving was obvious. In 1994 it was not. Online shopping barely existed, and a respected boss had given him a sensible reason to stay. What Bezos had was a clear way to weigh the choice.

Not every bold move should be made, and not every reader is in a position to leave a stable job. The framework does not say "always take the risk". It asks you to be honest about which kind of regret you can live with, and then to choose on purpose rather than by default.

title: Facebook rejected him in 2009. Five years later it paid up to $19 billion for his app.
seo_title: Brian Acton: rejected by Facebook, then WhatsApp's $19B sale
summary: In 2009 Twitter and Facebook both turned down engineer Brian Acton. He co-founded WhatsApp, which Facebook agreed to buy in 2014 for up to $19 billion.
intro: On 3 August 2009, a software engineer named Brian Acton posted a short update on Twitter: Facebook had turned him down for a job. He did not complain. He wrote that it had been a great opportunity to connect with some fantastic people, and that he was looking forward to life's next adventure.

Less than five years later, Facebook agreed to pay up to $19 billion for a company Acton had co-founded in the meantime. That company was WhatsApp, the messaging app that more than two billion people would go on to use. This is how a quiet job rejection turned into one of the most talked-about tech deals of its decade.

sections.h: Who is Brian Acton?
paras: Brian Acton is an American software engineer who studied computer science at Stanford. In the 1990s he joined Yahoo, then one of the biggest names on the internet, and stayed there as an engineer until 2007.

At Yahoo he met Jan Koum, a younger engineer who had moved to California from Ukraine as a teenager. The Associated Press later described how the two bonded over a shared, no-nonsense attitude to work, and how Acton stood by Koum when Koum's mother died of cancer in 2000.
In 2007 both men left Yahoo. They took roughly a year off, travelling in South America and playing Ultimate Frisbee, before thinking about what to do next.

sections.h: The two rejections of 2009
paras: By 2009 Acton was looking for work. He applied to Twitter first. On 23 May 2009 he tweeted that he had been "denied by Twitter HQ", adding, "That's ok. Would have been a long commute."

A few months later Facebook said no as well. His 3 August 2009 post, reported word for word by DNA India and BGR in 2014, read: "Facebook turned me down. It was a great opportunity to connect with some fantastic people. Looking forward to life's next adventure."

Both posts are short and good-humoured. There is no bitterness in them, no attack on the companies and no public self-pity. That tone is a big part of why the story spread so widely once the ending became known.

sections.h: How WhatsApp started
paras: The next adventure came from his friend. Jan Koum had noticed how the iPhone and its new App Store were changing what phones could do, and he had an idea for an app built around simple status messages. He started WhatsApp in 2009, and the name was a play on "What's up?"

According to the AP, Acton was jobless and working on a less promising start-up when Koum asked him to join. He did, becoming WhatsApp's co-founder later that year. The goal settled into something simple: let people send messages reliably to friends and family on almost any phone, anywhere in the world.

The two founders were strict about what WhatsApp would not do. Acton wrote a note with the line "No Ads. No Games. No Gimmicks.", and Koum kept it taped to his desk. Koum, who grew up in the Soviet Union, also said he did not want the company to pry into people's conversations. The investment firm Sequoia Capital backed the company early.

sections.h: The $19 billion deal with Facebook
paras: WhatsApp grew quickly, especially in countries where text messages were expensive. On 19 February 2014 Facebook announced it would buy the company. Its official press release, filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, set out the terms: $4 billion in cash and about $12 billion in Facebook shares, plus $3 billion in restricted stock units for WhatsApp's founders and staff, which together came to up to $19 billion.

At the time WhatsApp had more than 450 million monthly users, and more than a million new people were registering every day, according to the same release. Facebook said 70% of users were active on any given day.

Forbes reported that Koum, Acton and Sequoia's Jim Goetz signed the deal papers at a disused building in Mountain View that had once been a social services office, the place where Koum had queued for food stamps as a teenager. The company that had declined to hire Acton in 2009 was now the buyer.

sections.h: What Brian Acton did next
paras: Acton stayed on after the acquisition and left WhatsApp and Facebook in September 2017. In February 2018 he announced he was putting $50 million into a new non-profit, the Signal Foundation, to support the encrypted messaging app Signal. He became its executive chairman, and Signal's creator, Moxie Marlinspike, remained in charge of the app.

WhatsApp itself kept growing. In February 2020 it announced it had passed two billion users worldwide, making it the second app in Facebook's family to reach that mark, as Business Today and Bloomberg reported.

sections.h: Why this rejection story matters
paras: Rejection stories are easy to tell backwards, as if the happy ending was always obvious. It was not. In August 2009 Acton was an experienced engineer without a job, turned down by two of the hottest companies in Silicon Valley, helping a friend with a small app that few people had heard of.

What he controlled was his response. He treated each no as a closed door, not as a judgement on his worth. He stayed polite in public, kept good relationships and put his energy into the next real opportunity, even though it was smaller and far less certain than a job at Facebook.

Most rejections will not end in a billion-dollar deal, and that is not the point. The point is that a single no from a single company, on a single day, tells you very little about where you will be in five years.

title: Seven women, ₹80 and one rooftop: the Lijjat Papad story
seo_title: Lijjat Papad story: seven women, ₹80 and a rooftop
summary: In 1959 seven women in Mumbai borrowed ₹80 and made four packets of papad on a terrace. Lijjat now has about 45,000 women members who co-own it.
intro: On 15 March 1959, on the terrace of a residential building in Girgaum, in south Mumbai, seven women rolled out their first batch of papad. It came to four packets, and they sold them to a local shopkeeper.

The money to buy the flour and spices was a loan of ₹80. More than six decades later, the organisation those women started is reported to have a turnover of about ₹1,600 crore and around 45,000 women members, every one of them a co-owner.

sections.h: Who started Lijjat Papad?
paras: The founders were seven neighbours, Gujarati-speaking housewives with little formal education, who wanted to earn money of their own. The best known of them is Jaswantiben Jamnadas Popat. "We were semi-literate, which restricted our chances to get jobs," she told The Better India.

What they did have was a skill. Papad, the thin, crisp lentil wafer served with Indian meals, was something they already made well at home. "Making papads does not require education, which is why we started Lijjat," Jaswantiben said in an interview quoted by Business Insider India.

sections.h: The ₹80 loan and the first day
paras: The ₹80 came from Chhaganlal Karamsi Parekh, a social worker in the area known as Chhagan Bappa, who became the group's mentor. According to the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), he also helped shape the principles that guided it, including running it in a professional way and standing on its own feet rather than depending on donations.

The first sales were tiny. Jaswantiben recalled that on the first day they sold one kilo of papad and earned eight annas, half a rupee, and the next day two kilos brought in one rupee. Sales for the whole first year came to just over ₹6,000, according to The Better India and YourStory.

Early problems were practical ones. WIPO notes that the women first dried papad over charcoal, which left the wafers dirty, so within about a year they bought a covered stove. Not every step worked: an attempt to open a branch in Malad in 1961 failed. They learned from it and kept going.

sections.h: How the Lijjat cooperative model works
paras: Word spread among women in the neighbourhood, and within months dozens had joined. From the start, the group made a choice that shaped everything: women who join are not employees. They are members, known as 'sisters', who together own the organisation and share in its earnings.

In 1962 the group picked the brand name Lijjat, a Gujarati word for tasty, through a small prize contest among members. By 1962-63, annual sales had grown to close to ₹2 lakh. In 1966 it registered as a society, and the Khadi and Village Industries Commission recognised it as a village industry, which opened up better access to finance. In 1968 it opened its first branch outside Maharashtra, at Valod in Gujarat.

WIPO describes the work as split into processing, packaging and distribution, coordinated by a central managing committee in Mumbai, with branches that run themselves but follow the same rules. Members earn a wage for rolling, called vanai, and Business Insider India reports that a 21-member committee decides how profits are shared.

sections.h: Why Lijjat's quality stayed the same
paras: A brand made in thousands of homes could easily taste different from one packet to the next. Lijjat's answer was strict standardisation. The Better India reports that raw materials are bought from a single source and sent to all branches, each member gets a standard base and rolling pin so papads come out the same size, and finished products are tested in a laboratory in Mumbai.

WIPO's case study adds that daily samples are checked and substandard batches are destroyed. The organisation has also chosen to keep production by hand rather than move to mass machine production, so that the work stays with women members.

sections.h: How big is Lijjat Papad today?
paras: The numbers kept compounding. Recent reports by Business Insider India, The Better India and YourStory put Lijjat's turnover at about ₹1,600 crore and its membership at around 45,000 women. Reports give its branch count as 81 or 82, and it exports papad to countries including the United States, the United Kingdom and Singapore.

Lijjat has also expanded beyond papad into products such as spices, wheat flour and the Sasa range of detergents, which it launched in 1988. WIPO also notes that it runs scholarships and education grants for members and their families, especially daughters.
In 2021 Jaswantiben Popat, then 91, received the Padma Shri, one of India's highest civilian honours. "The credit of Lijjat Papad goes to every woman working here," she said afterwards.

sections.h: What the Lijjat story shows about starting small
paras: The founders did not wait for a factory, an investor or a business plan. They started with a skill they already had, a loan small enough to repay and a product they could make the next morning.
The capital was the least important part. What mattered was showing up every day, holding the quality steady, and building a structure where every new member had a real stake in the result.

It also shows how structure can protect a habit. Because members own the work, the standards set on that first terrace, careful quality and steady daily effort, travelled with Lijjat into every new branch.

The brand name Lijjat is chosen through a members' contest

lesson: You don't need big money to start something. You need a skill, a small first step and people who keep showing up, with a stake in what they build.
check: What is the ₹80 version of your idea: the smallest test you could run this month?

title: He missed by 25 seconds. Two years later he ran a marathon under two hours.
seo_title: Eliud Kipchoge: from 2:00:25 to the first sub-2 marathon
summary: In 2017 Eliud Kipchoge missed a two-hour marathon by 25 seconds. On 12 October 2019 in Vienna he ran 1:59:40, the first human under two hours.
intro: On the morning of 6 May 2017, on the motor-racing circuit at Monza in Italy, Eliud Kipchoge was on the last of his laps, chasing a number no human had ever beaten. He crossed the line in 2:00:25. After 42.195 kilometres, he had missed by 25 seconds.
Asked about it afterwards, he did not talk about failure. According to World Athletics, his words were: "We are now just 25 seconds away." Two and a half years later, in Vienna, he closed the gap.

sections.h: Who is Eliud Kipchoge?
paras: Kipchoge is a Kenyan distance runner who started on the track. At 18 he won the 5,000 metres at the 2003 World Championships in Paris, beating two of the greatest runners of the era, Hicham El Guerrouj and Kenenisa Bekele. He then took Olympic bronze in 2004 and silver in 2008 over the same distance. Later he moved up to the marathon.

The switch transformed his career. He won Olympic marathon gold in Rio in 2016 and became known for an almost unbroken run of wins in the world's biggest city marathons. He grew up on a farm in Kenya and, as a boy, ran to school each day.

sections.h: Why two hours looked impossible
paras: To run a marathon in under two hours, you have to average a little under 2 minutes 51 seconds for every kilometre, for nearly 42 kilometres without a break. That is about 21 kilometres an hour, the speed many fit people manage only for a short sprint.

For decades the official world record sat several minutes outside that mark. At the time of the Monza attempt it was 2:02:57, set by Dennis Kimetto in Berlin in 2014. Many coaches and scientists thought sub-two was decades away, if it was possible at all.

sections.h: Breaking2: what happened at Monza in 2017
paras: Nike organised the 2017 attempt, called Breaking2, as a laboratory-style race. The course was a loop of the Monza Formula One circuit, about 2.4 kilometres long, run 17.5 times. Three runners took part: Kipchoge, Zersenay Tadese of Eritrea and Lelisa Desisa of Ethiopia, protected from the wind by rotating teams of pacemakers.

Kipchoge passed halfway in 59:57, right on schedule. Tadese and Desisa dropped back, and he ran the second half alone with his pacers. He reached 40 km in 1:54:00, which left him needing to cover the last 2.2 km in under six minutes. It took him 6:25. "On the last lap I lost 10 seconds and the time escaped," he told World Athletics. He finished in 2:00:25; Tadese ran 2:06:51 and Desisa 2:14:10.

It was the fastest marathon distance anyone had ever covered, but it could not count as a world record: rotating pacemakers and the special drinks set-up were outside the rules. Kipchoge told World Athletics the preparation had taken "seven good months" and that he hoped people would now believe it was possible.

sections.h: From near miss to new plan
paras: What Kipchoge did next is the useful part. He went back to normal racing, and at the 2018 Berlin Marathon set an official world record of 2:01:39. That proved his body could run close to the pace in real competition, without a laboratory set-up.
Then he lined up a second attempt. The INEOS 1:59 Challenge was set in Vienna, on the Hauptallee, a long, straight, flat and tree-lined avenue in the city's Prater park that could be run in loops.

sections.h: How Kipchoge ran 1:59:40 in Vienna
paras: The run started at 8:15 am on 12 October 2019 on the Reichsbrücke bridge over the Danube, in cool, nearly still air. The course then ran into the Prater for about 4.4 laps of the Hauptallee. World Athletics and the Olympic Games website both put the pacing squad at 41 elite runners, who took turns running in a V-shaped formation around him. An electric car ahead projected green laser lines on the road to mark the target pace of about 2:50 per kilometre.

Kipchoge held that pace almost exactly. In the final few hundred metres he moved clear of the pacemakers and crossed the line alone in 1:59:40, the first person ever to cover the marathon distance in under two hours. "No human is limited," he said afterwards. He told World Athletics he expected "more people all over the world to run under two hours after today."

As at Monza, the time was never going to be an official world record. Kenya's Daily Nation listed the reasons: rotating pacers, a pace vehicle, drinks handed over from a bicycle and no rival competitors, none of which standard race rules allow.

sections.h: What came next, and why it matters
paras: The Vienna run changed what people believed, and Kipchoge kept racing under normal rules. On 25 September 2022, at 37, he won the Berlin Marathon in 2:01:09, cutting 30 seconds off his own world record. By then he was a double Olympic marathon champion.

The 25 seconds at Monza could have been read as proof the goal was out of reach. Kipchoge read them as a measurement of how close he was, and used the gap to plan the next attempt. That is a habit anyone can borrow: when you fall short, write down the exact size of the gap before deciding what it means.

timeline: Wins the 5,000m world title as a teenager
Wins Olympic marathon gold in Rio
Runs 2:00:25 at Breaking2 in Monza, 25 seconds outside two hours
Sets the official marathon world record of 2:01:39 in Berlin
Runs 1:59:40 at the INEOS 1:59 Challenge in Vienna
Lowers his world record to 2:01:09 in Berlin
lesson: A near miss is not a verdict; it is a measurement. Kipchoge treated 25 seconds as the exact size of the problem left to solve.
check: What did you almost do that you could try again with one change?
How far away are you, really, from the goal you gave up on?
