title: He lost almost everything. A year later, he invented instant noodles.
seo_title: Momofuku Ando: from losing everything to instant noodles
summary: In 1957 Momofuku Ando lost nearly all he owned. After a year of experiments in a backyard shed, he launched Chicken Ramen in 1958, the first instant noodles.
intro: In 1958, in a small shed behind a rented house in Ikeda, near Osaka, a man in his late forties was frying noodles. He had been at it for about a year, sleeping around four hours a night and, by some accounts, never taking a day off.

A year earlier, Momofuku Ando had lost nearly everything he owned. That August, the noodles from his shed went on sale as Chicken Ramen, the world's first instant noodles. Today people eat more than 120 billion servings of instant noodles a year.

sections.h: Who was Momofuku Ando?
paras: Momofuku Ando was born on 5 March 1910 in Taiwan, which was then under Japanese rule. His parents died when he was very young, and he was raised by his grandparents, who ran a cloth and kimono shop.

He was a businessman from an early age. At 22 he founded a company selling knitted fabrics and soon opened a branch in Osaka. After the Second World War he tried many ventures, from basic housing to salt production, with mixed results.

sections.h: How Momofuku Ando lost everything
paras: In 1957, a credit union in which Ando held a senior role collapsed. He lost almost all of his wealth. According to both Nissin and the Japanese site Nippon.com, the only thing he kept was a rented house in Ikeda, a city in Osaka Prefecture.
He was approaching 50, with no business left. It is the kind of moment when many people decide their best years are behind them.

sections.h: The idea behind instant noodles
paras: Ando had been thinking about food for years. Nippon.com and The Japan Times both describe a scene he remembered from the hungry years after the war: a long line of people on a cold night, waiting for bowls of ramen at a black-market stall near Osaka's main station.

He wanted to make a noodle that people could prepare at home easily. Nissin says he set himself five goals: it had to taste good, keep for a long time, be quick to prepare, be cheap, and be safe and hygienic.
According to The Japan Times, Nissin traced his drive back to that memory of the food stall and to a belief Ando often repeated: that peace will come to the world when people have enough to eat.
Ando later summed up his approach in a line Nissin still quotes: "Tenacity is the breeding ground for inspiration."

sections.h: How Chicken Ramen was invented in a backyard shed
paras: Ando built a small shed in his backyard and worked there alone. Batch after batch failed. The noodles would not keep, or they would not soften properly in hot water.

The breakthrough came from his kitchen. Watching his wife, Masako, make tempura, he noticed how the batter bubbled in hot oil as the water was driven out. He tried flash-frying seasoned noodles. Frying removed the moisture, so the noodles stayed dry and kept for a long time, yet softened again in hot water within minutes.

Chicken Ramen went on sale in August 1958, when Ando was 48. It was not cheap at first. Smithsonian Magazine reports it cost about six times as much as a bowl of fresh noodles, and Nissin's own figures, ¥35 a serving when a bundle of udon cost ¥6, tell the same story. Smithsonian notes the high price made investors wary. Shoppers, though, took to what Nippon.com says was nicknamed "magic ramen", and his company became Nissin Food Products.

sections.h: Cup Noodles and what came next
paras: Sales in Japan eventually slowed, and Ando looked abroad. On a trip to the United States to promote Chicken Ramen, he noticed Americans breaking the noodles into cups and pouring hot water over them instead of using a pot and a bowl, according to Smithsonian Magazine.
That idea became Cup Noodles, launched in Japan on 18 September 1971 in a waterproof foam cup. It went on sale in the United States in 1973 as Cup O'Noodles.

Ando never really stopped inventing. In July 2005, at the age of 95, he saw Nissin's vacuum-packed Space Ram noodles eaten by astronaut Soichi Noguchi aboard the space shuttle Discovery. "I'm happy I've realized my dream that noodles can go into space," he said, as reported by The Japan Times. He died in January 2007, aged 96.

His invention travelled far beyond Japan. The World Instant Noodles Association counts India among the biggest markets, though published figures for India's 2024 demand vary between about 8.3 and 8.8 billion servings, depending on the release.

sections.h: Why Momofuku Ando's story matters
paras: Ando's story is usually told as a product story. The more useful part is where he started from. He did not begin with money, a factory or a team. He began after a public failure, with one clear problem, a tiny workspace and a year of steady work.

According to Nippon.com, Ando later said that in life it is never too late, and that it took him 48 years to invent his product. Every failed business before 1958 had taught him something about selling, making and running things. Starting over did not mean starting from nothing.

lesson: Losing everything can be a starting line, not a finish line, if you pick one clear problem and give it focused, daily work.
check: What one problem could you work on, a little every day, for the next year?
What is your version of a backyard shed: the small space or time you already have?

title: Homemade detergent at ₹3 a kilo: how Karsanbhai Patel's Nirma beat the big brands
seo_title: Karsanbhai Patel: how Nirma started at ₹3 a kilo
summary: In 1969 lab technician Karsanbhai Patel mixed detergent in his backyard and sold it door to door at about ₹3 a kilo. Nirma went on to overtake Surf.
intro: In 1969, a government lab technician in Gujarat started mixing detergent powder by hand in the backyard of his home near Ahmedabad. After work, he packed it into simple packets and sold it door to door, cycling from one neighbourhood to the next.

The big detergent brands of the day cost around ₹13 a kilo. His cost about ₹3. Within roughly a decade, that homemade powder, Nirma, had overtaken Hindustan Lever's Surf, then the leading brand in India.

sections.h: Who is Karsanbhai Patel?
paras: Karsanbhai Patel was born in 1945 into a farming family in Gujarat. He studied chemistry and earned a BSc, which led to a job as a lab technician at New Cotton Mills in Ahmedabad, part of the Lalbhai group.

He later moved to the Gujarat government's Department of Geology and Mining, again working in a laboratory. It was a steady, modest job. Nothing about it suggested he would one day build one of India's best-known consumer brands.

sections.h: How Nirma started in a backyard
paras: In the late 1960s, washing powder was a premium product in India. Most households washed clothes with bar soap, and the main detergent brands were sold by large multinational companies to better-off buyers.

Patel used his chemistry training to make a detergent powder of his own. He mixed it in the backyard of his house in Khokra, near Ahmedabad, and packed it by hand. He named it after his daughter, Nirupama.

He did not quit his job to do this. Nirma began as a side venture, and Patel sold it himself, cycling through neighbourhoods and selling packets door to door. He left government service only once the product had become popular.

sections.h: Why Nirma was priced at ₹3 a kilo
paras: Price was the whole idea. Nirma's own company history says the powder sold at ₹3 a kilo when the cheapest competing brand cost ₹13. Most accounts give the same figures, though Business Today puts Nirma's starting price slightly higher, at ₹3.50 a kilo.

Either way, it cost roughly a quarter to a third of what the established brands charged. Patel kept costs low by keeping production, packaging and distribution simple. For millions of families who had never bought detergent powder, Nirma made it affordable for the first time.

sections.h: How Nirma beat Surf
paras: The low price opened up a market the big brands had largely ignored: lower-income households in small towns and villages. As demand spread beyond Ahmedabad, Nirma grew from a one-man business into a regional, then national, brand.

Advertising helped it go national in the 1980s. The television jingle ending in "Sabki Pasand Nirma" and the image of a little girl, known as the Nirma Girl, became among the most recognisable in Indian advertising. The girl on the pack was based on Patel's daughter.

In the 1980s, Nirma overtook Surf to become India's largest-selling detergent. Hindustan Lever, which made Surf, eventually answered with its own low-priced detergent, Wheel. When a giant copies a newcomer's strategy, that is a sign the newcomer got something important right.

The low-price model was not a permanent shield, though. A 2014 report in Retail4Growth noted that Wheel and later Ghadi, another value detergent, competed with Nirma on price in the 2000s, and that Nirma's share of a crowded market had fallen. The same strategy that lifted Nirma could be copied by others.

sections.h: What Nirma became
paras: From detergent, the business expanded into toilet soaps and other consumer products, and later into industrial materials such as soda ash, one of the raw materials used in making detergent. Nirma's company site says it runs eleven production facilities.

The group grew into a large employer. Both the company's own site and DNA India put its workforce at around 18,000 people, and Patel's son Hiren Patel later took on a leading role in the business, including the effort to refresh the Nirma brand for a new generation of shoppers.

In July 2016, Nirma agreed to buy Lafarge India's cement business from LafargeHolcim at an enterprise value of about $1.4 billion. Patel also turned to education, founding the Nirma Institute of Technology in Ahmedabad in 1995, which became part of Nirma University in 2003.
In 2010 the Government of India awarded him the Padma Shri, one of the country's highest civilian honours.

sections.h: What Karsanbhai Patel understood early
paras: Patel did not try to beat the big brands at their own game. He did not compete for the same affluent shoppers with fancier packaging or bigger advertising budgets, at least not at first. He served the much larger group of people those brands had priced out.

He also tested his idea without risking everything. He kept his job, made the product himself, sold it with his own hands, and went full time only after people kept buying. The overlooked market turned out to be the biggest one.
None of this needed a big idea or a large investment at the start. It needed a clear view of who was being left out, a product priced for them, and the patience to grow one neighbourhood at a time.

lesson: Build for the people the big players ignore. An overlooked market can turn out to be the biggest one.

title: At 49, she quit a top banking job and started Nykaa
seo_title: Falguni Nayar: quit banking at 49, built Nykaa
summary: Falguni Nayar left her post as MD of Kotak Mahindra Capital in 2012, at 49, to start Nykaa. Nine years later it was one of India's most watched listings.
intro: On 31 March 2012, Falguni Nayar walked out of Kotak Mahindra, where she had spent close to two decades and risen to managing director. The next morning she was already registering a new company. "I left Kotak on March 31 and on April 1, I was in the process of incorporating the company," she later told Business Today.

She was 49, a few months short of 50, and by her own admission had no experience of retail or technology. The company she started was Nykaa, an online shop for beauty products. Many people doubted Indians would buy lipstick on the internet.

sections.h: Who is Falguni Nayar?
paras: Nayar grew up in a Gujarati family in Mumbai and studied management at IIM Ahmedabad, graduating in 1985. Business Today notes she was one of only nine women in a batch of about 150.

She joined the Kotak Mahindra group and stayed for nearly two decades; Business Today puts it at 18 years and Business Standard at 19. Along the way she helped set up Kotak's international offices in London and New York. By the time she left, she was managing director of Kotak Mahindra Capital, running its institutional equities and investment banking work. Part of her job was helping companies prepare to go public.

sections.h: Why she started Nykaa at 49
paras: Nayar saw that India's beauty market was fragmented, with most products sold through small family-run neighbourhood shops. Her idea was a multi-brand beauty retailer built on technology: one trusted place that offered many brands, genuine stock and help choosing.

Leaving a senior, secure post to test that idea was a real risk. EY, which later gave her its Entrepreneur of the Year award, notes that she had no earlier experience as a founder and no background in retail or technology, and that investors were sceptical that people would buy beauty products online.

The name came from a friend from her IIM Ahmedabad batch. Nykaa is drawn from the Sanskrit word nayika, meaning a heroine or leading lady, which matched the brand's aim of putting the customer at the centre of her own story.

sections.h: How Nykaa started: a borrowed office and three employees
paras: The beginning was small. About a month after leaving Kotak, Nayar and three employees set up in her father's old office in Lower Parel, Mumbai, according to Business Today. The website went live at the end of October 2012.
In the early days she handled almost every part of the operation herself. EY's profile says she often stayed up until 3 a.m. to check that orders went out correctly.

Nykaa built its approach on what it calls curation, content and convenience: selling authentic products held in its own inventory, publishing tutorials and guides so customers knew what to buy, and making ordering simple. Over time it added its own product lines, a men's range, a fashion marketplace launched in 2018, and physical stores. By the time it listed, it had around 80 shops across India.

sections.h: The Nykaa IPO in 2021
paras: In late 2021, Nykaa's parent company, FSN E-Commerce Ventures, went to the stock market. The public offer opened on 28 October and closed on 1 November, and was subscribed about 82 times over. It raised about 53.5 billion rupees, roughly $720 million.

The shares began trading on 10 November 2021, priced at Rs 1,125 in the offer. They nearly doubled on day one: Bloomberg and Fortune reported a rise of about 96%, while Business Today put the day's gain at 89%.

Because Nayar and her family still owned about half the company, the listing took her personal net worth to roughly $7 billion. The Bloomberg Billionaires Index named her India's wealthiest self-made woman. That same year she won the EY Entrepreneur of the Year award in India.

sections.h: What she said after the listing
paras: Nayar's comments on the day were less about money than about permission. "I hope more women like me dare to dream for themselves," she said, as reported by both Bloomberg and Fortune.
She also told Bloomberg that being rewarded for doing what she loved was the key, and that share prices were the bonus. In other words, the listing was a result, not the reason she started.
Her children, Adwaita and Anchit, later took senior roles at the company, while Nayar continued to lead it as founder and chief executive.

sections.h: Why her late start was an advantage
paras: It is tempting to read Nayar's story as a fairy tale about a sudden change of life. It was not sudden. Two decades in finance taught her how companies raise money, how investors think and how to build a team. She later took her own company through the same listing process she had once guided others through.

Her experience did not make the risk disappear. Nykaa could have failed, and many online retailers of that era did. But it did give her skills that a 25-year-old founder would have had to learn on the job. The years before 49 were not lost time. They were preparation for the thing she had not yet started.

lesson: 49 isn't late. It's experienced. What you already know can be your edge in something new.

title: Stephen King threw Carrie in the trash. His wife pulled it out.
seo_title: Stephen King's Carrie: the novel he threw in the trash
summary: Stephen King threw the first pages of Carrie in the bin. His wife Tabitha pulled them out. The paperback rights later sold for $400,000.
intro: In the early 1970s, a young high school English teacher in Maine typed a few pages of a story, decided they were no good, and threw them in the wastebasket. The next day his wife found them, brushed off the cigarette ash, and read them.

The teacher was Stephen King. The pages became Carrie, his first published novel, and the start of one of the best-selling writing careers in the world. In a 2024 interview with The Boston Globe, King put it simply: Tabby literally picked it out of the wastebasket.

sections.h: Who was Stephen King before Carrie?
paras: Before he was famous, King was a teacher at Hampden Academy, a high school in Maine, and money was tight. In a 1979 excerpt published by Yankee Magazine, he recalled working in a laundry during the summer to help make ends meet. The Boston Globe reported that he also wrote while working in a commercial laundry.

The family lived in a trailer. Tabitha King later wrote that he worked in a tiny room meant to be the laundry room, even though they had no washer or dryer, according to the Globe. King told the newspaper, "We were scraping bottom."
He wrote at night and in spare moments, and he had been writing for years. Kirkus Reviews noted that by the early 1970s he already had several unpublished novels in a desk drawer.

sections.h: Why Stephen King threw Carrie away
paras: Carrie began as an idea for a short story about a bullied teenage girl who discovers she has telekinetic powers. King did not think it was working. He told The Boston Globe that it was too hard and already too long for a short story.

Accounts of exactly how much he had written vary slightly. In the Yankee Magazine excerpt he says he threw out four pages; Mental Floss, drawing on his memoir On Writing, describes three single-spaced pages. Either way, it was the very start of the book, and he was ready to give up on it.

Mental Floss quotes King's own explanation from On Writing: he threw it away because he doubted anyone would want to read a book about a poor, awkward girl like Carrie. He could not see past his own doubts.

sections.h: How Tabitha King saved Carrie
paras: Tabitha King, known as Tabby, found the crumpled pages in the bin, smoothed them out and read them. She saw something in them that her husband had missed.
In the 1979 Yankee Magazine account, King says she left him a note: "Please keep going—it's good." In On Writing, as quoted by Mental Floss, he remembers her telling him that he had something there.

King has said that her praise was rare, which made it count. He went back to the manuscript and kept going. Kirkus Reviews reported that the story grew from a short story into a full novel. Every edition of Carrie carries a dedication to Tabby, thanking her for getting him into it and then bailing him out of it.

sections.h: The $2,500 advance and the $400,000 phone call
paras: King sent the finished manuscript to Doubleday. Editor Bill Thompson accepted it and offered an advance of $2,500, a figure reported by The Boston Globe, Kirkus Reviews and Yankee Magazine. Mental Floss reports that King used the money to buy a car and move the family out of the trailer.

Carrie was published in April 1974. The bigger news came with the paperback. The paperback rights sold for $400,000, as both Yankee Magazine and Mental Floss report; Mental Floss names the buyer as Signet Books.

In the Yankee account, King says he first misheard the figure as $40,000. When he understood it was $400,000, he realised he would not have to teach anymore. He soon left the classroom to write full-time, as Kirkus Reviews and Mental Floss also note.

sections.h: What happened after Carrie
paras: The hardcover sold slowly at first. Kirkus Reviews contributing editor Gregory McNamee recalled selling only a copy or two a day at a bookshop, far fewer than the hit novel Jaws. The paperback did much better, and King told the Globe it became a bestseller after the 1976 film adaptation directed by Brian De Palma.
Within a few years, Kirkus Reviews notes, King had also published 'Salem's Lot, The Shining and The Stand. Carrie had opened the door, and he walked through it with book after book.
Despite all that, King has mixed feelings about his first novel. He told the Globe that Carrie changed his life, but that he has never really liked it all that much.

sections.h: Why this story matters to anyone who makes things
paras: There was no lucky meeting here and no famous mentor. The turning point was a few crumpled sheets of paper and one honest reader at home. The person closest to a piece of work is often its harshest judge, and a second pair of eyes can see what the creator cannot.

It also says something about the reader. Tabitha did not flatter him; King has said her praise was rare. What she offered was an honest second opinion at the moment he was about to quit. If you make things, it is worth having one person like that, and it is worth being that person for someone else.

timeline: Early 1970s
Teaching at Hampden Academy, King starts Carrie, throws out the first pages, and Tabitha retrieves them
Early 1970s
Doubleday accepts Carrie with a $2,500 advance

Carrie is published in hardcover by Doubleday
Mid-1970s
Paperback rights sell for $400,000 and King leaves teaching to write full-time
Brian De Palma's film of Carrie is released
lesson: What you are about to throw away might be the one. Let someone you trust read it before you decide.
check: What draft, idea or project is sitting in your bin right now?
Who could you show it to before you give up on it?
faq: Did Stephen King throw Carrie away?
Yes. He threw the first few pages in the wastebasket because he thought they were not working. His wife Tabitha pulled them out, read them and urged him to keep going.
How much was Stephen King paid for Carrie?

Doubleday paid him a $2,500 advance for Carrie. The paperback rights were later sold for $400,000 (Mental Floss names the buyer as Signet Books), the deal that let King give up teaching. Our sources confirm those two figures; reports of exactly how the $400,000 was split between Doubleday and King vary, so we don't state a number for his share.
When was Carrie published?
Carrie was published in hardcover by Doubleday in April 1974. It was Stephen King's first published novel.
What did Tabitha King say about Carrie?
In a 1979 account published by Yankee Magazine, King said she left him a note reading "Please keep going—it's good." In his memoir On Writing he recalls her telling him he had something there.
What was Stephen King's job when he wrote Carrie?
He was a high school English teacher at Hampden Academy in Maine, and he also worked in a laundry to make ends meet. The family lived in a trailer.

title: No brewery would hire her. So she built Biocon.
seo_title: Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw: from a ₹10,000 garage start to Biocon
summary: Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw trained as a master brewer but no Indian brewery would hire her. In 1978 she started Biocon in a garage with ₹10,000.
intro: In 1978, a young woman in Bangalore set up a company in the garage of her rented house with ₹10,000. She ran newspaper advertisements describing it as a multinational company, according to the Science History Institute. The advertisements did not mention the garage.
She had not planned to be an entrepreneur at all. Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw had trained to be a master brewer, and she started Biocon only after the brewing industry would not give her a job.

sections.h: Who is Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw?
paras: Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw grew up in Bangalore, now Bengaluru. Her father was a brewmaster at United Breweries, and his work shaped her choices. After studying biology in Bangalore, she went to Ballarat in Australia to study malting and brewing, the same field as her father.

Domain-b reported that she was the only woman in her class and finished at the top of it, qualifying as a master brewer. The Science History Institute also records that she earned the master brewer title at Ballarat, and notes that her family supported the choice, though with some worry about where it would lead.

sections.h: Why no brewery would hire her
paras: Back in India in the 1970s, she looked for work in brewing and kept running into the same wall. "I was finding it very difficult to get a job as a brew master," she told CNN in 2012.

The reason was not her training. Business Today reported that brewing was a male-dominated industry at the time, and that she was told a woman would find it hard to manage labour unions on a brewery floor. Employers saw hiring her as a risk. Domain-b gave the same account.
With doors in India closing, she began looking at jobs abroad. The Science History Institute notes that she was considering a move to Europe when a chance meeting changed her direction.

sections.h: How Biocon started in a garage with ₹10,000
paras: That meeting was with Leslie Auchincloss, founder of an Irish company called Biocon Biochemicals, which made enzymes. He suggested she set up a company in India. In 1978, Biocon India was formed as a joint venture between Mazumdar-Shaw and the Irish firm, according to Biocon's own history and the Science History Institute.

The start was small. Business Today and domain-b both report that she began in the garage of her rented home in Bangalore with ₹10,000. Accounts of the first team differ slightly: Biocon's history says it started with three employees, while the Science History Institute says two.

The first work drew directly on her brewing training. Biocon's company history says it began by making and exporting papain and isinglass, enzyme and clarifying products used in brewing and food processing. The Science History Institute describes the early business as industrial enzymes for food and textile makers.

sections.h: The early struggles
paras: Being young, a woman and in an unfamiliar industry made almost everything harder. CNN reported that she faced problems with credibility, funding and hiring staff in Biocon's early years.

Money was a constant hurdle. Business Today recounted that when she approached a bank for a loan, it wanted her father to stand as guarantor. She argued that, as managing director, she should be the guarantor herself, and after she took the matter to a senior manager at Canara Bank the loan was approved.

Support came from people who were willing to back her. Business Today reported that Narayanan Vaghul, a former chairman of ICICI Bank, funded a technology she needed to scale up, which Biocon used to develop an enzyme for the American juice company Ocean Spray. Her father also kept encouraging her, and she recalled his advice about the people she worked with: "Treat them with respect. Everyone has something to contribute."
She has described her mindset at the start in plain terms. Speaking to CNN, she said she began the company with a lot of foolish courage.

sections.h: From enzymes to medicines
paras: For about two decades, enzymes were Biocon's core business. In the late 1990s the company moved into biopharmaceuticals, a shift Business Today credits with giving Biocon global scale. Biocon's own history records its first biopharmaceutical products, statins, from 1996.

In 2004 Biocon went public. Its market value at the close of the first day of trading was about $1.11 billion, according to Biocon, and domain-b reported it as more than $1.1 billion. Mazumdar-Shaw told Business Today that the listing was when she truly understood the value of what she had built.
Today Biocon is best known for affordable insulin and biosimilars, near-copies of complex biological medicines. The Science History Institute describes it as India's largest insulin producer.

sections.h: What her story shows
paras: The job she was refused would have used part of her training. The company she built instead used all of it, and much more. In 2012 she told CNN it had taken her more than 30 years to get from a garage to the large campus Biocon has today.
She did not wait for the brewing industry to change its mind. She asked where else her skills were valuable, accepted a small and uncertain start, and kept building.

timeline: Qualifies as a master brewer at Ballarat, Australia, but cannot get a brewing job in India
Starts Biocon in the garage of her rented Bangalore home with ₹10,000, in a joint venture with Ireland's Biocon Biochemicals
Biocon enters biopharmaceuticals with statins
Biocon becomes an independent, privately owned company after Unilever exits the joint venture
Biocon lists on the stock market; first-day market value about $1.11 billion
lesson: If no one gives you the job, look at who else needs the skill. A closed door in one industry can be the start of a company in another.
check: Who said no to you, and what could you build instead with the same skill?
What is the smallest, cheapest version of that idea you could start this month?
faq: How did Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw start Biocon?
She set up Biocon in 1978 in the garage of her rented home in Bangalore with ₹10,000. It began as a joint venture with an Irish enzyme company, Biocon Biochemicals.
Was Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw a brewer?

Yes. She studied malting and brewing at Ballarat in Australia and qualified as a master brewer, but breweries in India would not hire her, reportedly because they doubted a woman could manage the labour side of the job.
What did Biocon make at first?
Enzymes. Biocon's company history says its first products were papain and isinglass, used in brewing and food processing. It moved into medicines in the late 1990s.
When did Biocon go public?
Biocon listed in 2004. Its market value at the close of the first trading day was about $1.11 billion.
What is Biocon known for today?
Biocon is known for biopharmaceuticals, especially insulin and biosimilars. The Science History Institute describes it as India's largest insulin producer.

title: $50 from his dad. Shoes in his trunk. It became Nike.
seo_title: Phil Knight's $50 start: shoes from a car trunk to Nike
summary: Phil Knight borrowed $50 from his father to order running shoes from Japan and sold them from his car trunk. That tiny import business became Nike.
intro: In 1962 Phil Knight was 24, had a fresh MBA from Stanford and was living in his parents' house in Oregon. He also had what he would later call a crazy idea: importing good, low-cost running shoes from Japan and selling them to American runners.
To test it, he borrowed $50 from his father. That money paid for his first order of shoes. The company it started is now known around the world as Nike.

sections.h: Who is Phil Knight?
paras: Before he sold shoes, Knight ran in them. He was a middle-distance runner at the University of Oregon, coached by Bill Bowerman, the university's demanding and inventive track coach. Knight later called Bowerman "part genius, part madman and the best coach I ever had."
Knight then went to Stanford for an MBA. The shoe idea first took shape during his studies, and after graduating he decided to try it for real rather than take a safe job.

sections.h: The trip to Japan and the $50 order
paras: After graduating, Knight travelled the world, backpacking through Asia, Europe and Africa. In Kobe, Japan, he visited Onitsuka, the company that made Tiger running shoes (it is now part of Asics), and talked his way into a deal to distribute them in the United States.
He named his tiny business Blue Ribbon Sports, of Portland, Oregon. His first order was paid for with the $50 he borrowed from his father.
Then he waited. The shoes took about a year to arrive, far longer than he expected. When they came, Knight sent a pair to his old coach, Bowerman.

sections.h: Selling shoes from a Plymouth Valiant
paras: Bowerman liked the shoes enough to ask to be part of the business. In 1964 the two became partners in Blue Ribbon Sports, with Bowerman matching Knight's investment, according to the Oregon Sports Hall of Fame.

There was no shop and no warehouse. Knight sold the shoes from the trunk of his Plymouth Valiant, directly to runners who could see and feel the product. In the company's first year of sales, he grossed about $8,000.

The sources disagree slightly about which year that was: the publisher's description of Knight's memoir says 1963, while other histories date the first full year of sales to 1964. Either way, it was a very small business, run by people who still had other jobs. For extra money, Knight also taught accounting at Portland State University.

Slowly, the numbers grew. Blue Ribbon hired a small and eclectic staff, and in 1966 it opened its first retail store. Every pair still came from Onitsuka, which meant the business depended entirely on a supplier thousands of miles away.

sections.h: How Blue Ribbon Sports became Nike
paras: Growth brought its own problems. In his memoir, Shoe Dog, Knight describes years of cash shortages, banks unwilling to lend more, late deliveries and unclear contracts with Onitsuka. By the early 1970s the relationship with the Japanese supplier had broken down, and Blue Ribbon needed its own brand.

In 1971 Knight met Carolyn Davidson, a design student at Portland State, after overhearing her say she could not afford an oil-painting class. He offered her freelance work, and she designed a stripe for the side of a shoe that suggested movement. She sketched ideas on tissue paper laid over a shoe and presented several options. The company picked one, and she charged $35. It became the Swoosh, first used commercially in June 1971, according to ESPN and Business Insider.
The new name came from Jeff Johnson, one of Blue Ribbon's early employees, who said it came to him in a dream: Nike, after the winged Greek goddess of victory.

sections.h: Where Nike is today
paras: Blue Ribbon Sports eventually took the Nike name for the whole company. By 2016, when Shoe Dog was published, Nike's annual sales topped $30 billion, according to the publisher. In 1983 the company gave Davidson a gold Swoosh ring and Nike shares to thank her for the logo.

Knight's memoir stands out because it does not pretend the path was smooth. For most of the first decade, the company was small, short of cash and dependent on a supplier it did not control. As Kirkus Reviews summarises it, sales grew through the 1960s, but bankers and Onitsuka itself kept holding the business back, and the memoir ends only when Blue Ribbon becomes Nike.

sections.h: What the $50 start teaches
paras: The useful part of this story is not the size of Nike. It is how little Knight needed to begin finding out whether his idea worked: a loan from his father, one order of shoes, a car and runners who would buy them.
Starting small kept his early mistakes small too. He learned what customers wanted, what suppliers could deliver and how cash moved through a business, long before any of it was worth much money.

It also shows that the first version of a big company can look nothing like the final one. Blue Ribbon was a distributor of someone else's shoes for years. Knight did not need the whole plan at the start; he needed a first step he could afford, and the willingness to keep taking the next one.

timeline: Knight, 24 and newly graduated from Stanford, visits Onitsuka in Japan and orders shoes with $50 from his father
Knight and Bill Bowerman become partners in Blue Ribbon Sports
Knight sells shoes from the trunk of his Plymouth Valiant, grossing about $8,000 in the first year
Carolyn Davidson designs the Swoosh for $35
Early 1970s
The Onitsuka partnership ends and the Nike brand is launched
Knight publishes his memoir, Shoe Dog
lesson: Start with what fits in your car. A small start you keep going beats a big plan you never begin.
check: What could you start this week with almost nothing?
What are you waiting for that you don't actually need?

What book tells the Nike origin story?

title: Vera Wang started her company at 40. And she almost didn't.
seo_title: Vera Wang started her company at 40: the late-starter story
summary: Vera Wang missed the Olympic team and the top job at Vogue. At 40 she feared it was too late, then opened her own bridal salon in New York in 1990.
intro: In 1989, a 39-year-old fashion editor turned designer went shopping for a wedding dress in New York and could not find one she liked. She had spent nearly two decades at Vogue. She knew fabric, fit and every major designer in the city. Still, she later told CNBC, "I couldn't find anything I wanted."
Her father thought there might be a business in that gap. She was not so sure. "I thought maybe it's just too late for me," Vera Wang said. A year later, she opened her own bridal salon.

sections.h: Who is Vera Wang?
paras: Vera Wang was born in New York City on 27 June 1949. Her parents had moved to the United States from China in the 1940s; her father ran a pharmaceutical company and her mother worked as a translator at the United Nations.
Her first dream was not fashion. She started figure skating as a young child and competed seriously as a pairs skater through her teens.

sections.h: Did Vera Wang skate in the Olympics?
paras: No. At the 1968 U.S. Figure Skating Championships, Wang and her partner did not place high enough to qualify for the Olympic team. She stopped competing soon after.

"I didn't make the Olympic team," she told CNBC in 2021, listing it among the disappointments of her early life. Skating did not leave her, though. Years later, as a designer, she made costumes that the American figure skater Nancy Kerrigan wore at the 1992 and 1994 Winter Olympics.

sections.h: Vera Wang's years at Vogue
paras: Wang studied at Sarah Lawrence College, spending time at the Sorbonne in Paris, where her interest in fashion grew. After graduating in 1971, she joined Vogue as an assistant. Within about a year, at 23, she was promoted to fashion editor, working on the magazine's fashion shoots.

She stayed at Vogue for 17 years. When the editor-in-chief job came open, it went to someone else. "I didn't become editor-in-chief at Vogue," she said. "I really blamed it on myself that I didn't make the cut, and you get motivated from that."

sections.h: From Ralph Lauren to her own wedding dress
paras: In 1987 Wang left Vogue for Ralph Lauren, where she worked as a design director. Britannica and Biography.com describe her role as designing accessories, while CNBC says she oversaw women's clothing, so reports differ on its exact scope. Either way, it gave her experience on the design and business side of fashion, not just the editorial side.

In 1989 she married Arthur Becker. She was 39. She has said that 39 does not seem old for a bride today, but in 1989 it did. Shopping for a gown, she felt out of place in the bridal departments and found nothing that suited her. In the end she designed her own dress.

sections.h: How Vera Wang started her company at 40
paras: Her father saw an opening. As Wang recalled, he told her he thought there was probably a serious business opportunity in what she had found. He encouraged her to leave Ralph Lauren and gave her the seed money to start.

In 1990 she opened the Vera Wang Bridal House in the Carlyle Hotel on Madison Avenue in New York. According to Britannica, the salon first sold gowns by other designers before moving on to her own designs.

Recognition built over the next decade. Kerrigan's Olympic costumes brought her wider attention, and she showed her first ready-to-wear collection in 2000. The Council of Fashion Designers of America named her Womenswear Designer of the Year in 2005 and gave her a lifetime achievement award in 2013. Her name now appears on clothing, fragrances, homeware and wedding rings.

The brand also reached beyond luxury buyers. Britannica notes a more affordable line, Simply Vera, sold through the department store Kohl's from 2006, and both Britannica and WWD record a partnership with the jeweller Zales on engagement and wedding rings in 2011. More than three decades after she opened that first salon, CNBC reported in 2021 that Wang was still the sole owner of her company, and she described herself as learning new lessons, as a designer and as an entrepreneur, every day.

sections.h: Is 40 too late to start a business?
paras: Wang's story suggests the question is often framed the wrong way. She did not start from zero at 40. She brought 17 years of editorial judgment from Vogue, design experience from Ralph Lauren, a network across the industry, and a problem she had just faced as a customer. The detours were the preparation.

The skating years mattered too. Reaching a national championship as a teenager takes years of practice, and missing the Olympic cut taught her to live with a result that did not go her way. Those habits are useful for anyone building a business from scratch, at any age.

She has also been honest that the road was not smooth. "There have been a million days where I said to myself, 'What was I thinking?'" she told CNBC. Her advice to younger people is that regret is far worse than never having tried, and worse than failure.
If you are wondering whether it is too late for you, it may help to list what your earlier years have already taught you. Those lessons may be the head start you have not noticed.

Graduates from Sarah Lawrence College and joins Vogue
Leaves Vogue after 17 years and joins Ralph Lauren
Marries at 39 and designs her own wedding dress
Opens her bridal salon in the Carlyle Hotel, New York
Named CFDA Womenswear Designer of the Year
lesson: Your plan B can be the real plan. And the years you think you lost may be the training you needed.
check: What would you start if age didn't matter?
What have your past jobs and disappointments taught you that you could build on?

title: Two friends, one small flat and a few books: how Flipkart began
seo_title: Flipkart story: from a small flat to Walmart's $16B deal
summary: In 2007 Sachin and Binny Bansal started Flipkart as an online bookstore from a Bengaluru flat. In 2018 Walmart paid $16 billion for about 77% of it.
intro: In late October 2007, a customer in Mahabubnagar, a town in what was then Andhra Pradesh, ordered a book he could not find in nearby Hyderabad: John Wood's memoir Leaving Microsoft to Change the World. The website he ordered from was brand new and run by two young engineers from a flat in Bengaluru.

To fill the order, co-founder Binny Bansal went from bookshop to bookshop around the city until he found a copy. It reached the customer a day late. That small, slightly clumsy first sale was the start of Flipkart, which Walmart bought a controlling stake in eleven years later for $16 billion.

sections.h: Who are Sachin Bansal and Binny Bansal?
paras: Sachin Bansal and Binny Bansal share a surname but are not related. They met at IIT Delhi in 2005, while finishing their engineering degrees, and both later moved to Bengaluru for work.

Sachin joined Amazon first, and Binny joined the same team in 2007. Working there gave them a close view of how online shopping worked. According to YourStory, their first idea was a price-comparison website, but their research pushed them towards running an online store themselves.

Leaving a steady job at a global company was a real risk. YourStory, looking back at the founders' story in 2018, described 2007 as a time "when entrepreneurship was not yet cool" in India. YourStory reports they built the first version of the site on two computers in their flat.

sections.h: How Flipkart started as an online bookstore
paras: The two friends left Amazon and launched Flipkart in 2007 from a two-bedroom flat in Koramangala, Bengaluru. Reports differ slightly on the exact date: Deccan Herald and Quartz give 15 September 2007, while Business Today and YourStory say October 2007, when the site opened for business.

There was no warehouse and no big brand. Flipkart sold one thing: books. Books were a sensible first product because they are easy to list, easy to describe and hard to damage in transit, and many Indian towns had no good bookshop nearby.
Growth was slow at first. Business Today and Quartz both report that Flipkart made just 20 shipments in its first year.

sections.h: The first order and the bookmarks on Church Street
paras: That first customer was V V K Chandra, a web consultant who wrote a blog. As he later told India TV, he found Flipkart through a comment left under one of his blog posts by someone called Sachin, with a link to the new site. He ordered the John Wood book, and Flipkart shipped it on 31 October 2007.

India TV's account says Binny searched shop after shop before finding a copy at Sapna Book Store, and that a Karnataka state holiday on 1 November delayed delivery by a day. Flipkart apologised and gave Chandra a discount. He was happy enough to write a review that the company showed on its homepage.

Finding more customers took the same hands-on effort. Business Today reported that the founders stood outside a bookshop on Church Street in Bengaluru and handed Flipkart bookmarks to people walking out with new books. The idea was simple: these were people who already bought books, so tell them there was another way to get them.

sections.h: How Flipkart grew beyond books
paras: In 2009 the venture capital firm Accel Partners invested $1 million, Flipkart's first outside funding, as Business Today, Deccan Herald and Quartz all report. The team grew and opened offices in Delhi and Mumbai.

Around 2010 Flipkart introduced cash on delivery. Many Indian shoppers at the time did not have credit cards or did not trust paying online, and letting them pay when the parcel arrived helped build trust. The same year it began selling electronics, mobile phones, music and movies.

New categories kept coming once the last one worked: appliances, laptops and cameras, then fashion and a mobile app. In 2014 Flipkart bought the fashion site Myntra and ran its first Big Billion Day sale. It later bought Jabong and the payments app PhonePe.

sections.h: The Walmart deal
paras: On 9 May 2018 Walmart announced it would pay about $16 billion for an initial stake of roughly 77% in Flipkart, including $2 billion of new money for the business. The deal valued Flipkart at around $20 billion; TechCrunch put the figure at $20.8 billion.

Walmart completed the deal in August 2018. Binny Bansal stayed on as a shareholder, alongside investors such as Tencent, Tiger Global and Microsoft. Sachin Bansal sold his stake and said goodbye to the company in a Facebook post.

sections.h: What the Flipkart story teaches
paras: The founders did not start with everything. They started with one category they could manage, learned how to source, pack and deliver it well, and only then added the next. Each step was built on something that already worked.

The early details are worth noticing too: a first order that arrived late, a co-founder walking from shop to shop to find one book, and two engineers handing out bookmarks on a pavement. None of it looks like a future $20 billion company. It looks like people doing small, practical things carefully and then doing them again.
If you have an idea that feels too big to start, it can help to ask what the books version of it would be: the one product or service you could sell and deliver well this month.

lesson: Start with one thing you can do well, get it right for real customers, and only then add the next.

The first order was John Wood's book Leaving Microsoft to Change the World, bought by V V K Chandra in Mahabubnagar. It was shipped on 31 October 2007 and arrived a day late.

title: Bankrupt in 1996. Sold to Disney for $4 billion in 2009.
seo_title: Marvel comeback: 1996 bankruptcy to Disney's $4 billion
summary: Marvel filed for bankruptcy in 1996 and sold Spider-Man's film rights. It bet on the heroes it kept, made Iron Man, and Disney paid about $4 billion in 2009.
intro: In 1998, a company still recovering from bankruptcy reportedly offered Sony the film rights to almost its entire roster of superheroes, including Iron Man, Thor and Black Panther, for $25 million. Sony said no. It wanted only Spider-Man, and paid $10 million for him.
That company was Marvel. Eleven years later, built on the very characters Sony had passed over, it was bought by Disney for about $4 billion.

sections.h: Why did Marvel go bankrupt in 1996?
paras: In the early 1990s Marvel rode a boom in comics and trading cards. Many buyers were collectors and speculators hoping the issues would rise in value. When that market cooled, sales collapsed. Den of Geek reports that Marvel's comics and trading card sales fell by about 70% between 1993 and 1996.

The company had also borrowed heavily to buy other businesses under its owner, the financier Ronald Perelman. Its share price, which had climbed above $30 after its 1991 listing, fell to under $3 by late 1996, according to both the Deseret News and Den of Geek.
In December 1996 Marvel Entertainment Group filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in Delaware. The Deseret News reported liabilities far greater than its assets at the time of the filing.

sections.h: The fight for control and the Toy Biz rescue
paras: Bankruptcy set off a long contest among Marvel's owner, its bondholders, including the investor Carl Icahn, and its banks. Control passed through several hands over the following months.

The way out came through Toy Biz, the toy company that made Marvel's action figures and was run by Isaac Perlmutter and Avi Arad. In 1998, after a court fight that ran for well over a year, Marvel and Toy Biz merged and the combined company came out of Chapter 11, as Den of Geek recounts. By the time it spoke to Sony that year, Quartz notes, Marvel had only just emerged from bankruptcy and was in a rather desperate position.

sections.h: Selling the crown jewels: Spider-Man, X-Men and the film rights
paras: The new Marvel was short of cash, and its most valuable assets were its characters. Licensing their film rights to Hollywood studios brought in money quickly, and over the 1990s and early 2000s many of its biggest names went elsewhere: the X-Men to 20th Century Fox and Spider-Man to Sony.

The Sony deal shows how little the rest of the roster was valued then. According to Wall Street Journal reporter Ben Fritz's book The Big Picture, as reported by Quartz and The A.V. Club, Marvel offered Sony nearly all of its characters for $25 million in 1998. Sony took only Spider-Man, for $10 million plus a share of the films' revenue.
The licensing brought hits, but Marvel saw only a small slice of the profits from films made with its own characters.

sections.h: The 2005 bet: making its own films
paras: By the mid-2000s Marvel's leaders decided to stop only licensing and start producing. In September 2005 the company announced a $525 million financing deal arranged by Merrill Lynch to make up to ten films itself, according to Marvel's own press release filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission and to Den of Geek.

The loan was secured against the film rights to a group of characters it still controlled, including Captain America and the Avengers. If the films failed, Marvel risked losing those characters too. Paramount agreed to distribute the films, with the first expected in summer 2008.

It was a large risk for a company that had been in bankruptcy less than a decade earlier. But it changed Marvel's position from a supplier collecting licence fees to the owner of the films, their profits and their creative direction.

sections.h: How Iron Man launched the Marvel Cinematic Universe
paras: Iron Man was not an obvious lead. One Marvel executive, quoted in Ben Fritz's book, recalled of the character's toys: "We couldn't give Iron Man away, nobody wanted it." According to Ben Fritz's book, as reported by Quartz, Marvel chose him partly after showing children pictures of its heroes and asking which they would most like as a toy; Iron Man came out on top.

Iron Man opened in the United States on 2 May 2008. It earned about $585 million worldwide, according to both Quartz and Den of Geek, roughly four times its budget by Quartz's estimate. The film became the first chapter of what is now known as the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

sections.h: Disney buys Marvel for $4 billion
paras: On 31 August 2009, little more than a year after Iron Man's release, Disney announced it would buy Marvel Entertainment in a cash-and-stock deal worth about $4 billion. Marvel shareholders would receive $30 in cash plus about 0.745 Disney shares for each Marvel share, as reported by The Next Web at the announcement and confirmed in Disney's completion statement.

Disney completed the purchase on 31 December 2009, gaining a library of more than 5,000 characters. The company that had sold its most famous hero's film rights to survive had turned the rest of its roster into one of the most valuable collections of stories in entertainment.

The lesson of Marvel's turnaround is not that it got back what it lost. It did not need to. It took the characters it still had seriously, invested in making one good film with them, and built from there.

Marvel merges with Toy Biz and leaves bankruptcy; Sony buys Spider-Man film rights for $10 million
Marvel secures $525 million from Merrill Lynch to make its own films

Disney completes the acquisition
lesson: Build with what you still have. Marvel's comeback came from the heroes no one wanted, not from winning back the ones it had sold.
check: What do you still have that you have been treating as second best?
If you lost your biggest asset tomorrow, what would you build with the rest?

title: The first mile under four minutes, run by a medical student
seo_title: Roger Bannister: the first four-minute mile, 3:59.4 in 1954
summary: Roger Bannister missed the medals at the 1952 Olympics. Training in short lunch-break sessions around medical school, he ran the first sub-four-minute mile.
intro: On the afternoon of 6 May 1954, a 25-year-old medical student stood near the Iffley Road track in Oxford watching a flag on a nearby church tower. It was whipping hard in the wind. Roger Bannister feared he would have to call off his attempt at the most famous target in athletics: a mile in under four minutes.

Shortly before the 6pm start, the wind dropped. He decided to run. A little under four minutes later, the announcer began to read out his time, got as far as the word "three", and was drowned out by the crowd.

sections.h: Who was Roger Bannister?
paras: Roger Bannister was born in Harrow, near London, in 1929. He took up running seriously as a teenager and, as a student at Oxford, became one of Britain's best middle-distance runners while also training to be a doctor.

He was unusual for his time. Al Jazeera's obituary notes he was nicknamed the "lone wolf miler" because he preferred to work out his own training rather than follow a coach. As a medical student, he used what he was learning about the body to design his programme and study the mechanics of running, according to World Athletics.

sections.h: The disappointment of Helsinki 1952
paras: Bannister went to the 1952 Olympic Games in Helsinki as one of the favourites in the 1,500 metres. Olympedia, the Olympic history database, records that the organisers rescheduled the event so that a heat, a semi-final and the final fell on consecutive days, which proved too much for him.

He finished fourth, just outside the medals. He was criticised in the press for his training methods. Associated Press and Sports Illustrated both report that it was after Helsinki that he set his sights on a single, clear goal: the first mile under four minutes.

sections.h: How Roger Bannister trained around medical school
paras: Bannister did not have the luxury of training all day. Sports Illustrated reports that medical school sometimes left him only 30 to 40 minutes a day, so he often ran hard during his lunch break rather than following long, finely tuned workouts.

Those short sessions were intense. EBSCO's history summary describes a typical one as ten quarter-mile repetitions, each run in slightly under a minute, with short rests in between. The idea was to get used to running at four-minute pace and recovering quickly.

The record he was chasing, Gunder Hägg's 4:01.4, had stood for nine years. Australia's John Landy and America's Wes Santee were also closing in on the barrier, so Bannister knew he might not have long to be first.

sections.h: 6 May 1954: the day of the first sub-four-minute mile
paras: The race was a meeting between Oxford University and the Amateur Athletic Association. Bannister had been working in London that day and travelled up to Oxford by train. The weather was cool, wet and blustery, and reports of the crowd vary between about 1,200 and 3,000 people.

Two friends helped him. Chris Brasher, who later founded the London Marathon, set the pace for the first two laps, reaching halfway in about 1:58. Chris Chataway took over for the third lap. Partway through the final lap, Bannister moved past Chataway and ran for the line alone.

He finished in 3 minutes 59.4 seconds, recognised by Guinness World Records as the first mile ever run in under four minutes. "The world seemed to stand still, or did not exist," he later said of those final strides. He also said he felt that it was "my chance to do one thing supremely well."

sections.h: How long did Bannister's record last?
paras: Not long. On 21 June 1954, in Turku, Finland, John Landy ran the mile in about 3:58; sources give his time as either 3:57.9 or 3:58.0. Most reports say Bannister's record had lasted 46 days, though World Athletics puts it at 45.

The two men met in August 1954 at the British Empire and Commonwealth Games in Vancouver, in a race billed as the "Miracle Mile". Bannister won in 3:58.8, and Landy also finished under four minutes. It was the first race in which two men broke the barrier.
Bannister then won the European 1,500 metres title and retired from racing at the end of 1954, aged 25, to concentrate on medicine.

sections.h: The neurologist behind the record
paras: Bannister became a leading neurologist. He chaired Britain's Sports Council from 1971 to 1974, where he pushed for testing for anabolic steroids, and he was knighted in 1975. From 1985 to 1993 he was Master of Pembroke College, Oxford.

He always said his medical work meant more to him than his running. He died in Oxford on 3 March 2018, aged 88. Sebastian Coe's tribute, quoted by World Athletics, summed up what the run had meant: "On the 6 May 1954, Roger made the impossible possible."

What made his run possible was not a huge training load but a clear target, smart use of limited time, and friends who shared the effort on the day. After he showed it could be done, other runners stopped treating four minutes as a wall and started treating it as a target.

Aug 1954
Beats Landy in the 'Miracle Mile' in Vancouver; both run under four minutes
Knighted
Dies in Oxford, aged 88
lesson: A limit can look fixed until one person breaks it. A clear target, used with whatever time you actually have, can take you further than you expect.
check: Which 'impossible' goal in your own field has someone already broken, and what does that tell you?
If you only had 30 focused minutes a day, what would you spend them on?

Roger Bannister, a British medical student, ran 3:59.4 on 6 May 1954 at the Iffley Road track in Oxford, with Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway as pacemakers.
How long did Roger Bannister's mile record last?
About six and a half weeks. John Landy ran faster on 21 June 1954 in Finland; most reports say Bannister's record lasted 46 days, while World Athletics says 45.
How much did Roger Bannister train?
Medical school sometimes left him only 30 to 40 minutes a day, so he often trained hard in his lunch break, typically running repeated fast quarter-miles with short rests.
Did Roger Bannister win an Olympic medal?
No. He finished fourth in the 1,500 metres at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics and retired from racing at the end of 1954 to focus on medicine.
What did Roger Bannister do after running?
He became a consultant neurologist, chaired Britain's Sports Council, was knighted in 1975 and served as Master of Pembroke College, Oxford.

title: Kodak held back the digital camera. Its own engineer invented it.
seo_title: Steve Sasson: Kodak's first digital camera story (1975)
summary: In 1975 Kodak engineer Steve Sasson built the first self-contained digital camera. Kodak, a film company, moved slowly. What that teaches about best sellers.
intro: In December 1975, in a laboratory at Eastman Kodak in Rochester, New York, a young engineer named Steve Sasson tested a strange, toaster-sized box he had built from spare parts. Twenty-three seconds later, a black-and-white image of 100 by 100 pixels had been written onto a cassette tape. To see it, he played the tape back on a television set.
It was the world's first self-contained digital camera, and it was built by the world's best-known film company.

sections.h: Who is Steve Sasson?
paras: Steven Sasson was born in Brooklyn, New York, in 1950. As a teenager he built his own radio equipment, and he went on to study electrical engineering at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, earning a bachelor's degree in 1972 and a master's in 1973.

That year he joined Kodak's research laboratory. "The most amazing thing about being at Kodak was that they paid me to do what I loved," he told the National Inventors Hall of Fame. In 1974 his supervisor, Gareth Lloyd, gave him a loosely defined task: find out whether a new kind of electronic light sensor, the charge-coupled device or CCD, could be used to make images.

sections.h: How the first digital camera worked
paras: Sasson built his answer from parts. According to the National Inventors Hall of Fame and Snopes, the prototype combined a lens from a Super 8 movie camera, 16 nickel-cadmium batteries, an analogue-to-digital converter, a CCD sensor and dozens of circuits on six circuit boards.

It weighed about 8 pounds, roughly 3.6 kilograms. Its sensor captured 0.01 megapixels. Taking the picture took a fraction of a second, but writing it to the cassette took 23 seconds, and viewing it required a television set, as the IEEE's history of the camera explains.
Kodak filed a patent for the "electronic still camera" in May 1977, naming Lloyd and Sasson as inventors. It was granted in December 1978 as US patent 4,131,919.

sections.h: Why Kodak did not launch it
paras: Sasson showed the camera to groups of Kodak managers. Their questions were reasonable for the time: when would this be good enough for ordinary customers? He estimated 15 to 20 years.

There was also a deeper problem. Kodak made most of its money from film and photographic paper, the business of printed photographs. "Of course, that went against Kodak's business model at the time, so it wasn't too well received," Sasson told WTOP in 2023. Speaking to the New York Times years earlier, he recalled that executives "were convinced that no one would ever want to look at their pictures on a television set."

It is fair to add context. The fact-checking site Snopes rates the popular claim that Kodak 'buried' the camera as a mixture of true and false. The 1975 prototype was nowhere near ready to sell, and Kodak did keep researching digital imaging and earned large sums from its patents. But concern about film sales was clearly part of the picture. As Sasson put it: "We had the technology, we just didn't have the business plan on how to deal with it."

sections.h: What happened to Kodak after the digital camera
paras: Sasson kept working on digital imaging. In 1989 he and colleague Robert Hills built what is described as the first self-contained digital single-lens reflex camera, storing images on a memory card. According to the National Inventors Hall of Fame, Kodak initially declined to sell it, to protect its film business. "When we built that camera, the argument was over," Sasson later told the New York Times, as quoted by Business Insider.

Kodak did eventually move. Snopes notes that its first commercially available digital camera system appeared in 1991, priced at about $20,000 and aimed mainly at professionals. An Associated Press report dates Kodak's mass-market digital cameras to 2001.

As digital photography spread, the film business that had carried Kodak for decades shrank. Kodak filed for bankruptcy protection on 19 January 2012. As part of its restructuring it sold a package of digital-imaging patents, about 1,100 according to the Associated Press, for roughly $525 million to a group of technology companies. It emerged in September 2013 as a much smaller company focused on commercial imaging and printing.

sections.h: How Steve Sasson is remembered
paras: Sasson's work was recognised in full in later years. In 2009 he received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, and in 2011 he was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame. In 2022 the IEEE dedicated a milestone plaque in Rochester to the hand-held digital camera of 1975.
Asked in 2023 about modern phone cameras, he said: "I had no idea it would advance this fast in my lifetime."

sections.h: Why this story matters
paras: Kodak's leaders were not foolish. They were protecting a very profitable business against an idea that, in 1975, really was crude and years from being useful. At its 1980s peak, IndustryWeek reports, Kodak employed about 145,000 people, and most of that enterprise rested on film.

The lesson is about what happens next. When a new idea threatens your best seller, the safe-looking choice is to wait. But someone else is rarely waiting, and the people who own the old business are often the last to see the new one clearly.

lesson: If a new idea threatens your best seller, someone else will build it. Better that it's you, even if you start small.
check: What are you protecting that might be holding you back?
If a competitor launched your 'shelved' idea tomorrow, would you regret not building it first?

The prototype was far from ready to sell, and Sasson estimated consumer versions were 15 to 20 years away. Kodak also made most of its money from film and paper, so a filmless camera went against its business model.

title: 13 employees, $1 billion: how Instagram began by cutting almost everything
seo_title: Instagram's 13 employees and the $1 billion Facebook deal
summary: Instagram began as Burbn, a check-in app with too many features. Its founders kept only photos, and 18 months later Facebook agreed to pay $1 billion.
intro: In April 2012, Facebook agreed to pay about $1 billion in cash and stock for a company that had no revenue and, according to Business Standard and NPR, just 13 employees. The company was Instagram, and its app had been on sale for only about 18 months.

The deal made headlines because of the price. The more useful part of the story happened two years earlier, when the founders looked at the app they had built, decided it did too much, and threw most of it away.

sections.h: Who founded Instagram?
paras: Instagram was founded by Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger in San Francisco in 2010. Systrom was a Stanford graduate who had worked at Google, as both Business Standard and Bloomberg noted at the time of the sale. TechCrunch reported that he had also spent time at Nextstop, a travel startup that was later bought by Facebook.

Krieger had spent about a year and a half at the chat startup Meebo before joining Systrom, according to TechCrunch. Business Standard reported that the pair teamed up in early 2010. Systrom brought the product idea; Krieger, an engineer, helped build it.

sections.h: What was Burbn, the app before Instagram?
paras: The first product was not Instagram. It was called Burbn, a location-based app built for the mobile web. TechCrunch described its features: you could check in at places, post plans for future check-ins, earn points for spending time with friends, and share photos.

It was a crowded market. Foursquare and Gowalla were already popular check-in apps, and Burbn was arriving late. Even so, the founders raised a seed round of $500,000 from Baseline Ventures and Andreessen Horowitz, a figure reported by both TechCrunch and Business Standard.

Then they noticed something in how people used it. TechCrunch reported that users were mostly ignoring the check-ins and sharing everyday photos instead. The feature the founders had treated as one item on a long list was the one people kept coming back to.

sections.h: The decision to cut almost everything
paras: Systrom and Krieger stepped back and looked hard at the product. TechCrunch reported that Systrom felt the iPhone version had become cluttered and overrun with features. So they made a difficult call. They kept the photo, comment and like features and cut nearly everything else.

In his own account of the decision, quoted by TechCrunch in 2010, Systrom wrote: "We decided that if we were going to build a company, we wanted to focus on being really good at one thing." Their seed investors backed the change of direction.

The founders then studied the photo apps people already loved. TechCrunch described the gap they saw: some apps had fun filters but were not social, while Facebook was social but not built around photos. Instagram aimed for the space in between, with simple filters and quick sharing.

sections.h: How fast Instagram grew
paras: Instagram launched on Apple's App Store in October 2010. Demand on the first day was so heavy that the servers struggled; Systrom later told TechCrunch that he had never felt so sick. By February 2011, Business Standard reported, it had 1.75 million members.
Growth came without paid advertising. TechCrunch reported that Instagram did not pay to acquire users. People shared their photos, friends saw them, and friends downloaded the app.

By early 2012 the user base was large, though reports gave slightly different counts. TechCrunch cited 27 million registered iPhone users announced in March 2012, while Business Standard put the total at more than 30 million at the time of the deal. An Android version launched in April 2012 and, according to TechCrunch, passed a million users within 24 hours.

sections.h: Why Facebook paid $1 billion for Instagram
paras: In April 2012, Facebook announced it would buy Instagram for about $1 billion in cash and stock. TechCrunch and NPR both reported the deal. Mark Zuckerberg said in his announcement that Facebook was committed to building and growing Instagram independently.

The price looked startling. TechCrunch pointed out that Instagram had no revenue at all, and only a short time earlier investors had valued it at $500 million, according to TechCrunch and Business Standard. Business Standard and NPR, citing TechCrunch, counted 13 employees, a team small enough to fit in one room.

The final cost turned out lower. Facebook's share price fell after its stock market listing, which reduced the value of the stock part of the payment. When the deal closed in August 2012, Business Today reported it was worth about $715 million, a figure CNBC also cited later.

sections.h: What happened to Instagram after the sale
paras: Systrom and Krieger stayed on to run Instagram inside Facebook for about six years. In September 2018 they announced they were leaving. By then, CNBC reported, Instagram had more than one billion users.

The size of the deal is what people remember. The decision behind it is what is worth borrowing. A small team chose to do one thing well instead of many things adequately. That focus made the product easy to explain in one sentence, easy to use on a phone, and possible for 13 people to run while millions of people joined.

lesson: Sometimes the breakthrough is what you cut, not what you add. Watch what people actually use, and have the nerve to drop the rest.
check: What is one feature, task or commitment you could cut to make room for what is working?
Which part of your project do people actually use, and which part do you keep only because you built it?

title: They laughed at how he jumped: Dick Fosbury and the Fosbury Flop
seo_title: Dick Fosbury: the laughed-at flop that won Olympic gold
summary: Dick Fosbury went over the high-jump bar backwards and was mocked for it. In 1968 he won Olympic gold at 2.24 m, and the world copied his style.
intro: In October 1968, in the Olympic stadium in Mexico City, a tall American student ran at the high-jump bar in a curve, twisted, and went over it backwards, head first, landing on his shoulders. According to World Athletics, Dick Fosbury later recalled that the spectators were so surprised that they stopped cheering and just watched.

A few years earlier, a local newspaper had compared him to a fish flopping in a boat. That evening in Mexico City he won the gold medal with an Olympic record, and within a decade his odd-looking jump had become the way almost everyone did it.

sections.h: Who was Dick Fosbury?
paras: Richard Douglas Fosbury was born on 6 March 1947 in Portland, Oregon, and grew up in Medford, a small city in southern Oregon. The Oregon Encyclopedia and The Guardian both record those details. He was tall and thin, 6 feet 4 inches, which is a good build for high jump.

But he was not a natural at it. The standard technique at the time was the straddle, where the jumper goes over face down and rolls across the bar. Fosbury struggled with it. Olympics.com notes that as a high school athlete he even failed to make his local club team in the event.

sections.h: How the Fosbury Flop was invented
paras: There was no single flash of genius. In 1963, as a 16-year-old at Medford High School, Fosbury started with the old scissors style, which he found easier. As the bar went up, he leaned back a little further each time. Over a series of meets his body kept turning, until he was going over the bar backwards and landing on his back.

The Guardian points out that timing helped. For decades jumpers had landed in pits of sand or sawdust, but during the 1960s foam rubber mats began to replace them. Landing on your shoulders into sawdust would have been dangerous. Landing on thick foam made the new style possible.

Fosbury also noticed details others missed. CBC reported that he worked out that for higher bars he needed to take off from a point further back, while most jumpers planted their foot in the same spot every time.

sections.h: Why people laughed at the Fosbury Flop
paras: The jump looked strange, and people said so. After one high school meet, the Medford Mail Tribune ran the headline "Fosbury Flops Over Bar". CBC reported that the writer said he looked like a fish flopping in a boat. Fosbury later told World Athletics that the comparison made sense locally, because Medford sits on a river popular for fishing.

Coaches pushed back too. His high school coach urged him to switch to the straddle. At Oregon State University, coach Berny Wagner made him practise the conventional style, though he let him use the flop in meets because it scored points for the team, according to the Oregon Encyclopedia.

There were safety worries as well. Coaches and doctors warned that jumping backwards could cause serious neck injuries. CBC cited a letter, described in a book by journalist Richard Hoffer, that warned of "a rash of broken necks". Those feared injuries did not happen, a result usually credited to better landing mats.

sections.h: The 1968 Olympic high jump final
paras: Fosbury kept improving. At Oregon State he broke the school record and won national college titles in 1968 and 1969. In 1968 he made the US Olympic team for Mexico City.

Track and Field News had called the event one of the toughest fields ever assembled, Olympics.com notes. In the final, Fosbury cleared 2.24 metres on his third attempt, finishing ahead of Ed Caruthers of the United States and Valentin Gavrilov of the Soviet Union. It was a new Olympic record, as Olympics.com and CBC both confirm.

He then asked for the bar to go to 2.29 metres, to try for the world record, but missed all three attempts. It did not matter. The new style had worked on the biggest stage in the sport, in front of the whole world.

sections.h: How the world copied him
paras: Young jumpers studied film of Mexico City and started trying it themselves. At the next Olympics, in Munich in 1972, 28 of the 40 high jumpers used the flop, a figure reported by both Olympics.com and World Athletics. Olympics.com adds that the straddle was last seen at an Olympics in Seoul in 1988.

Fosbury himself did not make the 1972 team. He finished his engineering degree, became a civil engineer in Idaho and later served as a county commissioner in Blaine County, Idaho. He stayed involved in the Olympic movement and taught at clinics and track camps. He died in March 2023, aged 76. In 2014 he told World Athletics that he believed the flop was a natural style and he was simply the first to find it.

sections.h: What Fosbury understood before everyone else
paras: Fosbury did not set out to start a revolution. He was a teenager who could not make the accepted technique work, so he kept adjusting until he found something that worked for his body. The ridicule was real, but so was the steady progress on the scoreboard.
He also had help from timing he did not control, such as softer landing mats. The lesson is not that every strange idea wins. It is that a strange idea deserves a fair test before it is dismissed.

timeline: Dick Fosbury is born on 6 March in Portland, Oregon
Starts developing his backwards jumping style at Medford High School
Wins the NCAA high jump title for Oregon State
October 1968
Wins Olympic gold in Mexico City with an Olympic record of 2.24 m
At the Munich Olympics, 28 of 40 high jumpers use the flop
The straddle is seen for the last time at an Olympics, in Seoul
March 2023
Fosbury dies aged 76
lesson: Weird is often just early. Fosbury did not argue with the people laughing; he kept refining the jump until the results answered for him.
check: What are people laughing at you for trying?
Is it actually wrong, or just new, and what result would settle the question?
faq: Dick Fosbury lent his name to a "flop" in which Olympic event?
The high jump. Dick Fosbury went over the bar head-first and backwards, a style now called the Fosbury Flop, and used it to win high-jump gold at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, clearing 2.24 metres.
Who invented the Fosbury Flop?
American high jumper Dick Fosbury developed it gradually from 1963, as a teenager at Medford High School in Oregon. He adapted the older scissors style until he was going over the bar backwards.
When did Dick Fosbury win Olympic gold?
At the 1968 Mexico City Olympics. He cleared 2.24 metres on his third attempt, which was a new Olympic record.
Why is it called the Fosbury Flop?
The name came from a local newspaper headline, "Fosbury Flops Over Bar", in the Medford Mail Tribune. The writer compared him to a fish flopping in a boat.
How quickly did other jumpers adopt the flop?
By the 1972 Munich Olympics, 28 of the 40 high jumpers used it. Within about a decade it had become the standard technique.
Why did foam mats matter for the Fosbury Flop?
Jumpers once landed in sand or sawdust, which would have made landing on the back risky. Foam rubber mats spread during the 1960s and made the backwards landing much safer.
