title: He planted a forest by himself: Jadav Payeng and Molai forest
seo_title: Jadav Payeng: the Forest Man of India and Molai forest
summary: In 1979 teenager Jadav Payeng planted bamboo on a bare Brahmaputra sandbar in Assam. He kept planting, and Molai forest now covers about 1,360 acres.
intro: In the summer of 1979, after heavy floods and then a heatwave, a teenage boy walked onto a bare sandbar of the Brahmaputra river near Jorhat in Assam and found it covered in dead snakes. The floods had washed them up, and with no trees for shade, the heat had killed them.

The boy, Jadav Payeng, later told the Khaleej Times what went through his mind: "I thought even the human beings would die like this if nothing was done to save trees." He decided to plant some. He did not stop for the next four decades.

sections.h: Who is Jadav Payeng?
paras: Jadav Payeng, known locally by his nickname Molai, grew up in Jorhat district in Assam, in north-east India, close to the Brahmaputra. He left school early. Then and now, he has made his living as a small dairy farmer, keeping cows and buffaloes and selling milk, with his home near the forest at Kokilamukh.

Reports differ slightly on his age in 1979. The Khaleej Times says he was 15, and the Christian Science Monitor says 16. Either way, he was a teenager with no money and no official role, only a strong reaction to what he had seen.

sections.h: How Molai forest started with a handful of bamboo
paras: Payeng asked the village elders what could be done to stop animals dying like that. Their answer was practical: plant bamboo. It grows fast, holds sandy soil and gives shade quickly.

So he started with bamboo seedlings on the sand. Accounts of the exact number vary; the Christian Science Monitor reports about 50 bamboo shoots, while other retellings say around 20. What all accounts agree on is the scale: a few dozen plants on an empty river island.

Then he kept going, mostly alone. According to the Christian Science Monitor, he watered the young plants using earthen pots with small holes in the bottom, so water dripped slowly into the dry ground. The Khaleej Times reports that he even carried red ants from his village to the sandbar to help improve the soil.

He has since explained that a sapling needs several years of steady care before it can survive as a tree on its own, which is why the early years mattered so much. He also credits help he never planned for: "The birds, cows, deer, wind, water and elephants have helped me," he told The Hindu.

sections.h: How big is Molai forest today?
paras: As the bamboo took hold, Payeng planted more varied trees. The Christian Science Monitor lists species including teak, tamarind, jackfruit, mango, banyan, silk cotton and Indian rosewood. Year by year, the sandbar turned from bare sand into woodland.

Today the forest, called Molai forest or Molai Kathoni after him, covers about 1,360 acres, roughly 550 hectares. Both the Khaleej Times and the Christian Science Monitor give that figure, and the Monitor points out that it is bigger than New York's Central Park.

The wildlife followed the trees. Reported visitors and residents include Bengal tigers, one-horned rhinoceroses, deer, wild buffalo, vultures and many other birds, and herds of wild elephants pass through every year.

sections.h: How the world found out about the Forest Man
paras: For close to three decades, almost nobody outside the area knew the forest existed. That changed in the late 2000s, when Jitu Kalita, a local wildlife photographer and journalist, came across it while photographing birds along the river. Reports give different years for this, from 2007 to 2010. In the documentary Forest Man, Kalita remembers it simply: "I had found a dense forest in the middle of a barren wasteland."

In 2012 Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi invited Payeng to an Earth Day event and gave him the title he is now known by: the Forest Man of India. A short documentary, Forest Man, by Canadian filmmaker William Douglas McMaster, won an award at a Cannes Film Festival showcase in 2014 and carried his story around the world.
In 2015 the Government of India awarded him the Padma Shri, the country's fourth-highest civilian honour.

sections.h: What Jadav Payeng is doing now
paras: Recognition did not change his routine. The Khaleej Times reported that he asked organisers not to invite him to award ceremonies in April, May and June, because those are the best planting months in Assam.

Since 2012 he has also started planting on a sandbar near Majuli, one of the world's largest river islands, which faces serious erosion. He has spoken at environmental events abroad and urges schools to make children plant and look after trees themselves.

Asked what he wants from others, his answer is short. "I just plant trees, and I'd like all of you to do so," he told The Hindu. And about himself, Yahoo News quoted him in 2015: "I will continue to plant till my last breath."

sections.h: Why a forest is the right picture for small habits
paras: The forest is impressive, but the method is ordinary: plant something, water it, come back tomorrow. None of the individual days would have looked important. A bamboo shoot on a sandbar is not news.
What turned it into 1,360 acres was time and repetition, carried on for years before anyone was watching or giving credit.

lesson: Small things, done every day for long enough, become forests. Most of the growth happens long before anyone notices.
check: What small thing could you start today and repeat every day?
What would it look like after ten years if you never skipped it?

title: The avalanche hit. She kept climbing: Bachendri Pal on Everest
seo_title: Bachendri Pal: avalanche, then the Everest summit in 1984
summary: An avalanche hit her Everest camp in May 1984 and more than half the team turned back. A week later Bachendri Pal stood on the summit.
intro: At about half past midnight on 16 May 1984, the members of India's Everest expedition were asleep in their tents at Camp III, around 24,000 feet up on the Lhotse face. Then came a sound like an explosion. An avalanche tore through the camp, burying tents and injuring almost everyone inside.
Bachendri Pal was one of them. A week later, on 23 May, she was standing on the summit of Mount Everest, the first Indian woman ever to do so.

sections.h: Who is Bachendri Pal?
paras: Bachendri Pal was born on 24 May 1954 in Nakuri, a village in what is now Uttarakhand. She was one of seven children in a working-class family. Her father, Kishan Singh Pal, was a small border trader who carried groceries by mule into Tibet.

Money was always short, and Pal learned stitching and sewed clothes to help pay for her studies. She was a strong student and went on to earn an MA in Sanskrit and a B.Ed. She was the first person in her village to complete an MA.
The mountains came early. At about 12, she and a group of classmates climbed a peak of nearly 4,000 metres and ended up stranded overnight. It was an adventure that stayed with her.

sections.h: From teacher's path to mountaineer
paras: Her family expected her to become a teacher, and many relatives saw climbing as no career for a young woman. In a 2016 interview with The Week she remembered her mother calling the plan risky and doubting she would return alive. She later said: "Breaking the stereotype and coming out of that mindset was tougher than climbing Mount Everest."

She joined a course at the Nehru Institute of Mountaineering in Uttarkashi in 1982, at 28, and earned an A grade. Her performance there, and on a selection camp in the Garhwal Himalaya, earned her a place on Everest '84, India's first Everest expedition to include both men and women. The team included six women.

sections.h: What happened in the 1984 Everest avalanche?
paras: The expedition began its push up the mountain in early May 1984. On the night of 15-16 May, the avalanche struck Camp III on the Lhotse glacier. Pal later described being jolted awake by something hitting her hard. Everyone survived, but many were hurt, and more than half the team had to give up the climb because of injuries or exhaustion.

When she was asked whether she wanted to quit, Pal said no. Speaking to The Week years later, she explained her thinking simply: "I thought that since I did not die in this incident, I have no reason to step back."

It is worth noticing what that decision was not. It was not bravado or a refusal to feel fear; she has said she was scared. It was a calm judgement that the setback had not removed her ability to continue, so it should not remove her goal either.

sections.h: How Bachendri Pal reached the summit on 23 May 1984
paras: On 22 May she set off from the higher camps with the Sherpa sirdar Ang Dorjee and a few remaining climbers. She was the only woman in the group. They spent the night at the South Col, the last camp below the summit, and set out for the top at 6:20 the next morning, in temperatures well below minus 30 degrees Celsius.

In her autobiography, Everest: My Journey to the Top, she recorded the moment: "And at 1.07 pm on 23 May 1984, I stood on top of Everest, and I was the first Indian woman to have done so." The next day, 24 May, was her 30th birthday.
Later that year she received the Padma Shri, one of India's highest civilian honours.

sections.h: What Bachendri Pal did after Everest
paras: Pal did not treat the summit as an ending. She spent more than three decades with Tata Steel running its adventure programmes, becoming director of the Tata Steel Adventure Foundation in Jamshedpur, which trains people in mountaineering and leadership. She retired in May 2019. Climbers she trained include Arunima Sinha and Premlata Agarwal, both later Everest summiteers.

In 1993 she led the Indo-Nepalese Women's Everest Expedition. According to Tata Steel, 18 people reached the summit on that one expedition, seven of them women. In 1994 she led an all-women rafting voyage down the Ganga from Haridwar to Kolkata, and in 1997 an all-women trek across the length of the Himalayas, from Arunachal Pradesh to the Siachen Glacier.
The honours kept pace: the Arjuna Award in 1986 and the Padma Bhushan, India's third-highest civilian award, in 2019.

sections.h: Why her decision still matters
paras: Most of us will never stand on a collapsing ice slope at night. But almost everyone meets a moment when the team shrinks, a plan breaks or a project takes a hit, and the easy reading is that the attempt is over.

Pal's story separates two things that often get tangled: the setback and the goal. The avalanche changed her team, her plan and her odds. It did not change whether she could still climb. She checked that honestly, and kept going. That honest check, more than courage alone, is what turned a near-disaster into a first for India.

timeline: Born on 24 May in Nakuri, in today's Uttarakhand

lesson: A setback can shrink the team without ending the journey. Ask whether it has actually taken away your ability to continue, not just your comfort.
check: What setback are you treating like a stop sign, when it has only changed the plan?

On the night of 15-16 May 1984 an avalanche struck Camp III, at around 24,000 feet. Many climbers were injured and more than half the team withdrew, but Pal chose to continue.

She was 29. She reached the summit on 23 May 1984, and turned 30 the next day.
What awards has Bachendri Pal received?

What did Bachendri Pal do after climbing Everest?

She led adventure programmes at Tata Steel for decades and headed the Tata Steel Adventure Foundation until 2019. She also led the 1993 Indo-Nepalese Women's Everest Expedition and all-women expeditions on the Ganga and across the Himalayas.

title: From ticket collector to the World Cup-winning six: MS Dhoni
seo_title: MS Dhoni: ticket collector at Kharagpur to World Cup 2011
summary: MS Dhoni once checked train tickets at Kharagpur station and played for the railway team. In 2011 he hit the six that won India the World Cup.
intro: On the night of 2 April 2011, at Wankhede Stadium in Mumbai, India needed four runs from 11 balls to win the World Cup. Their captain swung the ball over long-on for six, and the country had its first 50-over world title in 28 years.

Less than a decade earlier, that captain had been checking passengers' tickets on trains out of Kharagpur, a railway town in West Bengal. Mahendra Singh Dhoni's road to that six ran through a government job, a railway cricket team and a lot of patient waiting.

sections.h: Was MS Dhoni a ticket collector?
paras: Yes. Dhoni, who grew up in Ranchi, worked as a travelling ticket examiner (TTE) for South Eastern Railway, based at Kharagpur station. Deccan Chronicle reported that he held the job from September 2001 to July 2004, before he made the Indian team. Deccan Herald put his stay in Kharagpur at about four years.

The work was ordinary. A TTE checks tickets and reservations on trains, often on long shifts. Deccan Herald reported that he carried out these duties with integrity, and that it was hard for people who later watched him lead India to imagine him walking down train corridors with a ticket chart.

sections.h: How cricket came with the railway job
paras: The job and the cricket were linked. Deccan Herald reported that Dhoni was hired by South Eastern Railway through its Divisional Railway Manager, a cricket fan, and that he became an integral part of the railway's cricket team.

He had already played age-group cricket before arriving. According to Deccan Herald, he had represented Bihar in the Cooch Behar Trophy, an Under-19 competition. In Kharagpur he kept playing as much as he could, including in local tennis-ball tournaments, while holding down his railway duties.

None of this was glamorous. Kharagpur was far from the big cricket centres, and there was no famous academy behind him. What he had was a steady income, regular matches and the chance to keep improving.

sections.h: From Kharagpur to the Indian team
paras: Dhoni left the railway in 2004, and late that year he was picked for India's tour of Bangladesh. His start was not promising. In his first one-day international, in December 2004, he was run out without scoring, as both the ICC and India TV recall.

He did not have to wait long for his breakthrough. A few months later, in 2005, he made his first international century against Pakistan at Visakhapatnam. India TV reported that later the same year he made 183 not out against Sri Lanka in Jaipur, which the ICC lists as the highest ODI score by a wicketkeeper in men's cricket.
In 2007 he was given the captaincy for the first ICC World Twenty20. India, with a young side, won the tournament by beating Pakistan in the final, according to the ICC and India TV.

sections.h: The 2011 World Cup final: Dhoni's 91 not out
paras: Four years later India reached the 50-over World Cup final against Sri Lanka at home. Sri Lanka made 274 for six in their 50 overs, built around an unbeaten century from Mahela Jayawardene, according to the BCCI match report and the ESPNcricinfo scorecard.

India's chase started badly. Virender Sehwag was out on the second ball, and Sachin Tendulkar fell in the seventh over, as Wisden and the BCCI both describe. Gautam Gambhir steadied the innings with 97.

Then Dhoni made an unexpected call. Wisden reported that he promoted himself to No. 5, ahead of the in-form Yuvraj Singh, partly because he expected Sri Lanka's off-spinners to trouble the two left-handers. It was a risk, because Dhoni himself had not scored many runs earlier in the tournament and had not yet played a big innings.

It worked. Dhoni finished on 91 not out from 79 balls, with eight fours and two sixes. The last of those sixes, off Nuwan Kulasekara, won the match. India won by six wickets with 10 balls to spare, and Dhoni was named player of the match, as the ESPNcricinfo scorecard and the BCCI record.

sections.h: What came after the World Cup
paras: In 2013 Dhoni led India to the ICC Champions Trophy as well. The ICC describes him as the only captain to win all three of its men's white-ball titles: the T20 World Cup, the 50-over World Cup and the Champions Trophy.

He played his last match for India in the 2019 World Cup semi-final against New Zealand, and retired from international cricket more than a year later. The ICC describes it as a career of 16 years, in which he was captain, wicketkeeper and batter.

sections.h: Why the ticket collector story matters
paras: The story is popular in India because it is so ordinary at the start. A steady job at a railway station did not stop him; it gave him a base from which to keep practising and playing until the bigger chance came. Where you start does not decide where you finish, but what you keep doing in the meantime often does.

It is also a reminder that a job and a dream do not always have to compete. For about three years, Dhoni did both: he checked tickets, collected a salary, and used the railway team as his training ground. When the call came from the national selectors, he was ready for it.

title: Eighteen years old, twenty thousand rupees, Ludhiana: how Sunil Mittal got to Airtel
seo_title: Sunil Mittal: ₹20,000 at 18 in Ludhiana to Bharti Airtel
summary: In 1976, 18-year-old Sunil Mittal borrowed ₹20,000 from his father to make bicycle parts in Ludhiana. A ban, a trade fair and a phone later, came Airtel.
intro: In the early 1980s, Sunil Mittal had a business that was working. He was importing portable generators from Japan and selling them across India. Then the government banned their import. In his own words to Knowledge at Wharton: "One fine day, there was no business."

He was in his mid-twenties, and it was not the first time he had started from scratch. It would also be the setback that pushed him, step by step, towards the telephone business that became Bharti Airtel.

sections.h: Who is Sunil Bharti Mittal?
paras: Sunil Bharti Mittal grew up in Ludhiana, Punjab, a city known for its small factories and workshops. He called it "a very industrious town" and "the bedrock of small-scale industry" in a 2008 interview with Knowledge at Wharton, the business journal of the Wharton School.

He is the founder and chairman of the Bharti group, best known for Bharti Airtel, one of India's largest mobile networks, with operations across South Asia and Africa. But his story begins far from mobile phones. The path from a Ludhiana workshop to that company ran through three very different businesses, and one of them was shut down by a single government decision.

sections.h: How Sunil Mittal started: ₹20,000 and bicycle crankshafts
paras: In April 1976, at 18, Mittal borrowed ₹20,000 and started his first business in Ludhiana, making parts for the city's bicycle makers. Business Insider India, India TV and domain-b all report the ₹20,000 figure and the bicycle business; Udayavani adds that the money came from his father and friends.

He described the product himself to Knowledge at Wharton: "I decided to manufacture bicycle parts, in particular crankshafts." India TV likewise reports that he made crankshafts for local bicycle manufacturers.
It was a real business, but he soon saw its limits. The big bicycle companies set the prices, and as he told Wharton, "just making shafts wouldn't have made you a player of any size or scale."

sections.h: The move to Bombay and the generator business
paras: So he left. "It was very clear that I had to get out of Ludhiana into a much bigger place, Delhi or Mumbai — Bombay at that time," he told Wharton. Accounts of the timing vary between 1980 and 1982.

In Bombay he turned to trading imported goods. His main product was portable generators made by Suzuki in Japan, which Knowledge at Wharton and India TV both describe. Business Insider India and Udayavani describe it as a full-scale business selling generators imported from Japan.

Then the rules changed. The government banned generator imports and gave licences to two Indian companies to make them locally, as Business Insider India and Udayavani report. India TV and domain-b date the ban to 1983. His business disappeared almost overnight.

sections.h: From a Taiwan trade fair to telephones
paras: Mittal did not wait for the rules to change back. He went back to Japan, Korea and Taiwan looking for a new product, ideally one that larger Indian companies were not already making, as he explained to Wharton.

At a trade fair in Taiwan he found it: push-button telephones. Indian homes still used rotary-dial phones, and he brought in what he describes as India's first push-button telephone set. India TV reports the phones were sold under the Beetel brand.

Telephone equipment led to a technical partnership with the German company Siemens, according to both domain-b and the ICMR case study on Airtel, and in the early 1990s the group also launched some of India's first fax machines and cordless phones, as India TV and Udayavani report.

sections.h: The 1992 mobile licence and the launch of Airtel
paras: When India began opening mobile telephony to private companies, Mittal decided to compete. He told Wharton he was bidding for a mobile licence "against all odds — in 1992, when I was a rank outsider." Udayavani and India TV both report that Bharti won the right to build a cellular network in Delhi in 1992.

It was a bold move for a company whose experience was in making and selling telephone handsets, not running networks. But each earlier venture had given Mittal something he now needed: an eye for products India did not yet have, experience with foreign technology partners, and a habit of moving quickly when an opening appeared.
The service launched in 1995 under the Airtel brand. The ICMR case study dates the Delhi launch to November 1995, and India TV also places the launch of Bharti Cellular's Airtel service in 1995.

From one city, the network spread across India through new licences and acquisitions, and later into other countries. Udayavani reports that in 2005 Airtel launched its first international mobile network, in Sri Lanka.

sections.h: Why each small business mattered
paras: Looked at in hindsight, none of Mittal's early ventures was wasted. The crankshaft workshop taught him manufacturing, pricing and dealing with bigger customers. The generator trade taught him imports, distribution and how quickly a government decision can wipe out a business.

That last lesson might have ended his career. Instead it sent him looking for a new product, and the one he found happened to be at the start of India's telecom boom. His own advice, given to Wharton, sums up the approach: "If you're caught between speed and perfection, always choose speed, and perfection will follow."

lesson: A small first business teaches you the big one, and a closed door is often the start of the next search.
check: What small business could you start with what you have now?
When a door last closed on you, did you go looking for the next one, or wait for the old one to reopen?

In the early 1980s he imported Suzuki portable generators from Japan and sold them in India. The government then banned generator imports, reportedly in 1983, and gave local manufacturing licences to two Indian companies, ending his business.
How did Sunil Mittal get into telecom?

After the generator ban he found push-button telephones at a trade fair in Taiwan and brought them to India, which replaced rotary phones. That led to telephone equipment, a partnership with Siemens, and then a bid for a mobile licence.

Bharti won the bid to build a cellular network in Delhi in 1992, and the Airtel mobile service launched in Delhi in 1995.

title: Free physics lessons, a phone and a whiteboard: how PhysicsWallah became a unicorn
seo_title: Alakh Pandey: free YouTube lessons to PhysicsWallah unicorn
summary: Alakh Pandey began posting free physics lessons on YouTube in 2016. By 2022 PhysicsWallah was a unicorn, and in 2025 it listed on the stock market.
intro: In 2016, a young physics teacher from Prayagraj set up a phone on a tripod, stood in front of a whiteboard and started recording lessons for YouTube. According to YourStory, that was close to the whole kit: a camera phone, a tripod, a whiteboard and a few books.

The teacher was Alakh Pandey, and the channel was called PhysicsWallah. Six years later, the company that grew out of it raised its first outside money at a valuation of $1.1 billion. In November 2025, it listed on India's stock exchanges.

sections.h: Who is Alakh Pandey?
paras: Alakh Pandey grew up in Allahabad, now Prayagraj, in Uttar Pradesh. Entrepreneur India reports that he started teaching very early, giving tuition to younger children while he was still at school himself.

He went to an engineering college in Kanpur but did not finish the course. In interviews he has described himself plainly as a college dropout who felt he had to prove himself. TechCrunch notes that he had not cleared the IIT entrance exam himself, which gave him a personal sense of what students without good coaching were up against.

Before YouTube, he taught physics at coaching institutes. That classroom experience, standing in front of real students and seeing where they got stuck, shaped the style that later made his videos popular: direct, energetic and focused on the exam syllabus.

sections.h: How the PhysicsWallah YouTube channel started
paras: Pandey started the PhysicsWallah channel in 2016, posting lessons for students preparing for the JEE and NEET entrance exams and for Class 11 and 12 physics. The videos were free. TechCrunch described the aim as helping students who could not afford premium coaching.

Growth was slow at first. Both YourStory and Entrepreneur India report that the channel took about a year to reach 10,000 subscribers. There was no marketing budget behind it, so most new viewers arrived because another student had shared a lesson with them.

He kept going anyway, recording video after video on the same simple setup. Over time he moved from classroom coaching to teaching on YouTube full-time. By 2020, TechCrunch later reported, PhysicsWallah had become the largest Indian education community on YouTube.

sections.h: From a YouTube channel to an app
paras: In May 2020, with schools and coaching centres shut by the pandemic, PhysicsWallah launched its own app for paid courses. The launch did not go smoothly. YourStory and Entrepreneur India both report that the app crashed when tens of thousands of students tried to join live classes at the same time, and the team had to fix it quickly.

Pandey had a co-founder by then: Prateek Maheshwari, who ran a small edtech firm called PenPencil and took charge of technology and business growth. The company was registered as PhysicsWallah Private Limited in 2020.

The paid courses were priced low compared with big coaching brands, and plenty of teaching stayed free on YouTube. Pandey summed up the shift in a line printed by Entrepreneur India: "Earlier, I was doing it for free and now I am doing it for a marginal amount of money."

sections.h: How PhysicsWallah became a unicorn
paras: For its first years the business ran without outside investors. In June 2022 it raised its first institutional round: $100 million from WestBridge Capital and GSV Ventures, at a valuation of $1.1 billion, as reported by Inc42 and later by Business Today. Both Inc42 and YourStory counted it as India's 101st unicorn.

The timing stood out, because the wider edtech sector was going through a hard period after the pandemic boom. YourStory reported that PhysicsWallah had been profitable since inception, with positive cash flows and reserves, which set it apart from many rivals that depended on investor money to keep running.

In September 2024 PhysicsWallah raised another $210 million, led by Hornbill Capital, which lifted its valuation to $2.8 billion. TechCrunch and Business Today both reported the round. TechCrunch, which described edtech funding as scarce at the time, noted that the company had also opened physical learning centres alongside its online classes.

sections.h: Where PhysicsWallah is today
paras: In November 2025, PhysicsWallah went public. Its initial public offering raised about ₹3,480 crore at ₹109 per share, and the shares began trading on 18 November, according to Business Standard and Business Today. On the first day the stock listed at a premium of more than 30 percent to the issue price.

The company now runs paid courses, many YouTube channels and offline centres. But its public story still begins with the same image: one teacher, a whiteboard and free lessons for students who needed them.

sections.h: Why the free lessons mattered
paras: It is easy to read this as a funding story. It is really a trust story. For years, students watched Pandey teach without paying anything, and many of them passed the lessons on to friends. By the time the app arrived, a large audience already knew his teaching and believed it worked.
He also started with what he had. He did not wait for a studio, a team or investors. He used a phone and a whiteboard, kept posting, and let the quality of the lessons do the spreading.

title: A rice farmer's daughter in cheap spikes: how Hima Das won world 400 m gold
seo_title: Hima Das: rice farmer's daughter to World U20 400m gold
summary: Hima Das, a rice farmer's daughter from Dhing, Assam, was no better than fourth on the last bend of the 2018 World U20 400m final. She won gold in 51.46.
intro: With one bend to go in the women's 400 m final at the 2018 World U20 Championships in Tampere, Finland, the 18-year-old from Assam was out of the medals. World Athletics reported that she was no better than fourth as she entered the final turn.

Then she ran down the home straight as if the race had just started. Hima Das crossed the line in 51.46 seconds, clear of the field, and became the first Indian, man or woman, to win a global title on the track. Only a few years earlier, she had been playing football in the mud beside her family's rice fields.

sections.h: Who is Hima Das?
paras: Hima Das grew up in Dhing village in the Nagaon district of Assam. She is the youngest child of Ronjit and Jomali Das; her father is a rice farmer, and the family had little money to spare for sport. Reports differ on the number of siblings, with some saying she is the youngest of five children and others the youngest of six.
Her first sport was football, not athletics. She played with boys on muddy ground beside the paddy fields and turned out for local clubs. Her nickname, the Dhing Express, comes from her home village.

sections.h: How Hima Das was discovered
paras: A local coach noticed how fast she was and suggested she try athletics. At an inter-district meet she won the 100 m and the 200 m while wearing cheap spikes, and that is where Nipon Das, an athletics coach with Assam's Directorate of Sports and Youth Welfare, saw her run.

He later told DNA: "She ran like the wind. I hadn't seen such a talent in ages." He asked her family to let her move about 140 km to Guwahati to train properly. Her parents were reluctant at first, but they agreed.

In Guwahati she lived in rented accommodation near the Sarusajai Sports Complex. Nipon Das persuaded officials to admit her to the state academy, even though it had no separate athletics wing at the time. With a second coach, Nabajit Malakar, he helped raise the money to send her to the 2017 World Youth Championships in Nairobi, where she finished fifth in the 200 m.

sections.h: Hima Das's road to Tampere
paras: Hima had only recently moved up to the 400 m. At the Commonwealth Games on the Gold Coast in April 2018, she reached the final and finished sixth in 51.32 seconds. It was a strong result for a teenager who had been running the distance for only a few months.

In June 2018, at the Inter-State Championships in Guwahati, she ran 51.13 seconds. That gave her the fastest personal best of anyone entered in the 400 m at the World U20 Championships a few weeks later. She won her heat in Tampere and was fastest through the semi-finals, though her times there were well off her best.

sections.h: How Hima Das won the 2018 World U20 400m final
paras: The final was held on 12 July 2018 at Ratina Stadium in Tampere. Hima did not lead early. She came into the final straight behind the leaders, then overtook them in the closing stretch and pulled away.

She won in 51.46 seconds. Andrea Miklos of Romania took silver in 52.07, a personal best, and Taylor Manson of the United States took bronze in 52.28. Hima told World Athletics that her biggest strength was the last 100 m, which is exactly where the race was won. Her coach, Nipon Das, put it another way to YourStory: "Her race begins in the final 80 metres." In Tampere, that was where she passed the runners ahead of her.

The result made history. World Athletics described her as the first Indian woman to win a global title of any kind and the first Indian to win a global title on the track. After the race, Hima said she was very proud to hold the Indian flag on her shoulders.

sections.h: What Hima Das did next
paras: Six weeks later she was racing seniors at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta. On 26 August she won silver in the women's 400 m in 50.79 seconds, a national record, behind Bahrain's Salwa Eid Naser. She also won gold in the women's 4x400 m relay and silver in the mixed 4x400 m relay.
When she returned to Assam, crowds lined the roads in Guwahati. At the Sarusajai Stadium, where she had trained, she kissed the track.

sections.h: Why the Hima Das story matters
paras: Very little about her start looked like the start of a world champion. She came late to athletics from another sport, trained far from home on a family budget, and ran her early races in basic shoes. What she had was raw speed, steady work and a coach who noticed and then made the effort to open doors.

The Tampere final is also a lesson about judging too early. Anyone who looked away at the last bend would have seen a fourth-placed runner. The finish told a different story. Many people stop counting themselves in long before the real race has been decided.

lesson: You don't need the perfect start to finish first. And never judge a race, or a person, at the last bend.
check: What are you waiting to have before you start: better shoes, more money, the right timing?

title: He mortgaged his house for a badminton academy: Pullela Gopichand
seo_title: Pullela Gopichand: the coach who mortgaged his house
summary: All England champion Pullela Gopichand mortgaged his home to finish a badminton academy in Hyderabad. Its players went on to win India's Olympic medals.
intro: The building was half finished, and the money had run out. Pullela Gopichand, India's All England badminton champion, had land from the state government and a plan for a world-class academy in Hyderabad. What he did not have was enough money for the courts.

"The building was half done but we needed the courts," he later recalled to Olympics.com. So he mortgaged his own home. A few years later, players from that academy would win India's first Olympic medals in badminton.

sections.h: Who is Pullela Gopichand?
paras: Gopichand grew up in Andhra Pradesh and, by Business Standard's account, preferred cricket as a child until his mother and brother steered him towards badminton at around 10. His family cut back on spending, even on meals out, to pay for his training.

His early career was shaped by injury. At the 1994 national games in Pune he collided with his doubles partner and badly damaged his left knee. Surgeons were unsure he would play again. Reports vary on the details, with Olympics.com describing three major operations and Business Standard four, but he spent years recovering. Former national coach Sanjay Sharma told Business Standard: "Everyone had written him off."

sections.h: Gopichand's All England win in 2001
paras: The comeback was not smooth. At the Sydney 2000 Olympics he went out before the quarter-finals; Olympics.com says he played with a swollen knee and a fever, and Deccan Chronicle notes he had no coach with him there. Within months, he would be playing for one of the sport's biggest titles.

He came back. In March 2001 in Birmingham, Gopichand played the All England Open, then one of the most prestigious titles in the sport, with his knee flaring up again. "I went through that All England tournament in a cloud of pain. But I remained totally focused," he told Olympics.com.

In the semi-final he beat Denmark's Peter Gade, one of the world's best players, 17-14, 17-15. On 11 March he beat China's Chen Hong 15-12, 15-6 in the final. He became only the second Indian to win the title, after his early mentor Prakash Padukone in 1980.
Around that time, according to Business Standard, he also turned down a soft drink endorsement because he did not believe in the product. It was an early sign of how he would run things later.

sections.h: Why Gopichand mortgaged his house
paras: After his All England win, the Andhra Pradesh government gave Gopichand five acres of land in Hyderabad, which he chose to use for a badminton centre. His goal was simple: Indian players should be able to train at world-class level at home, without having to go abroad.

Raising the money was slow and hard. Several sources, including Olympics.com, Business Standard and The Statesman, report that he could not find enough backers and mortgaged his family home to keep construction going. The Statesman says he wanted young players to get "nothing but the best training."

Help did come. Industrialist Nimmagadda Prasad agreed to back the project, and Indian press reports put his contribution at about Rs 5 crore. The Pullela Gopichand Badminton Academy opened in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, in 2008.

sections.h: How the academy worked
paras: Gopichand was not only the founder but the head coach, and he worked long hours. Both Business Standard and Deccan Chronicle report that he would be on court from about 4 a.m. for the first session of the day.

He was strict about details. Business Standard describes him studying match footage over and over, keeping fizzy drinks out of the cafeteria and controlling players' diets closely before big events. Players were expected to train hard, several sessions a day.

sections.h: Saina Nehwal, P V Sindhu and the Olympic medals
paras: The bet paid off in the most visible way possible. At the London 2012 Olympics, Saina Nehwal, who trained under Gopichand, won bronze in women's singles, the first Olympic medal by any Indian badminton player.

Four years later at Rio 2016, P V Sindhu, another of his students, reached the women's singles final and won silver after a three-game match against Spain's Carolina Marin. Sindhu later added a bronze at the Tokyo Games in 2021. Business Standard reports that Sindhu's family moved closer to the academy so she could train there, and Deccan Chronicle notes that her parents credited her Rio result to Gopichand.

The academy also trained leading men's players such as Parupalli Kashyap and Kidambi Srikanth. Gopichand went on to serve as India's chief national badminton coach, and he has received the Dronacharya Award and the Padma Bhushan.

sections.h: What Gopichand's bet teaches
paras: It would be wrong to read this as a story about one dramatic decision. The academy took years of planning and fundraising, and it needed land from the government, a generous backer and many coaches and staff to work.

But at the moment it mattered most, Gopichand put his own home on the line for players who had not yet won anything. Nobody should copy that literally; most families cannot take that risk. The useful part is the idea underneath it: real belief in someone else's potential usually costs something, whether that is money, time or a public vote of confidence.

lesson: Bet on the people you believe in. Belief that costs you something is the kind that changes outcomes.

title: He failed Class 12. Then he cleared UPSC: the real story of Manoj Kumar Sharma
seo_title: Manoj Kumar Sharma: the real 12th Fail IPS officer story
summary: Manoj Kumar Sharma from Morena failed Class 12, drove a tempo and walked dogs to pay for books, and cleared UPSC on his fourth attempt with AIR 121.
intro: In a small village in the Chambal region of Madhya Pradesh, copying in board exams was so common that many students expected to pass that way. Then, the year Manoj Kumar Sharma sat his Class 12 exam, a strict official put a stop to it. Without the usual help, he failed.

That result could easily have been the end of his education. Instead it became the first chapter of a story that took him to Delhi, through years of odd jobs and three unsuccessful attempts at India's toughest exam, and finally into the Indian Police Service. His life later inspired the award-winning film 12th Fail.

sections.h: Who is Manoj Kumar Sharma?
paras: Manoj Kumar Sharma is an Indian Police Service officer of the 2005 batch, Maharashtra cadre. He grew up in Bilgaon, a village in Morena district in the Chambal area of Madhya Pradesh. His father worked as a clerk, and the family had little money to spare.

School was a struggle. DNA India and Lokmat Times both report that he passed Classes 9 and 10 in the third division. Nothing in his early record suggested he would one day clear the Union Public Service Commission's civil services exam.

sections.h: Why Manoj Kumar Sharma failed Class 12
paras: According to The Pioneer and The Hitavada, cheating in exams was widespread in his area until a strict officer arrived and stopped it. The two papers differ on that officer's title, one calling him a DSP and the other an SDM. Either way, the copying ended, and Manoj failed his Class 12 board exam.

Reports also differ on the details of the result. DNA India says he failed only Hindi, while Lokmat Times says he failed every subject except Hindi. What they agree on is that he did not give up on school. Outlook India reports that he cleared Class 12 on his second attempt.

The Pioneer describes how that officer also made a lasting impression on him. When Manoj asked how he could become an officer himself, the advice he received was to stop cheating. He took it, and from then on he passed his exams honestly.

sections.h: Tempo driver, library worker, dog walker
paras: To prepare for the civil services exam, Manoj needed coaching and books, and he had very little money. He worked his way through it. Outlook India and DNA India both report that he drove a tempo, worked in a library and walked dogs for well-off families in Delhi to pay for his fees and study material.
There were times when he had nowhere proper to stay. Outlook India and Lokmat Times both report that he sometimes slept on the pavement during those years.

The library job turned out to be more than a wage. DNA India reports that he used the time there to read widely, from Maxim Gorky to Abraham Lincoln to the Hindi poet Muktibodh, building the general knowledge and writing ability the exam demands.

sections.h: Clearing UPSC on the fourth attempt
paras: The civil services exam did not reward him quickly. He was not selected on his first three attempts. Each failure meant another year of preparation while still earning his keep.
On his fourth attempt he cleared it, with an All India Rank of 121, as reported by Outlook India and Lokmat Times. He joined the Indian Police Service in 2005 and was allotted the Maharashtra cadre.

During his preparation years he met Shraddha Joshi, a fellow aspirant from Uttarakhand, who supported him through the hardest stretch. She went on to become an Indian Revenue Service officer, and the two later married. Their story is as central to the film as his exam journey.

sections.h: Is 12th Fail a true story?
paras: Yes. Author Anurag Pathak wrote about Manoj Kumar Sharma's life in the book 12th Fail, published in 2019. Director Vidhu Vinod Chopra adapted it into a Hindi film starring Vikrant Massey as Manoj, which released on 27 October 2023.

The film found a large audience, and at the 71st National Film Awards, announced on 1 August 2025, it was named Best Feature Film, while Vikrant Massey shared the Best Actor award, as Scroll reported.

Sharma's career continued alongside the film's success. Deccan Herald reported in January 2024 that he was heading CISF security at Mumbai airport on deputation and had been awarded the Medal for Meritorious Service on Republic Day. Lokmat Times reported his promotion to the rank of Inspector General in March 2024.

sections.h: What his story really shows
paras: The point is not that failing is good. Failing Class 12 was painful, and the years that followed were hard. The point is that a single result, even a public one like a board exam, is one page in a much longer story.
What decided Manoj's story was the set of choices he made on the pages after it: to study honestly, to take whatever work paid for books, and to sit the exam again after each disappointment.

It also shows how much the people and places around a struggling student matter: an officer who refused to allow cheating, a library that doubled as a classroom, and a partner who believed in him before any result did. If you are going through a hard stretch of your own, it is worth asking who and what you can lean on, and who might be leaning on you.

What was Manoj Kumar Sharma's UPSC rank?

What jobs did Manoj Kumar Sharma do while preparing for UPSC?

Why did Manoj Kumar Sharma fail Class 12?
Reports say copying was common in his area until a strict officer stopped it in the year of his exam, and he failed. He later cleared Class 12 on his second attempt.
Who is Manoj Kumar Sharma's wife?

title: He slept on the living room floor: Sundar Pichai's Chennai childhood
seo_title: Sundar Pichai's childhood: the living room floor in Chennai
summary: Google CEO Sundar Pichai grew up in a modest Chennai home, slept on the living room floor, queued for water in a drought and waited years for a phone.
intro: Long before he ran Google, Sundar Pichai was a boy in Chennai who slept on the floor. "We lived in a kind of modest house, shared with tenants," he told The New York Times in 2018. "We would sleep on the living room floor."

Today he leads one of the world's most valuable companies. But in interviews over the years he has kept coming back to that small house, the water queues and the long wait for a telephone, and to what those years taught him about attention, gratitude and hard work.

sections.h: Where did Sundar Pichai grow up?
paras: Pichai was born on 10 June 1972 in Madras, now Chennai, in Tamil Nadu. Britannica notes that his father was an electrical engineer at GEC, a British company. The family was middle class, and money was carefully spent.

In the 2018 New York Times interview, reported by Business Today and IBTimes, he described a simple life built around friends, books and the street. "Friends, playing street cricket, reading books — that was kind of the totality of life," he said. "There was a simplicity to my life."

sections.h: Queuing for water in a drought
paras: Water was not something the family could take for granted. On the Lex Fridman Podcast in 2025, Pichai recalled a severe drought when water was delivered by truck. "It was a massive drought, so they would get water in these trucks," he said, with only a few buckets for each household.

"Me and my brother, sometimes my mom, we would wait in line, get that and bring it back home," he told Fridman. Business Today, reporting on the interview, said the family waited for hours with containers for the water truck to arrive.
That experience stayed with him. "There was a drought when I was growing up, and we had anxiety," he told The New York Times. "Even now, I can never sleep without a bottle of water beside my bed."

sections.h: A refrigerator, a phone and a VCR
paras: Many everyday comforts arrived slowly. "Other houses had refrigerators, and then we finally got one," he told The New York Times. He described its arrival as "a big deal".
A telephone took even longer. "There was a five-year waiting list, and we got a rotary telephone," he told Lex Fridman, a detail Business Today also reported.

Television was similar. "We had to convince my dad for a long time to get a VCR," he said on the podcast, adding that before that there had been only one TV channel. He read widely instead, everything from philosophy to crime novels, as he put it.

sections.h: The plane ticket his father paid for
paras: Pichai studied metallurgical engineering at IIT Kharagpur and won a place at Stanford University in the United States for a master's degree.

Getting there was the family's biggest bet. In his online "Dear Class of 2020" graduation speech in June 2020, he said: "My father spent the equivalent of a year's salary on my plane ticket to the US so I could attend Stanford." It was his first time on a plane.

Life in America was expensive by his family's standards. "A phone call back home was more than $2 a minute, and a backpack cost the same as my dad's monthly salary in India," he told graduates, as The Tribune and The Federal reported.

Looking back on that journey, he told the graduates that what carried him was not money or connections. Other than luck, he said, the only thing that got him from there to here was "a deep passion for technology, and an open mind". His advice to them, as The Tribune summed it up in its headline, was to be impatient and open-minded.

sections.h: From Stanford to Google CEO
paras: After his master's degree in 1995, Pichai worked briefly at the chipmaker Applied Materials, then earned an MBA from the Wharton School and spent a short time at the consultancy McKinsey, according to Britannica.

He joined Google in 2004 and helped lead work on the Google Toolbar and then the Chrome browser, which launched in 2008. In August 2015 he became Google's CEO, and in December 2019 he also became CEO of its parent company, Alphabet, as Britannica and Stanford's own biography of him both record.

sections.h: What his childhood taught him
paras: Pichai does not describe his childhood as a hardship story. He describes it as simple, and he has spoken often about how it shaped him, making him value things that others might take for granted, from running water to a working phone line.

Notice, too, how ordinary most of his memories are. They are not about a single dramatic break. They are about waiting in a queue with his brother, a family getting its first fridge, a phone that took five years to arrive and a wide mix of books, from philosophy to crime novels. Small, everyday experiences like these quietly shape what a person pays attention to later in life.

The lesson for the rest of us is not that hardship is required for success. It is that what you lacked can sharpen what you notice, and what you are willing to work for. It is also a reminder that most big journeys start with someone else's sacrifice: in his case, a father who spent a year's pay on one plane ticket.

title: He left school and fixed calculators for ₹400 a month. Then came Quick Heal
seo_title: Kailash Katkar: from calculator repair to Quick Heal
summary: Kailash Katkar left school early and repaired calculators in Pune for ₹400 a month. With his brother Sanjay he built Quick Heal, which listed in 2016.
intro: In the early 1990s, the computers coming into a small repair business in Pune kept arriving with the same problem. They were not broken in the usual sense. They were infected with viruses.

The man running the business, Kailash Katkar, had left school as a teenager and learned his trade repairing radios and calculators for ₹400 a month. His younger brother Sanjay, a computer science student, started writing small programs to clean the infected machines. Those programs became Quick Heal, one of India's best-known antivirus brands.

sections.h: Who is Kailash Katkar?
paras: Kailash Katkar grew up in Pune in a family of modest means. His father, according to The Better India and YourStory, worked in a factory as a machine or tool setter.

He left school early because the family needed income. Reports differ slightly on when: YourStory and DNA say he left during Class 9, while The Better India and Business Standard describe him as educated up to Class 10. Either way, he did not go on to college.
His first job was at a shop that repaired radios and calculators. YourStory and DNA both report that it paid ₹400 a month. He stayed for several years and learned the work thoroughly.

sections.h: From a calculator repair shop to computers
paras: In 1991 he opened his own repair business in Pune, putting in ₹15,000, a figure reported by The Better India, YourStory and DNA. The Better India describes it as a 100 sq ft room fixing calculators, and says the business was profitable.
He then noticed where electronics were heading. In 1993 he set up CAT Computer Services to maintain and repair computers, as The Better India, DNA and MediaNama all record.
That shift put him in front of a new problem. As Sanjay told Business Standard: "I noticed that a lot of machines, which had come for repairs, were infected with viruses."

sections.h: How Sanjay Katkar wrote the first Quick Heal antivirus
paras: Sanjay was studying computer science in Pune and spent much of his spare time at his brother's shop. In a detailed 2017 profile in YourStory, he described cleaning infected floppy disks and hard drives by hand, then writing his own small tools in the C language to remove specific viruses. New viruses kept turning up, so the tools kept multiplying.

Kailash saw that this could be more than a repair service and asked his brother to turn the tools into a proper antivirus product. The first version of Quick Heal, for the MS-DOS operating system, was launched in 1995 at ₹700, according to YourStory and DNA. The Better India dates the first program to 1994, so it was likely written in 1994 and sold from 1995.
The name, Sanjay told YourStory, came from speed: because his tools looked for a smaller set of viruses than the big international products, they cleaned machines quickly.

sections.h: The hard early years
paras: Selling software was harder than writing it. Sanjay told YourStory that for the first two years almost nobody paid for the antivirus, because copying software was so common. As he put it: "We couldn't convince people to buy anti-virus."

The brothers kept the repair business going to pay the bills. Repair workshops also helped spread the software, Sanjay recalled, by passing it on to customers. By 1998 the product had proved itself, and Kailash told Business Standard: "By 1998, we stopped hardware repairing and moved focus to anti-virus."
The going was still not easy. Kailash told The Better India the company nearly shut down in 1999, and Sanjay told YourStory he almost quit around 2001 because he could not keep developers.

sections.h: How Quick Heal grew beyond Pune
paras: From 2002 the company began expanding beyond its home city, with Business Standard and The Better India both marking that year as the turning point. The Better India reports the first branch outside Pune opened in Nashik in 2003, followed by a network of offices across India.

In 2010 the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital invested in the company, as The Better India and MediaNama report. Business Standard reports it also moved into security products for businesses around 2011-12, alongside its home antivirus software.

Kailash became managing director and CEO, while Sanjay led technology. Business Standard quoted Sanjay looking back: "When we started we never thought of making it so big. We just wanted to develop a good product."

sections.h: The 2016 Quick Heal IPO
paras: In February 2016 Quick Heal Technologies held its initial public offering. The issue of about ₹451 crore was priced at ₹321 a share and was open from 8 to 10 February, according to Business Standard and MediaNama.

The shares listed on the BSE and NSE on 18 February 2016, opening at about ₹305, roughly 5% below the issue price. For a business that began as a calculator repair room, it was a remarkable milestone: an Indian-built software product company, run by its founding brothers, listed on the country's stock exchanges.

Looking back, the order of events is the useful part. Kailash did not set out to build a software company. He went where the repair work was moving, from calculators to computers, and paid attention when the same fault kept coming through the door. The product grew out of a problem his customers already had, and his brother already knew how to fix.

lesson: Fix the problem in front of you, then ask how many other people have it. Done well, a repair job can become a product.

title: Her first earnings came at 90, from a box of besan barfi
seo_title: Harbhajan Kaur: besan barfi business started at 90
summary: Harbhajan Kaur of Chandigarh never had money of her own. At about 90 she sold her father's besan barfi recipe at a market and earned ₹2,000 on day one.
intro: At around the age of 90, Harbhajan Kaur sat down at a stall in a local organic market in Chandigarh with boxes of home-made besan barfi. By the end of the day she had earned ₹2,000.

It was not a large sum. But it was the first money in her long life that she had earned herself, and it turned a grandmother's quiet regret into a small family brand that, a few years later, had one of India's best-known industrialists calling her his entrepreneur of the year.

sections.h: Who is Harbhajan Kaur?
paras: Harbhajan Kaur is a homemaker from Chandigarh who spent her life running a household and cooking for her family. Her daughters remember a home where they rarely needed to eat out. As her daughter Raveena Suri told YourStory, she was so talented at cooking that the family never went out to eat when the children were young.
Outlook Money describes her as a lifelong homemaker and keen cook who was always making sweets, cakes and pastries at home. SheThePeople reports that she has three daughters.

sections.h: The one regret that started it
paras: The business began with a remark, not a plan. Around 2016, when she was about 90, Harbhajan Kaur told her daughter that she had lived a full life but had one regret: she had never earned money of her own.

The Better India quotes her directly: "I had a fulfilling life, but my only regret is that I never earned any money on my own. I wish I had." News Bharati and Outlook Money describe the same conversation, and SheThePeople quotes Raveena Suri saying it all started with an innocuous utterance by her mother when she turned 90.
Raveena did not treat it as a passing comment. She asked what her mother could make and sell, and the answer was already in the kitchen.

sections.h: Why besan barfi?
paras: Besan barfi is a traditional north Indian sweet made from roasted gram (chickpea) flour, ghee and sugar, set and cut into squares. It is common, which makes a good one hard to stand out with. Harbhajan Kaur's version had family history behind it.

Both Outlook Money and SheThePeople report that the recipe came from her father. Outlook Money adds that her daughter described it as more than 100 years old. For decades it had been made only for the household; as Raveena told News Bharati, though her mother had been making barfi for ages, it was only for the members of the house.

sections.h: How the first day went: ₹2,000 at an organic market
paras: The family took her barfi to a local organic market in Chandigarh. According to both The Better India and Outlook Money, she earned ₹2,000 on that first outing. Outlook Money notes that she financed the early stage from her own savings.
The money mattered less for its size than for what it represented. For the first time, she had been paid for her own work, by strangers who chose to buy what she made.

From there the range widened. The Better India and Outlook Money both report that she added chutneys and pickles, and SheThePeople mentions marmalades as well. Over time the business moved to an order-based model, with sweets made fresh and collected by customers, as News Bharati and Outlook Money describe.

sections.h: Building the Harbhajan's brand
paras: Her family helped give the business a name and a face. It was called Harbhajan's, and The Better India reports that her granddaughter helped with the branding and packaging.

The tagline was "Bachpan yaad aa jayegi", roughly "you will remember your childhood". The exact Hindi spelling varies slightly between reports, but The Better India, Outlook Money, SheThePeople and News Bharati all carry it. It is a well-chosen line: it sells the taste of a home kitchen, which is exactly what a grandmother's barfi offers and a factory product cannot.
Every account stresses that the business was a family effort. Her daughters handled sales and the market stall, while she kept to what she knew best, the cooking.

sections.h: When Anand Mahindra called her entrepreneur of the year
paras: For about four years Harbhajan's grew quietly. Then, in early January 2020, a video about her was shared on Twitter and Anand Mahindra, chairman of the Mahindra Group, was tagged. On 7 January 2020 he replied, as Republic World and News Bharati report.

His post said that the word start-up usually brings to mind young people in Silicon Valley or Bengaluru, and that from now on it should also include a 94-year-old woman who does not think it is too late to start one. "She's my entrepreneur of the year," he wrote, a line quoted by Republic World, Outlook Money and News Bharati.

The story spread widely. By then she was 94, which is why many headlines from 2020 say she started at 94. The fuller accounts, including The Better India, YourStory and SheThePeople, make clear she had begun about four years earlier, at around 90.

What makes the story useful is how ordinary the ingredients were. There was no investor, no shop lease and no new product to invent. There was one recipe she had made for decades, a daughter willing to help, a local market nearby and a willingness to sit at a stall and see whether strangers would pay.

lesson: It is never too late to be paid for what you are good at. Harbhajan Kaur did not learn a new skill at 90; she finally put a price on one she had practised all her life.

title: Famous People Who Failed Before They Succeeded: 15 True Stories (With Sources)
seo_title: Famous People Who Failed Before They Succeeded: 15 Stories
summary: 15 famous people who failed first: rejected manuscripts, lost jobs, bankrupt studios and missed selections, each with the real numbers and sources.
intro: In 1923 a young cartoonist in Kansas City watched his first studio go bankrupt. He left for California carrying little more than an unfinished reel of film. Five years later, his new studio released Steamboat Willie. His name was Walt Disney.

Stories like his get passed around so often that the details blur, and some popular versions are simply untrue. So we went back to the record. Every person below failed, was rejected or was pushed out before the work they are known for, and every number has been checked against reputable sources, listed at the end. Where sources disagree, we say so.

sections.h: 1. J.K. Rowling: Harry Potter was turned down by a string of publishers
paras: Before Harry Potter was a phenomenon, it was a manuscript that kept coming back. Voice of America reports that 12 publishers rejected the first book. Bloomsbury's founder Nigel Newton remembers a smaller number: he told the New Zealand Herald that "eight others turned J K Rowling down; ie, the whole lot." The exact count differs, but the pattern is the same: almost everyone said no.

Bloomsbury said yes partly because Newton's eight-year-old daughter, Alice, read a chapter and loved it. Rowling received an advance of £2,500, a figure both the New Zealand Herald and The Express Tribune report. The first book came out in 1997, and VOA notes that only 500 copies went to bookshops in Britain at first.

sections.h: 2. Walt Disney: his first studio went bankrupt in 1923
paras: Disney's first company, Laugh-O-Gram Films in Kansas City, made short cartoons. According to Britannica, a New York distributor cheated the young producers, and Disney was forced to file for bankruptcy in 1923. The US National Archives at Kansas City still holds the bankruptcy case file.

The Walt Disney Family Museum describes him in July 1923 struggling to pay for regular meals. When he left for California, he carried a reel of Alice's Wonderland, the last cartoon he made in Kansas City. In California he and his brother Roy started again, and in 1928 Steamboat Willie, starring Mickey Mouse, was, in Britannica's word, a sensation.

sections.h: 3. Oprah Winfrey: removed from the evening news after less than eight months
paras: In August 1976, WJZ-TV in Baltimore paired 22-year-old Oprah Winfrey with veteran anchor Jerry Turner on its evening news. Baltimore Magazine reports that less than eight months later, the station took her off the newscast hours before airtime and moved her to short morning news updates. Adweek's TVSpy dates the change to 1 April 1977.

It looked like a demotion, and she has described it as one. But in 1978 the station gave her a local talk show, People Are Talking, co-hosted with Richard Sher. That format suited her. In January 1984 she left Baltimore to host A.M. Chicago.

sections.h: 4. Michael Jordan: left off the varsity list as a 15-year-old
paras: The popular version says Michael Jordan was cut from his high school team. Sports Illustrated calls that a myth, but the real story is still useful. In 1978, at Laney High School in North Carolina, about 50 boys tried out for 15 varsity places. Jordan was about 5 feet 10 inches tall. His friend Leroy Smith, a 6-foot-7 sophomore, made the varsity; Jordan was placed on the junior varsity.

"It was embarrassing not making the team," Jordan later said, as quoted by Newsweek. He became the star of the JV side, scoring 40 points or more in several games, and Newsweek reports that he made the varsity as a junior. He mentioned the episode again in his 2009 Hall of Fame speech.

sections.h: 5. Steve Jobs: pushed out of the company he co-founded at 30
paras: After a boardroom power struggle, Steve Jobs left Apple in September 1985, as Britannica records. In his 2005 Stanford commencement speech, published by NPR, he put it bluntly: "I had just turned 30, and then I got fired," adding that he was "very publicly out."

In the next five years he started a company called NeXT and took over a small computer graphics studio called Pixar. In 1996 Apple bought NeXT, and in 1997 Jobs returned to lead the company. The years that followed brought the iMac, the iPod and the iPhone.

sections.h: 6. Jack Ma: 24 people applied to KFC, 23 were hired
paras: Jack Ma once applied for a job at KFC. CNBC reports Ma's account that 24 people applied and 23 were hired. He was the one who was not. Entrepreneur tells the same story, and both also describe him being turned down when he tried to join the police.

Ma also failed China's university entrance exam twice, according to both Entrepreneur and a CNN fact file, getting into Hangzhou Teachers College on his third try. He became an English teacher. In 1999 he and a group of co-founders started Alibaba out of an apartment in Hangzhou.

sections.h: 7. Soichiro Honda: his first piston rings were rejected by Toyota
paras: In the 1930s, Soichiro Honda set up a company to make piston rings and hoped to supply Toyota. His first order was rejected. The American Society of Mechanical Engineers says Honda refined the process after the rejection, and a history published by the Association for Asian Studies explains that his early rings failed Toyota's inspection.

Instead of quitting, he went back to study engineering part-time, as both the Association for Asian Studies and EBSCO's biography describe. His business later became a major parts supplier. After the war he started again: the Honda Technical Research Institute opened in 1946, and Honda Motor Company was incorporated in 1948.

sections.h: 8. Amitabh Bachchan: a failed company, heavy debt and a comeback
paras: In 1996, already one of India's biggest film stars, Amitabh Bachchan launched his own entertainment company, ABCL. It went badly wrong. Business Today reports that by 1999 the company had losses of ₹70.82 crore and debts of about ₹70 crore. WION, drawing on Bachchan's own interviews, puts the debt at around ₹90 crore and says he faced 55 legal cases. The figures differ, but both describe a serious crisis.

He went looking for work. Yash Chopra cast him in Mohabbatein (2000), and the same year he began hosting Kaun Banega Crorepati. Business Today says the show revived his fortunes, and endorsements helped him repay creditors. WION quotes him calling KBC his lifeline.

sections.h: 9. APJ Abdul Kalam: ninth in a selection with eight places
paras: As a young engineer, APJ Abdul Kalam dreamed of flying. In his memoir My Journey, he described going to Dehradun for the Indian Air Force selection. Millennium Post and OneIndia both report that he finished ninth out of 25 candidates when only eight places were available. "I had failed to realise my dream of becoming an air force pilot," he wrote.

He took a job as a senior scientific assistant at the Directorate of Technical Development and Production instead. Britannica records where that road led: he became project director of SLV-III, India's first home-built satellite launch vehicle, which put the Rohini satellite into orbit in 1980. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1997.

sections.h: 10. Narayana Murthy: his first company closed in less than a year
paras: Long before Infosys, Narayana Murthy started a company called Softronics in the 1970s to sell software to Indian businesses. In an oral history for the Computer History Museum, he said that within about seven or eight months he realised there was no domestic market, because there were hardly any computers in India. He closed it in less than a year. YourStory also reports that Softronics shut down for lack of demand.

He named his mistake as "not ascertaining the size of the market" and went to work at Patni Computer Systems to learn how companies ran. In 1981 he and his colleagues founded Infosys. Business Standard and Business Today both report that it started with a ₹10,000 loan from his wife, Sudha Murty.

sections.h: 11. Sachin Tendulkar: told to give up fast bowling at 14
paras: In 1987, a 14-year-old Sachin Tendulkar went to the MRF Pace Foundation in Chennai wanting to be a fast bowler. Its coaching director was the Australian great Dennis Lillee. As The Week and cricket.com.au both report, Lillee advised him to forget bowling and concentrate on batting. Tendulkar recalled Lillee's words: "I think this young lad should go out and bat, forget about bowling."

It was the end of one dream, and the start of another. On 16 March 2012, against Bangladesh in Mirpur, Tendulkar became the first player to score 100 international centuries, as The Irish Times and the BCCI reported at the time.

sections.h: 12. Stephen King: his first novel's opening pages went in the bin
paras: Stephen King was a schoolteacher living in a trailer when he gave up on a story about a teenage girl and threw the pages away. His wife, Tabitha, took them out, read them and told him to keep going. The novel was Carrie, and Kirkus describes it facing rejection after rejection before Doubleday paid a $2,500 advance.

Carrie was published in April 1974. The sale of its paperback rights let King leave teaching and write full-time. The full story: https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/stephen-king-carrie-first-novel-in-the-trash-story/

sections.h: 13. James Dyson: 5,127 prototypes before one worked
paras: James Dyson's bagless vacuum did not work the first time, or the hundredth. Both Gizmodo and Entrepreneur report that he built 5,127 prototypes before he got it right. Large manufacturers then turned the design down, so he licensed it in Japan and later made it himself.

His first Dyson-made model, the DC01, arrived in 1993. Dyson told Gizmodo that the process, not the final prototype, was what made the struggle worthwhile. Read more: https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/james-dyson-5127-prototypes/

sections.h: 14. Colonel Sanders: starting over at 65 on $105 a month
paras: In 1955, a new highway bypass took traffic away from Harland Sanders's restaurant and motel in Corbin, Kentucky. He sold up. The Scribner Encyclopedia of American Lives describes him as 65 years old and living on $105 a month from Social Security.

He took his chicken recipe on the road and signed up restaurants to use it. By 1964 there were more than 600 franchised outlets, and he sold most of the business for $2 million, as Britannica records. The full story: https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/colonel-sanders-started-over-at-65-kfc-story/

sections.h: 15. Manoj Kumar Sharma: failed Class 12, cleared UPSC on his fourth attempt
paras: Manoj Kumar Sharma, from Morena in Madhya Pradesh, failed his Class 12 board exams. Outlook and DNA both report that while preparing for the civil services in Delhi he drove a tempo, worked in a library and walked dogs to pay for coaching and books.

He failed the UPSC exam more than once and cleared it on his fourth attempt, joining the Indian Police Service. His life inspired the 2023 film 12th Fail. Read his story: https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/manoj-kumar-sharma-12th-fail-ips-upsc-fourth-attempt/

lesson: In almost every one of these stories, the rejection was a verdict on one attempt, not on the person. What they shared was not talent alone but the willingness to change the plan, learn from the no, and try again.
check: Which rejection in your own life have you treated as a final verdict, when it may only have been feedback on one attempt?
Like Murthy and Tendulkar, is there a different version of your goal that fits your real strengths better?
faq: Which famous people failed before they succeeded?

Well-documented examples include J.K. Rowling, whose first Harry Potter book was rejected by several publishers; Walt Disney, whose first studio went bankrupt in 1923; Steve Jobs, who was pushed out of Apple in 1985; and APJ Abdul Kalam, who missed selection as an Indian Air Force pilot by one place.
How many publishers rejected Harry Potter?

Voice of America and many other reports say 12 publishers rejected the first book. Bloomsbury founder Nigel Newton has recalled the number as eight. Either way, Bloomsbury accepted it and paid Rowling a £2,500 advance.
Was Michael Jordan really cut from his high school team?

Not exactly. In 1978 he was left off the varsity team at Laney High School as a sophomore and placed on the junior varsity, where he starred. Sports Illustrated calls the 'cut' story a myth, though Jordan himself has spoken of it as being cut.
Did Jack Ma really get rejected by KFC?
Yes, by his own account. Ma has said that 24 people applied for a job at KFC and 23 were hired; he was the only one turned down. CNBC and Entrepreneur both report the story.
Which famous Indians failed before success?

APJ Abdul Kalam finished ninth when the Air Force had eight places, Narayana Murthy closed his first company Softronics within a year, Amitabh Bachchan rebuilt after his company ABCL ran into heavy debt, and Manoj Kumar Sharma failed Class 12 before clearing UPSC.
