title: USC Film School Said No to Steven Spielberg. Twice. He Finished His Degree at 55
seo_title: Spielberg Rejected by USC Film School Twice: The True Story
summary: Steven Spielberg was rejected twice by USC's film school. He kept filming, made Jaws, and finished his college degree in 2002 at the age of 55.
intro: The most famous film director of his generation could not get into film school. The University of Southern California's School of Cinema turned Steven Spielberg down, and then turned him down again.

He did not wait for a second opinion. He went to a state college nearby, kept making films, signed a studio contract before he graduated, and was directing Jaws before he turned 30. Then, in 2002, at 55, he quietly went back and finished his degree.

sections.h: Was Steven Spielberg really rejected by USC film school?
paras: Yes. CNN's fact file on Spielberg states that the USC School of Cinema rejected him twice, and Business Insider describes the rejection as happening "not once, but twice." UPI's 2002 report on his graduation and ET Online also record that USC's film school turned down his application.

That rejection is easy to misread with hindsight. USC was, and is, one of the most selective film schools in America. A no from them did not mean he had no talent; it meant one admissions process, on one day, did not pick him.

sections.h: What had he done before film school?
paras: Plenty. Born in Cincinnati, Ohio, on 18 December 1946, Spielberg filmed family events with an 8 mm camera as a child, according to CNN. Britannica notes that as a teenager he made Escape to Nowhere (1962), a 40-minute war film that won first prize at a film festival.

In 1964, at 17, he released Firelight, a feature-length science-fiction film. CNN and Britannica both list it as his first feature. He had made a full-length film before he finished school. In other words, he already had a body of work when the top film school said no. The work was real; the rejection was an opinion.

sections.h: Where did Spielberg go instead, and how did Amblin' get him into Hollywood?
paras: He enrolled at California State College, Long Beach (now California State University, Long Beach), starting in 1965, according to UPI. Britannica and ET Online confirm he studied there after the USC rejection.

In 1968 he made Amblin', a short film about two hitchhikers. Britannica reports that a Universal executive saw it and offered him a contract, and /Film describes Universal signing him straight away after seeing it.

He left college to take the job. UPI says he left school after three years to pursue his career; Hello! magazine dates his departure to 1968. Years later, in 1984, he named his production company Amblin Entertainment after that same student short, as CNN notes.

sections.h: What happened after he left college?
paras: At Universal he started in television, directing episodes of shows such as Columbo, according to Britannica. His TV film Duel premiered on 13 November 1971 (CNN; Britannica). The Sugarland Express followed in 1974.

Then came Jaws in 1975. Britannica calls it one of the highest-grossing films ever made, and CNN notes it is considered the first summer blockbuster, taking $60 million in its first month. The student USC turned down was now the director every studio wanted.

The run continued: Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977), E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982) and Jurassic Park (1993). For Schindler's List he won the Oscars for Best Picture and Best Director, and he won Best Director again for Saving Private Ryan, as both CNN and TODAY record.

sections.h: Why did Spielberg go back to finish his degree at 55?
paras: He did not need the paper for his career. Still, in 2001 he re-enrolled at Cal State Long Beach and completed the requirements, according to UPI and Hello!. In May 2002 he received a bachelor's degree in film and electronic arts, at 55.

UPI quoted him saying the degree came "33 years after finishing my principal education." It is the quiet end of the story: the man the film school would not admit still chose to finish what he had started, on his own terms.

sections.h: What can you learn from Spielberg's rejection? (Myth vs fact)
paras: First, separate the verdict from the work. USC's decision told Spielberg nothing about the films he had already made or the ones he would make next. He kept his attention on the camera, not on the letter.

Second, the second-choice path can be the faster one. At Long Beach he was free to keep shooting, and it was a short film made outside any famous programme that put him in front of a studio executive.

Third, unfinished things can still be finished later. Going back at 55 was not about proving anything to USC. It was a choice to complete his own story. If a door has closed on you, the useful question is not "Why did they say no?" but "What can I make this week anyway?"

Fourth, a no is information about fit, not about worth. His road ran through a state college, a short film and a studio television department, and it still led to some of the most-watched films ever made.
Myth: Spielberg dropped out because he failed at college. Fact: he left because a studio offered him a contract after seeing his short film, and he came back decades later to finish.
Myth: getting rejected by a top school means you are not good enough. Fact: Spielberg had already made a feature-length film when USC said no. One panel's decision did not measure what he could do.

timeline: Born in Cincinnati, Ohio, on 18 December
Releases Firelight, his first feature-length film, at 17
Starts at California State College, Long Beach, after USC's film school rejects him
Makes the short film Amblin'; Universal offers him a contract and he leaves college
His TV film Duel premieres
Jaws becomes one of the highest-grossing films ever made
Wins the Oscars for Best Picture and Best Director for Schindler's List
Graduates from Cal State Long Beach at 55
lesson: A rejection is one opinion, not your future. Keep making the work, and let the work answer.
check: Which "no" are you still treating as a final verdict?
What is one small piece of work you could make this week that answers it?
faq: How many times was Steven Spielberg rejected by USC?
Two times. CNN's Spielberg fact file and Business Insider both report that USC's School of Cinema rejected him twice.
Did Steven Spielberg finish college?
Yes. He left California State College, Long Beach, in 1968 for a Universal contract, re-enrolled in 2001 and received a bachelor's degree in film and electronic arts in 2002, at 55 (UPI; Britannica).
What film got Steven Spielberg his first Hollywood contract?
Amblin' (1968), a short film about two hitchhikers. A Universal executive saw it and offered him a contract (Britannica; /Film).
Which college did Steven Spielberg go to?
California State College, Long Beach, now California State University, Long Beach, from 1965 (UPI; Britannica).
What is the lesson from Spielberg's USC rejection?
A rejection reflects one panel's decision at one moment. Spielberg already had a feature film behind him, kept making films at a state college, and was directing Jaws within a decade.

title: Jensen Huang Cleaned Toilets as a Boy. Then He Built the First $5 Trillion Company
seo_title: Jensen Huang Cleaned Toilets: From Denny's to Nvidia
summary: As a boy Jensen Huang cleaned school bathrooms; as a teen he washed dishes at Denny's. At 30 he co-founded Nvidia, the first company worth $5 trillion.
intro: Long before he ran the world's most valuable chip company, Jensen Huang had a mop. As a boy at a boarding school in Kentucky, he was given the job of cleaning the bathrooms. "You can't unsee that kind of stuff," he later told an audience, as reported by Fortune. "But that was my job and so I did it delightfully."

A few years later he was washing dishes at Denny's. At 30, he sat in a Denny's booth with two friends and planned a company called Nvidia. On 29 October 2025, Nvidia became the first company in history worth five trillion dollars (AP; Global News). This is how the boy with the bathroom job got there, and what most retellings of the story leave out.

sections.h: Did Jensen Huang really clean toilets as a child?
paras: Yes, and he has told the story himself many times. Huang was born in Taiwan in 1963 and was sent to the United States as a young boy; Global News notes he was raised in the US from age nine. He and his older brother were enrolled at the Oneida Baptist Institute, a small boarding school in rural Kentucky.

Every student there had a chore. According to Fortune, the older students got heavier work such as farm jobs, and the youngest boy on campus was handed the bathrooms. Fortune's December 2025 account of his interview with Joe Rogan describes him as, in effect, the school's janitor.
What stands out is how he describes it. Not as a hardship story, but as a job he chose to do well. "That was my job and so I did it delightfully," he said.

sections.h: What did Jensen Huang do at Denny's?
paras: As a teenager, Huang took a job at Denny's, the American diner chain. Fortune reports that he started as a dishwasher, became a busboy and later a waiter. A CNBC report adds that the busboy job meant clearing tables, washing dishes and, yes, cleaning toilets again.

He has said he wanted to be the best at each of those jobs. In a March 2024 interview at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, quoted by CNBC and by Fortune, he put it this way: "To me, no task is beneath me because, remember, I used to be a dishwasher [and] I used to clean toilets."
He went on to study electrical engineering and spent years working as a chip designer in Silicon Valley before he started a company of his own.

sections.h: How was Nvidia started in a Denny's booth?
paras: In 1993, Huang met two engineers he knew from work, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, at a Denny's. Over coffee they talked through what would become the core idea of Nvidia: chips that make computer graphics much faster. Fortune and CNBC both describe the plan being sketched in a Denny's booth, and Global News confirms the company was founded in 1993.
Huang was 30 years old. The diner where he once cleared tables became the place where he planned his company, a detail he clearly enjoys repeating.

sections.h: Was it a straight line to the top?
paras: No. Fortune's 2025 account recalls that when Nvidia introduced its CUDA software platform in 2006, its chips cost more to make, revenue did not move, and the company's market value fell from about $12 billion to roughly $2 to $3 billion. Huang kept investing in it anyway.

That long bet later became the base for the boom in artificial intelligence, where Nvidia's chips are used to train and run AI models. The company passed $3 trillion in value in June 2024, then $4 trillion, and on 29 October 2025 it closed at a market value of about $5.03 trillion, making it the first company ever to cross $5 trillion (Global News; AP via The Washington Times).

sections.h: Myth vs fact: what the viral posts get wrong
paras: Myth: he cleaned toilets at Denny's and then founded Nvidia the next year. Fact: the bathroom job came first, as a child at boarding school, and Denny's came in his teens. Nvidia was founded more than a decade later, after an engineering degree and years of work as a chip designer.
Myth: he got lucky with AI. Fact: Nvidia spent years investing in tools like CUDA while its value fell, long before AI made those tools famous.
The real lesson is less about luck and more about how he treated the small jobs: as work worth doing well.

sections.h: What can you learn from Jensen Huang's first jobs?
paras: The useful part of this story is not the fortune. It is the attitude Huang brought to work that most people would rush through. He describes cleaning bathrooms and washing dishes as jobs he wanted to do well, and he credits those years for how he leads today: he told the Stanford audience that no task is beneath him.

If you are in a first job, a side job or a role that feels too small, that is the borrowed hindsight. The skills you practise there, showing up, finishing the job properly and learning from the people around you, are the same ones you will need when the work gets bigger. Nobody can promise you a $5 trillion company. But doing small work well is something you can start today.

29 October: Nvidia becomes the first company worth $5 trillion
lesson: Do the small job well. It is training for the big one, and the habits you build there come with you.
check: Which part of your current job do you do half-heartedly because it feels small?
What would doing it "delightfully" for one week look like?

Yes. As a boy at a Kentucky boarding school he was given the job of cleaning the bathrooms, and as a teenager at Denny's his work included washing dishes and cleaning toilets, as reported by Fortune and CNBC.
What job did Jensen Huang have at Denny's?
He started as a dishwasher, then worked as a busboy and later as a waiter, according to Fortune.
Was Nvidia founded at a Denny's?
The idea was planned in a Denny's booth in 1993, where Huang met his co-founders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem over coffee, as reported by Fortune and CNBC.
How old was Jensen Huang when he started Nvidia?
He was 30. He was born in early 1963 and Nvidia was founded in 1993.
When did Nvidia become a $5 trillion company?
On 29 October 2025, Nvidia became the first company ever worth $5 trillion, closing at a market value of about $5.03 trillion (AP; Global News).

title: Late Bloomers: 15 People Who Found Success After 50
seo_title: Late Bloomers: 15 People Who Found Success After 50
summary: 15 true late bloomers who found success after 50: a milkshake-mixer salesman, a 65-year-old author, a 96-year-old student and more, with sources.
intro: In April 1955 a 52-year-old salesman who had spent decades selling paper cups and milkshake mixers opened a hamburger restaurant in Des Plaines, Illinois. His name was Ray Kroc, and that restaurant was the first McDonald's he franchised.

Kroc is not unusual. Below are 15 people, from America and Britain to Kenya and India, who found the work they are remembered for after the age of 50, some of them after 90. We checked every age, year and number against at least two reputable sources, listed at the end, and left out popular versions that we could not confirm.

sections.h: 1. Ray Kroc: a milkshake-mixer salesman who opened his first McDonald's at 52
paras: For most of his working life, Ray Kroc was a travelling salesman. TIME and Biography.com both describe him selling paper cups and then Multi-Mixer milkshake machines to restaurants and soda fountains.

In 1954 he visited the McDonald brothers' busy hamburger restaurant in San Bernardino, California. He came away with a deal to franchise their system, and on 15 April 1955, aged 52, he opened his own McDonald's in Des Plaines, Illinois. In 1961 he bought the business from the brothers outright.

sections.h: 2. Colonel Harland Sanders: lost his customers in his 60s, then sold the recipe on the road
paras: Harland Sanders had run a roadside restaurant in Corbin, Kentucky, for about 25 years. His first franchise, run by Pete Harman near Salt Lake City, opened in 1952, when Sanders was already in his early sixties. Then, in the mid-1950s, a new highway route took the traffic away from his corner of Corbin.

At 65 he sold the cafe and took to the road, cooking his chicken for restaurant owners and signing up franchisees one by one. By 1964 there were more than 600 outlets and he sold the company. We tell the full story, with its myths and facts, in https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/colonel-sanders-started-over-at-65-kfc-story/ .

sections.h: 3. Julia Child: first cookbook at 49, a hit TV show at 50
paras: Julia Child, born in 1912, did not train as a cook until she moved to Paris with her husband in 1948 and enrolled at the Cordon Bleu. Encyclopedia.com and Biography.com both date her first book, Mastering the Art of French Cooking, to 1961, when she was 49.

On 11 February 1963, at 50, she premiered The French Chef on Boston's WGBH. The show won her a Peabody Award in 1965 and an Emmy in 1966, and made French cooking feel possible in ordinary American kitchens.

sections.h: 4. Laura Ingalls Wilder: her first Little House book came out when she was 65
paras: Laura Ingalls Wilder grew up on the American frontier, and in her 40s she began writing columns for small farming publications in Missouri, according to PBS American Masters.
Her first book, Little House in the Big Woods, was published in 1932, when she was 65. PBS and Colorado State University both give the same year and age.

sections.h: 5. Frank McCourt: a retired schoolteacher who won the Pulitzer at 66
paras: Frank McCourt spent most of his career teaching English in New York City public high schools, including Stuyvesant High School, according to EBSCO's biography. He had grown up poor in Limerick, Ireland.
Angela's Ashes, his memoir of that childhood, came out in 1996, when he was 66. NPR reports that it stayed on the best-seller lists for two years, and in 1997 it won the Pulitzer Prize for biography.

sections.h: 6. Peter Mark Roget: published his famous thesaurus at 73
paras: Peter Mark Roget was a London physician. Britannica says he began sorting words by meaning in 1805. Cambridge University Press notes that he thought about the work for nearly fifty years.
Only after he retired did he turn the list into a book. The first edition of Roget's Thesaurus appeared in 1852, when he was 73, and it has never gone out of print.

sections.h: 7. Grandma Moses: began painting in her late 70s, first solo show at 80
paras: Anna Mary Robertson Moses, born in 1860, spent most of her life working on farms. When arthritis made embroidery too painful, she took up painting in her late 70s, as both the Smithsonian American Art Museum and CBS News report.

In 1940, at 80, she had her first solo exhibition, 'What a Farmwife Painted', at Galerie St. Etienne in New York. Smithsonian magazine says she went on to make more than 1,500 paintings, and the press nicknamed her Grandma Moses.

sections.h: 8. Harry Bernstein: started writing at 93, published at 96
paras: Harry Bernstein grew up in Stockport, a mill town near Manchester, England, and spent his working life in New York as a script reader for film studios and an editor of trade magazines. Feeling lonely after almost seven decades of marriage, he began writing about his childhood at 93.
The result, The Invisible Wall, was published in 2007, when he was 96. CBS News and the Associated Press both report his age, and AP adds that three more books followed.

sections.h: 9. Nola Ochs: a college degree at 95
paras: Nola Ochs, from Kansas, began taking occasional college classes in the 1970s, a few at a time, according to The Spokesman-Review.

In May 2007, at 95, she graduated from Fort Hays State University with a degree in general studies and history, in the same ceremony as her granddaughter Alexandra. CBS News reports that Guinness World Records recognised her at the time as the world's oldest college graduate.

sections.h: 10. Kimani Maruge: started primary school at 84
paras: On 12 January 2004, Kimani Ng'ang'a Maruge walked into Kapkenduiyo Primary School in Eldoret, Kenya, in a school uniform and joined Standard One, the first year of primary school. He was 84.

Guinness World Records lists him as the oldest person to begin primary school, and Kenya's Standard newspaper notes that his story later became the film The First Grader. When Google marked the anniversary with a doodle, the message was simple: it is never too late to learn.

sections.h: 11. Chandro Tomar, 'Shooter Dadi': picked up a pistol at 65
paras: In the late 1990s, Chandro Tomar went with her granddaughter Shefali to the Johri Rifle Club range in her village in Uttar Pradesh. Al Jazeera and The Better India both say she was 65 at the time. She lifted a pistol for the first time and hit the bull's eye, and the coach told her to keep going.

Her family was not keen at first, and The Better India reports that she practised quietly until they came round. She went on to win veterans' shooting championships, became known across India as 'Shooter Dadi' and coached several members of her own family.

sections.h: 12. Man Kaur: started running at 93, won world masters gold at 101
paras: Man Kaur took up athletics at 93, when her son Gurdev Singh, himself a masters athlete, suggested she join him at competitions. SBS News and YourStory both report the age and the son's role.

At the 2016 Americas Masters Games in Vancouver she won the 100 metres in her age group, and at 101 she won the 100 metres again at the 2017 World Masters Games in Auckland. SBS says it was her 17th athletics gold.

sections.h: 13. Karthyayani Amma: topped a literacy exam at 96
paras: In 2018, Karthyayani Amma from Haripad in Kerala's Alappuzha district sat Aksharalaksham, the Kerala literacy mission's test at fourth-standard level, covering reading, writing and maths. She was 96, the oldest of 43,330 candidates.
She scored 98 out of 100, full marks in reading and maths, as The Week and Onmanorama both report. Her next goal, she said, was the tenth-standard equivalency exam at 100.

sections.h: 14. Mastanamma: a YouTube cooking star at 106
paras: Karre Mastanamma had cooked for her family in Gudivada village, Andhra Pradesh, for most of a century. In 2016 her grandson Laxman and his friend Srinath Reddy started a YouTube channel, Country Foods, to film her cooking outdoors in the village.

Her 'watermelon chicken' video went viral, and by 2017, at 106, she had hundreds of thousands of subscribers. Tubefilter called her the oldest creator on YouTube, and Onmanorama says she had been cooking for close to 95 years.

sections.h: 15. Harbhajan Kaur: started a sweets business at about 90
paras: At around 90, Harbhajan Kaur told her daughter that she had never earned money of her own. So she made besan barfi at home in Chandigarh and took it to a local organic market. On the first day she earned ₹2,000.

Harbhajan's grew by word of mouth into chutneys and pickles, and in January 2020 Anand Mahindra called the 94-year-old his entrepreneur of the year. Her full story is at https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/harbhajan-kaur-besan-barfi-chandigarh-started-business-in-her-nineties/ .

sections.h: What do late bloomers have in common?
paras: Almost none of them started from zero. Kroc knew restaurants from years of selling to them. Child had cooked for more than a decade before her book. McCourt had spent a lifetime remembering his childhood before he wrote it down. Late success usually rests on everything a person learned earlier, even when it looked like a detour.

Many also started small and stayed curious: one class at a time for Nola Ochs, one market stall for Harbhajan Kaur, one pistol shot for Chandro Tomar. If 50 still feels late, remember that Falguni Nayar founded Nykaa at 49 (https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/falguni-nayar-nykaa-started-at-49-story/ ) and Vera Wang opened her bridal salon at 40 (https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/vera-wang-started-her-company-at-40-story/ ).

lesson: Age changed how these people started, not whether they could. Each of them used what a long life had already taught them, began with one small step, and kept going.
check: What have you been telling yourself you are 'too old' to start, and what would the smallest first step look like this week?
Which skill from your earlier years, like Kroc's selling or Child's cooking, could become the base for something new?
faq: Who are famous late bloomers who succeeded after 50?

Well-documented examples include Ray Kroc, who opened his first McDonald's franchise at 52; Julia Child, whose TV show The French Chef began when she was 50; Laura Ingalls Wilder, who published her first book at 65; and Grandma Moses, who had her first solo exhibition at 80.
Is it too late to start something new after 50?

The people in this list suggest not. Frank McCourt won a Pulitzer Prize for a first book published at 66, Peter Mark Roget published his thesaurus at 73, and Man Kaur took up running at 93. What they shared was a small first step and years of earlier experience.
How old was Ray Kroc when he started McDonald's?

Ray Kroc was 52 when he opened his first McDonald's franchise in Des Plaines, Illinois, on 15 April 1955. He had spent years selling paper cups and Multi-Mixer milkshake machines, and he bought the business from the McDonald brothers in 1961.
Did Colonel Sanders start KFC at 65?

Not exactly. The first Kentucky Fried Chicken franchise opened in 1952, when Sanders was in his early sixties. At 65, after a new highway took traffic away from his cafe in Corbin, Kentucky, he sold the cafe and began selling franchises full-time.
Who is the oldest person to start primary school?
Guinness World Records lists Kimani Maruge of Kenya, who enrolled in Standard One at Kapkenduiyo Primary School in Eldoret on 12 January 2004, at the age of 84.

title: How Infosys Started With ₹10,000 From Sudha Murty (1981)
seo_title: How Infosys Started With ₹10,000 From Sudha Murty in 1981
summary: In 1981 Sudha Murty had ₹10,250 in savings. She kept ₹250 and gave the rest to Narayana Murthy. That money helped start Infosys. The true story, with sources.
intro: In 1981, Sudha Murty checked her savings. She had ₹10,250. She kept ₹250 for herself and handed the other ₹10,000 to her husband, N. R. Narayana Murthy, so that he and six fellow engineers could start a software company. That company was Infosys.

Today Infosys employs more than three lakh people and reports annual revenue of about US$20 billion. But the first office was a home in Pune, the first years were slow, and the person who funded it called her ₹10,000 "a risk". Here is how it really happened, and what most retellings leave out.

sections.h: Who gave Narayana Murthy the money to start Infosys?
paras: Sudha Murty did. Speaking at the India Today Conclave in March 2024, she said: "I had Rs 10,250 in my savings. I saved Rs 250 for myself and gave him the rest." Business Standard and Deccan Herald both carried her words, and Business Today reported the same figures.

She was not a passive bystander. She was an engineer herself, working at TELCO (now Tata Motors) at the time, according to The Week. When her husband said in 1981 that he wanted to start a software company, she pointed out that they both already had well-paying jobs. He promised he would not go ahead without her agreement, and warned her to expect a bumpy ride for about three years.

sections.h: Why did Sudha Murty call it a risk?
paras: Because it was. Narayana Murthy had tried a business before. In her words, as reported by Business Standard and Deccan Herald, "he failed in his earlier venture Softronics, so I took a risk."

This is the part of the story that gets lost. Infosys was not a sure thing backed by a confident investor. It was a second attempt by someone whose first attempt had not worked, funded by the savings of a person who had doubts and said yes anyway. At the same event, Narayana Murthy said his wife was "much more qualified than all the founders", Business Today reported.

sections.h: Who were the seven founders of Infosys?
paras: Infosys's own history page says the company was founded in Pune in 1981 by N. R. Narayana Murthy and six engineers. Mint lists all seven: Narayana Murthy, Nandan Nilekani, N. S. Raghavan, S. Gopalakrishnan (Kris), S. D. Shibulal, K. Dinesh and Ashok Arora.

The Week and Oneindia both report that the founding took place in July 1981 and that the first headquarters was the Murthys' home. "The first headquarters was our house in Pune, near Deccan Gymkhana," Sudha Murty recalled at the company's 40th anniversary. In 1983, the company moved its base to Bangalore, according to Infosys's own history.

sections.h: What were the hardest parts of the early years?
paras: Not the coding. The paperwork. In India in the early 1980s, a small private software firm needed government permission for almost everything. The Week and Oneindia both report that importing a computer took multiple trips to Delhi and that getting a telephone connection took several years. "People were very sceptical about any software developed in India," Sudha Murty said, and "getting the first customer was very challenging."

Money was tight too. Once, when a client's payment was late and the company needed around ₹20,000 to pay salaries, Sudha Murty went to a bank and offered her jewellery as security, both outlets report. Her husband's rule, she said, was that "we should be able to pay our employees on time."

The first client was Data Basics Corporation in New York, according to Infosys and The Week. Proving that world-class software could be written in India, for a customer on the other side of the world, was the whole bet.

sections.h: How did Infosys grow from a Pune home to a global company?
paras: Slowly, then quickly. In 1993 Infosys went public in India and introduced an employee stock option plan, which Mint describes as the first in India's IT sector, so that ordinary engineers could own a piece of what they were building. On 11 March 1999, its shares began trading on Nasdaq; its annual report filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission called it "the first Indian-registered company to be listed on a stock exchange in the United States". The same year, Infosys says, its revenue crossed US$100 million.

If the climb sounds familiar, it is a pattern we see again and again on this site: Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw started Biocon in a garage with ₹10,000 (https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/kiran-mazumdar-shaw-biocon-garage-10000-rupees-story/), and Flipkart began as two friends packing books in a small flat (https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/flipkart-story-two-friends-small-flat-online-bookstore/). The starting amount is small in every one of these stories. What is large is the number of years the founders kept going.

sections.h: Myth vs fact: did ₹10,000 build Infosys?
paras: Myth: a ₹10,000 loan turned into a giant company. Fact: the ₹10,000 got seven engineers through the door. What built Infosys was years of slow, unglamorous work: chasing permissions, waiting for a phone line, finding a first client abroad and paying salaries on time when money was late. Sudha Murty herself framed it as a responsibility rather than a windfall: "My life drastically changed when he started Infosys, it was a responsibility, a commitment," she said in 2024.

And the most quoted detail is the one worth remembering: she kept ₹250 back. The first investor in Infosys was not reckless. She took a measured risk on someone who had already failed once, and kept a little aside for herself. That is a very different lesson from "bet everything", and a far more useful one. For more people who failed first and won later, read our list of famous people who failed before they succeeded (https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/famous-people-who-failed-before-they-succeeded/).

lesson: A first failure is not a verdict. Infosys was a second attempt, funded by someone who had doubts, kept ₹250 back, and said yes anyway.
check: Is there an idea you dropped after one failure that deserves a second, smaller, more careful attempt?
Who in your life has backed you before you had proof, and have you told them?
faq: How much money did Sudha Murty give to start Infosys?
₹10,000. She has said she had ₹10,250 in savings in 1981, kept ₹250 for herself and gave the rest to N. R. Narayana Murthy, as reported by Business Standard, Deccan Herald and Business Today.
When and where was Infosys founded?

In 1981 in Pune. Infosys's own history says it was founded in Pune that year by Narayana Murthy and six engineers; The Week and Oneindia report the first headquarters was the Murthys' home near Deccan Gymkhana. It moved its base to Bangalore in 1983.
Who are the 7 founders of Infosys?
N. R. Narayana Murthy, Nandan Nilekani, N. S. Raghavan, S. Gopalakrishnan, S. D. Shibulal, K. Dinesh and Ashok Arora, according to Mint and Infosys's history page.
What was Infosys's first client?
Data Basics Corporation in New York, according to Infosys's own history and The Week.
When did Infosys list on Nasdaq?
On 11 March 1999. Its filing with the US SEC described it as the first Indian-registered company to list on a US stock exchange. It had gone public in India in 1993.

title: Alex Honnold: 3,000 Feet, No Rope, and the Year of Practice Nobody Saw
seo_title: Alex Honnold Free Solo of El Capitan: How He Prepared
summary: Alex Honnold climbed El Capitan with no rope in 3 h 56 min in 2017. His first try ended in under an hour. Here is the practice behind it.
intro: At 5:32 in the morning on 3 June 2017, Alex Honnold started up a granite wall in Yosemite National Park with no rope, no harness and no partner. At 9:28 he stood on top. Three hours and fifty-six minutes for a wall of nearly 3,000 feet: the first free solo of El Capitan, a climb Alpinist magazine called the greatest free solo of all time.

What looks like pure nerve was something else. His first attempt, the previous November, ended in less than an hour. What happened between that turn-back and the summit is the useful part of the story.

sections.h: Who is Alex Honnold?
paras: Alex Honnold was born on 17 August 1985 in Sacramento, California. He started climbing in a gym as a child and was soon climbing several times a week. He enrolled at the University of California, Berkeley, to study civil engineering, then left to climb full time.

For years he lived out of a van, driving between climbing areas. In 2008 he made his name with two ropeless climbs that shocked the climbing world: Moonlight Buttress in Utah and the Regular Northwest Face of Half Dome in Yosemite. Both were huge walls that very few people would attempt even with a rope.

sections.h: What is a free solo, and what makes El Capitan different?
paras: In a free solo the climber uses only hands and feet, with no rope, harness or protective gear. Every move has to be right. Most climbers, even world-class ones, never free solo anything big.

El Capitan is a different scale. National Geographic describes the wall as nearly 3,000 feet tall, more than half a mile of granite; Guinness World Records lists it at 2,900 feet. Honnold chose Freerider, a 30-pitch route that includes sections of smooth, glassy rock. He told National Geographic that parts of it felt "like walking up glass." He had been thinking about a ropeless ascent for years before he committed to it.

sections.h: Did Alex Honnold fail his first attempt on El Capitan?
paras: Yes, in a sense. In November 2016 he set off on his first attempt and backed off in less than an hour because conditions did not feel right, according to National Geographic. He climbed down, went home and kept training.

That decision matters more than it first appears. The person famous for having no fear was the same person who turned around when something felt wrong. Turning back was not the end of the plan. It was part of it.

sections.h: How did Alex Honnold prepare for the El Capitan free solo?
paras: National Geographic reports that he trained for more than a year, on rock in the United States, China, Europe and Morocco. He rehearsed the hand and foot sequences of the hardest pitches again and again with a rope, until each move was automatic. He did long fingertip hangs and pull-ups on a training rig bolted inside his van, and he logged his workouts in a journal.

Over Memorial Day weekend in 2017, a week before the real climb, he made a practice run of Freerider with his friend Tommy Caldwell, roped up, in just over five and a half hours. Days before the ascent he rappelled down the route to check that the chalk marks he relied on had survived a rainstorm. By the morning of 3 June, nothing on the wall was new to him.

sections.h: What happened on 3 June 2017?
paras: He started at 5:32 a.m. and topped out at 9:28 a.m. Pacific time, 3 hours and 56 minutes for the whole wall, as reported by NPR and National Geographic. Guinness World Records lists it as the first free solo climb of El Capitan. On Facebook that day he wrote that he was "so stoked to realize a life dream," NPR reported.

The climb was filmed by Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi. Their documentary, Free Solo, won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature in February 2019, which is how millions of people who have never touched a climbing wall first heard his name.

sections.h: What did Alex Honnold do after El Capitan?
paras: He kept using the same method: rehearse, fail, adjust, try again. In June 2018, just a year after the free solo, he and Tommy Caldwell climbed The Nose, the most famous route on El Capitan, with ropes this time, in 1 hour, 58 minutes and 7 seconds. Caldwell wrote in the American Alpine Journal that they managed it after 11 previous attempts. It was the first time anyone had climbed the route in under two hours.

Away from the rock, he set up the Honnold Foundation in 2012, years before he was famous outside climbing. It focuses on solar energy, helping communities get access to clean power. The climber people call fearless spends much of his time on something slow and patient.

sections.h: Myth vs fact: was it fearlessness?
paras: Myth: Honnold climbed El Capitan because he simply does not feel fear. Fact: the record shows a man who abandoned his first attempt in under an hour, spent more than a year rehearsing, wrote down his training and checked his chalk marks after rain. National Geographic quotes him saying fear was "only hindering my performance," so he set it aside. He did that after the preparation, not instead of it.

That is the borrowed hindsight. What strangers call fearless is usually practice they never saw. If something big scares you, the useful question is not "am I brave enough?" but "what can I rehearse until it is ordinary?" And turning back on a bad day is not failure. It can be the first step of the plan that works.

title: Ray Kroc Was 52: How a Milkshake-Mixer Salesman Built McDonald's
seo_title: Ray Kroc at 52: How a Mixer Salesman Built McDonald's
summary: Ray Kroc was a 52-year-old milkshake-mixer salesman when he met the McDonald brothers in 1954. How a late start built 43,000+ restaurants.
intro: In 1954, a travelling salesman drove to a busy hamburger stand in San Bernardino, California. He sold milkshake mixers, and this one small restaurant was running several of his machines at once. He wanted to see why. He was 52 years old.

His name was Ray Kroc. He did not invent McDonald's, and he did not start young. But the next three decades turned a single California drive-in into a system with about 7,500 restaurants by the time he died in 1984. At the end of 2024 McDonald's reported 43,477 restaurants in more than 100 countries. This is how a late start, built on 30 years of selling, became one of the biggest businesses in the world.

sections.h: Who was Ray Kroc before McDonald's?
paras: Raymond Albert Kroc was born on 5 October 1902 in Oak Park, Illinois. At 15 he lied about his age to train as a Red Cross ambulance driver in the First World War, but the war ended before he was sent overseas.

In 1922 he took a job selling paper cups for the Lily-Tulip Cup Company and rose to Midwest sales manager. Selling cups meant years of visiting soda fountains, cafés and restaurant counters: he learned how food businesses ran, what slowed them down and what owners would pay for.

Around 1940 he switched to selling the Prince Castle Multimixer, a machine that could make five milkshakes at once, and carried it from kitchen to kitchen for more than a decade. By 1954 he was in his fifties, an age when most people are planning to retire, not to start.

sections.h: What did Ray Kroc see in San Bernardino in 1954?
paras: The restaurant belonged to two brothers, Dick and Mac McDonald, who had opened a drive-in in San Bernardino in 1940. In 1948 they closed it for three months and reopened with a radical idea: self-service windows instead of carhops, a menu cut to nine items and lower prices. They called it the Speedee Service System.

Kroc noticed the restaurant because it kept ordering more of his mixers. When he arrived, he saw an assembly line for food: a short menu, fast, consistent and cheap, with crowds at the windows. Many people had seen that stand. Kroc saw it with 30 years of restaurant visits in his head, and understood it could be copied town by town.
He offered to become the brothers' franchising agent. He was 52, according to McDonald's own history page and to London Business School's profile of him.

sections.h: How did the first McDonald's franchise deal work?
paras: Under the deal, a franchisee paid a $950 fee and 1.9% of gross sales. Of that 1.9%, 0.5% went to the McDonald brothers and the rest to Kroc's company.

On 15 April 1955 Kroc opened his own McDonald's in Des Plaines, Illinois, the first one east of the Mississippi River. McDonald's records its first-day sales as $366.12. He used it as a model restaurant: proof that the system worked far from California, and a place to train others.

The pattern will feel familiar if you know how Colonel Sanders started over at 65 (https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/colonel-sanders-started-over-at-65-kfc-story/): decades of hands-on experience in one industry, turned into a recipe other people could run.

sections.h: How did McDonald's grow so fast in the 1950s and 1960s?
paras: The turning point was money, not burgers. Harry Sonneborn, who joined Kroc in the mid-1950s for about $100 a week, set up a real-estate model: the company bought or leased the land and buildings and rented them to franchisees. The rent gave McDonald's steady income and the capital to keep opening new restaurants.

Growth followed. The chain went from a handful of restaurants to 228 by 1960. In 1961, according to McDonald's, Hamburger University opened in the basement of a restaurant in Elk Grove Village, Illinois, to train operators. The same year Kroc agreed to buy out the McDonald brothers for $2.7 million, a price Dick McDonald named. In 1965 the company went public at $22.50 a share.
Kroc kept working into old age. He published his autobiography, Grinding It Out, in 1977 and was senior chairman until he died on 14 January 1984, aged 81.

sections.h: Did Ray Kroc found McDonald's? Myth vs fact
paras: Myth: Ray Kroc invented McDonald's. Fact: Dick and Mac McDonald created the restaurant, its name and the Speedee system. Kroc built the company that franchised it nationally and then worldwide, and he bought the rights in 1961. The 2016 film The Founder, with Michael Keaton as Kroc, dramatised this story; for exact facts, rely on the sources below rather than on the film.
Myth: success came from one lucky break. Fact: the growth came from the land-and-lease model and from training people to run every restaurant the same way, year after year.

Myth: 52 is too late. Fact: the most valuable thing Kroc brought to San Bernardino was everything he had learned before he got there. Our list of late bloomers who found success after 50 (https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/late-bloomers-people-who-found-success-after-50/) shows the same thing again and again.

sections.h: What can you learn from Ray Kroc's late start?
paras: Kroc did not have a new idea. He had a trained eye. Years of watching kitchens told him that a stand ordering several mixers at once was unusual, and that a fast, simple, consistent kitchen could be copied. Your own years in a job or a trade are the same kind of data: you notice what customers keep asking for, and where things go wrong.

The second lesson is about systems. Kroc's restaurants did not depend on one talented cook; they depended on a method other people could learn. Write down how you do the thing that works, so someone else can do it too. For smaller starts in the same spirit, read how Phil Knight began with $50 and a car boot of shoes (https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/phil-knight-50-dollars-shoes-car-trunk-nike-story/) and how Falguni Nayar started Nykaa at 49 (https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/falguni-nayar-nykaa-started-at-49-story/).

timeline: Ray Kroc is born in Oak Park, Illinois (5 October).
Starts selling paper cups for the Lily-Tulip Cup Company.
Dick and Mac McDonald reopen their San Bernardino drive-in with the self-service Speedee Service System.
Kroc, 52, visits the brothers and becomes their franchising agent.
Opens his first McDonald's in Des Plaines, Illinois (15 April); first-day sales $366.12.
Buys out the McDonald brothers for $2.7 million; Hamburger University opens.
McDonald's goes public at $22.50 a share.
Kroc dies on 14 January, aged 81; about 7,500 restaurants worldwide.
lesson: A late start is not a blank start. Everything you have learned so far is the advantage a younger person doesn't have yet.
check: What have you watched up close for years that most people have never noticed?
Which part of what you do well could you write down as steps someone else could follow?
faq: How old was Ray Kroc when he started McDonald's?
Ray Kroc was 52 when he visited the McDonald brothers in San Bernardino in 1954 and became their franchising agent. He opened his first McDonald's in Des Plaines, Illinois, on 15 April 1955.
What did Ray Kroc do before McDonald's?

He sold paper cups for the Lily-Tulip Cup Company from 1922, rising to Midwest sales manager, and then sold the Prince Castle Multimixer, a machine that made five milkshakes at once. That is how he came across the McDonald brothers' busy restaurant.
Did Ray Kroc found McDonald's?

No. Dick and Mac McDonald opened the original restaurant in San Bernardino in 1940 and created its fast self-service system in 1948. Kroc franchised the system, built McDonald's into a national company and bought the brothers' rights in 1961.
How much did Ray Kroc pay the McDonald brothers?
$2.7 million in 1961, the price Dick McDonald asked, according to McDonald's corporate history and other accounts based on Kroc's autobiography.
How many McDonald's restaurants are there today?
McDonald's reported 43,477 restaurants in more than 100 countries at the end of 2024, about 95% of them franchised. When Kroc died in 1984 there were about 7,500.

title: Mirabai Chanu: Five Failed Lifts in Rio, Then World Champion and Tokyo Silver
seo_title: Mirabai Chanu: From Rio 2016 DNF to Tokyo Olympic Silver
summary: At Rio 2016 Mirabai Chanu made one valid lift of six and did not finish. A year later she was world champion; in Tokyo she won India's first medal.
intro: On the scoreboard at the Rio 2016 Olympics, the row for India's Saikhom Mirabai Chanu ended with three letters: DNF. Did not finish. In the women's 48 kg event she made one snatch, at 82 kg, and then missed all three of her clean-and-jerk attempts. One valid lift out of six, and no total.

Fifteen months later she was world champion. Five years later, at the Tokyo Olympics, she lifted 202 kg in total and won silver: India's first medal of those Games. This is how a lifter from a small village in Manipur turned the worst day of her career into the start of her best years.

sections.h: Who is Mirabai Chanu?
paras: Mirabai Chanu grew up in Nongpok Kakching, a village outside Imphal, the capital of Manipur in north-east India. Her family was not wealthy; according to The Better India, her father worked for the Public Works Department in Imphal and her mother ran a small shop in the village.

Her strength showed early. Her brother told the International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) that when she was about 12, she picked up and carried home a bundle of firewood he could not lift, a walk of about two kilometres. She was inspired by Kunjarani Devi, one of India's great weightlifters, who later coached her.

Getting to training was its own challenge. Her academy was in Imphal, a long way from home. For years, truck drivers on that road gave her free rides. In August 2021, after Tokyo, she invited about 150 truck drivers and helpers to thank them with a meal and gifts, Tribune India and The Quint reported.

sections.h: What happened to Mirabai Chanu at the Rio 2016 Olympics?
paras: Mirabai went to Rio as a medal hope after winning silver at the 2014 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. In the snatch she missed 82 kg on her first attempt, made it on her second and missed 84 kg on her third, according to PTI's report in Deccan Herald.

In the clean and jerk, her stronger lift, she missed 104 kg and then 106 kg twice. ESPN reported the same sequence. Without a valid clean and jerk there is no total, so she was listed as did not finish.
For an athlete who had trained most of her life for that stage, it was as public a failure as sport gets. What she did next is why her story is worth knowing.

sections.h: How did she come back after Rio?
paras: She went back to the training hall. On 30 November 2017, at the World Weightlifting Championships in Anaheim, USA, she won gold in the 48 kg class with a total of 194 kg (85 kg snatch, 109 kg clean and jerk). The Week and the IWF both describe it as India's first world title in the sport in 22 years, since Karnam Malleswari in the 1990s.

In 2018 she won gold at the Commonwealth Games on the Gold Coast with 196 kg. Then her body pushed back: a lower back injury kept her out of competition for much of 2018, the IWF reported. She returned, and in 2018 she also received the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna, India's highest sporting honour.

sections.h: How much did Mirabai Chanu lift at the Tokyo Olympics?
paras: On 24 July 2021, in the women's 49 kg event at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics (held a year late), Mirabai lifted 87 kg in the snatch and 115 kg in the clean and jerk: 202 kg in total. China's Hou Zihui won gold with 210 kg and Indonesia's Aisah Windy Cantika took bronze with 194 kg, according to Olympics.com and Gulf News.
The silver was India's first medal of the Tokyo Games. She was 26. It was also only the second Olympic weightlifting medal ever won by an Indian, after Karnam Malleswari's bronze at Sydney 2000.

sections.h: What people get wrong about her story
paras: It is easy to tell this as a story of one magic comeback day in Tokyo. The record shows something slower. Between Rio and Tokyo there were five years of competitions, a world title, a Commonwealth gold, an injury and long stretches of rehabilitation. The silver was the visible end of a lot of unseen work.

It is also easy to read Rio as the moment she was proven not good enough. The scoreboard said something narrower: on that day, at those weights, the clean and jerk did not go up. She treated it as information about her lifting, not as a judgement on her.

sections.h: The borrowed hindsight
paras: One bad day is data, not a verdict. A failed attempt tells you what broke, under what conditions. It does not tell you what you are capable of. The useful question after a setback is not "am I good enough?" but "what exactly went wrong, and what will I change before the next attempt?" A simple habit helps: within a day of a bad result, write down the plain facts of what happened, while the details are still fresh, and one change you will test next time.
Mirabai's story also has a quieter lesson: the people who helped her early, the truck drivers on a Manipur road, were part of the medal too, and she went back to thank them.

faq: Did Mirabai Chanu fail at the Rio Olympics?
Yes. At Rio 2016 in the women's 48 kg event she made one snatch at 82 kg but missed all three clean-and-jerk attempts, so she had no total and was listed as did not finish (Deccan Herald/PTI, ESPN).
What medal did Mirabai Chanu win at Tokyo 2020?
Silver in the women's 49 kg weightlifting event on 24 July 2021, with a total of 202 kg (87 kg snatch, 115 kg clean and jerk). It was India's first medal of the Tokyo Games.
When did Mirabai Chanu become world champion?
On 30 November 2017 at the World Weightlifting Championships in Anaheim, USA, in the 48 kg class, with a total of 194 kg.
Where is Mirabai Chanu from?
Nongpok Kakching, a village outside Imphal in Manipur, India. As a young lifter she got free rides from truck drivers to her training academy in Imphal.
Why did Mirabai Chanu thank truck drivers?

For years, truck drivers gave her free rides to training in Imphal. After Tokyo, in August 2021, she invited about 150 drivers and helpers to thank them with a meal and gifts (Tribune India, The Quint).

title: The Amul Story: How 247 Litres of Milk From Two Villages Became India's Biggest Dairy Brand
seo_title: Amul Story: From 247 Litres of Milk to India's Top Dairy
summary: In 1946, farmers in Kheda formed a cooperative with two village societies and 247 litres of milk. It became Amul. The true story, with sources.
intro: In 1946, a group of dairy farmers in Kheda district, Gujarat, were tired of selling their milk for whatever one buyer offered. So they started their own cooperative. It began with just two village dairy societies and 247 litres of milk, according to Outlook and the dairy trade paper DairyNews7x7.

That cooperative is Amul. In 2025-26 the Amul brand's turnover crossed ₹1 lakh crore, and it is owned by about 36 lakh dairy farmers, Lokmat Times and AgroSpectrum reported in April 2026. Here is how a few cans of milk became India's biggest dairy brand, and what most retellings get wrong.

sections.h: Why did the farmers of Kheda start their own dairy?
paras: In the 1940s, milk from Kheda (then called Kaira) went to the city through one private dairy, Polson, which held a monopoly on collecting it, ThePrint reports. Under the government's Bombay Milk Scheme, Kaira's milk was shipped to the city through that one dairy, and the farmers who produced it had almost no say in the price.

In 1946 the farmers refused to sell to the monopoly and went on a milk strike, both ThePrint and DairyNews7x7 report. Led by Tribhuvandas Patel, who became the founder chairman, they registered the Kaira District Co-operative Milk Producers' Union by December 1946. The idea was simple: the farmers would own the dairy, so the money from their milk would come back to them.

sections.h: Who built Amul: Tribhuvandas Patel, Verghese Kurien and H. M. Dalaya
paras: Verghese Kurien did not plan to stay. Britannica says he came to Anand in 1949 to work at a government creamery as a condition of his scholarship to Michigan State University. The farmers' cooperative asked for his help, and he became its manager; the government's New India Samachar dates his joining to 1 January 1950, and Outlook also puts it in 1950.

He worked with chairman Tribhuvandas Patel and dairy engineer Harichand Megha Dalaya. DairyNews7x7 credits the three of them, together, with building the dairy. None of them owned it. That was the point: the owners were the farmers who poured milk into the cans every morning and evening.

sections.h: What was Amul's 'impossible' breakthrough?
paras: Most of Kheda's milk came from buffaloes, and experts abroad believed milk powder could only be made from cow's milk. Kurien and Dalaya proved them wrong, says New India Samachar. ThePrint describes Dalaya's method of spray-drying buffalo milk into powder as something dairy technologists had thought could not be done.

Amul Dairy's own history says the world's first buffalo-milk spray dryer was installed in Anand in 1955. It mattered for a practical reason: in the flush season farmers produced more milk than the city could drink. Turning the surplus into powder meant the cooperative could keep buying from them all year.

sections.h: Where did the name Amul and the Amul girl come from?
paras: The name comes from the Sanskrit word 'amulya', meaning priceless, ThePrint reports. Sources differ on the year: New India Samachar says the brand was named in 1955, while ThePrint says it was registered in 1957.

The famous mascot came later. In 1966, Sylvester daCunha of the agency Advertising and Sales Promotion conceived the chubby girl in a polka-dot dress, and art director Eustace Fernandes drew her, Khaleej Times and Storyboard18 report. Because television sets and print ads were out of reach for many households, she first appeared on hoardings, and she has been commenting on the news with a pun ever since.

sections.h: How did the Amul model spread across India?
paras: Once Anand worked, the country copied it. In 1965 Kurien became the first chairman of the National Dairy Development Board, set up to build cooperatives on the Anand pattern, Britannica and New India Samachar report. Operation Flood, the programme that linked village cooperatives to cities across India, began at the start of the 1970s.

The result is one of the great turnarounds in food history. India became the world's largest milk producer, overtaking the United States in 1998, according to New India Samachar and DailyO. Even the film about the movement was farmer-owned: Shyam Benegal's Manthan (1976) was paid for by about five lakh dairy farmers who gave ₹2 each, Deccan Herald and The Tribune report. A restored version screened at Cannes in 2024.

sections.h: How big is Amul today, and what do people get wrong?
paras: Today the Gujarat Co-operative Milk Marketing Federation (GCMMF), which markets Amul, has 18 member district unions. Its own turnover was ₹73,450 crore in 2025-26, up from ₹65,911 crore, and the wider Amul brand passed ₹1 lakh crore, Lokmat Times and AgroSpectrum report. The Week (PTI) says the network collects milk from about 36 lakh farmers.

The common myth is that Kurien founded Amul. He did not: the farmers had already formed their union in 1946, before he arrived, and he built it as their employee. The other myth is that big brands need big money to start. Amul started with 247 litres. Like Lijjat Papad (https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/lijjat-papad-seven-women-80-rupees-story/) and Nirma (https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/karsanbhai-patel-nirma-detergent-3-rupees-story/), it grew because ordinary people kept showing up, day after day.

That is the borrowed hindsight in this story. The farmers of Kheda did not wait for a big investor or a perfect plan. They had a problem they all shared, a small amount of milk each, and a decision to work together. If you have a small idea and two or three people who care about it as much as you do, that is a real start, not a weak one.

Kurien becomes the first chairman of the National Dairy Development Board
The Amul girl first appears on hoardings
Manthan, paid for by about five lakh farmers at ₹2 each, is released
India becomes the world's largest milk producer
lesson: You don't need big money to build something big. You need a small group who own it together and keep showing up.
check: What could you start this month with the small amount you already have?
Who are the two or three people who would build it with you?
faq: How did Amul start?

Amul started in 1946 when dairy farmers in Kheda (Kaira) district, Gujarat, formed the Kaira District Co-operative Milk Producers' Union after a milk strike against a monopoly buyer. It began with two village dairy societies and 247 litres of milk.
Who is the founder of Amul?

The farmers' union was founded in 1946 with Tribhuvandas Patel as its founder chairman. Verghese Kurien joined as manager around 1950 and, with engineer H. M. Dalaya, built it into a modern dairy. The farmers have always been its owners.
What is the full form or meaning of Amul?
Amul comes from the Sanskrit word 'amulya', meaning priceless. Sources differ on whether the brand name was adopted in 1955 or registered in 1957.
Who owns Amul?
Amul is owned by about 36 lakh dairy farmers through their village societies and district unions. The Gujarat Co-operative Milk Marketing Federation (GCMMF), with 18 member unions, markets the brand.
What is Amul's turnover?
In 2025-26, GCMMF's turnover was ₹73,450 crore and the Amul brand's total turnover crossed ₹1 lakh crore, up about 11% from the previous year.

title: Inky the Octopus: The Night He Slipped Out of New Zealand's National Aquarium and Went Back to the Sea
seo_title: Inky the Octopus Escape: How He Got Back to the Sea
summary: Inky the octopus slipped out of his tank at New Zealand's National Aquarium, crossed the floor and went down a 50-metre drain pipe to the Pacific. The true story.
intro: One night, after the staff at the National Aquarium of New Zealand in Napier had gone home, a common octopus called Inky found that the top of his tank was not quite closed. By the next morning he was gone. The only clue was a trail across the floor, leading to a drain hole about 15 centimetres wide.

That drain fed a pipe of about 50 metres that ran straight back to the Pacific Ocean. Nobody saw him leave, and he was never seen again. When the aquarium told the story in April 2016, about three months later, it travelled around the world.

sections.h: Who was Inky the octopus?
paras: Inky was a common New Zealand octopus who had lived at the National Aquarium in Napier since 2014. He did not arrive in perfect shape. Fishermen caught him in a crayfish (rock lobster) pot off Pania Reef, near Napier, and he came in scarred and battle-worn. The Associated Press reported that two of his arms were about half their normal length, probably after an attack by a fish.

He recovered at the aquarium and became a favourite with staff and visitors. The aquarium's manager, Rob Yarrall, described him to National Geographic as "very inquisitive", an octopus who "liked to push boundaries". He also told the AP that Inky would come up to the surface so keepers could hand-feed him.

sections.h: How did Inky escape from the aquarium?
paras: Reports agree on the main steps. During maintenance work, the lid of Inky's tank was left slightly open (RNZ, TIME and CBC all describe it this way; the AP describes a small gap at the top of the tank). At some point after dark, Inky climbed out through that gap.

He then crossed the floor to one of the drain holes used to return water to the sea. The hole was about 150 millimetres (6 inches) across, according to both RNZ and the AP. He squeezed into it and travelled down a pipe of roughly 50 metres (164 feet), reported by both CBC and the AP, which empties into the Pacific Ocean off Napier.
Nobody watched any of this happen. Staff worked out the route the next day from the wet trail he left behind. When they checked the pipework, he was already gone.

sections.h: How can an octopus fit through such a small hole?
paras: An octopus has no bones. Its body is soft, so it can change shape and push through openings that look far too small for it. National Geographic noted that this is exactly why octopuses are such good escape artists, and Yarrall told the AP that an octopus can get through almost any opening larger than its beak, the one hard part of its body.
Inky's body was described by the AP as about the size of a rugby ball. A 6-inch drain looks impossible for an animal that size. For an octopus, it was simply a way through.

sections.h: Was the escape surprising to scientists?
paras: Not really. James Wood, a marine biologist quoted by National Geographic, said Inky's escape was not surprising, because octopuses are very intelligent and learn quickly. He described octopuses that had escaped from closed tanks before, including one in Bermuda that repeatedly left its own tank to eat animals in nearby ones.

The aquarium said Inky was not unhappy or lonely; octopuses live alone in the wild, and Yarrall's view was that Inky simply wanted to know what was outside. The aquarium also said it did not plan to replace him.

sections.h: Myth vs fact: what the viral versions get wrong
paras: Myth: someone saw Inky make a daring dash across the room. Fact: no one saw him leave. The whole route was reconstructed later from his trail.

Myth: he planned the escape for months. Fact: nobody can know what an octopus planned. What is reported is simpler and more useful: the lid was not fully closed, a drain was nearby, and he used both. We have stuck to what the sources printed.

sections.h: What Inky's escape teaches us (and how to find your own gap)
paras: We usually look for a big, obvious door: the perfect job offer, the big break, the person who opens everything for us. Inky did not need a big door. He needed one small gap and the willingness to squeeze through it.

Most of us have a few gaps like that already: an email we never followed up, a person who once said "ask me anytime", a short course, a small side project. They don't look like much. That is exactly why they get ignored. If you want to see how small starts grow, read how Payeng planted a forest by himself at https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/jadav-payeng-forest-man-of-india-molai-forest-assam/.

Try a simple exercise. Write down three doors that are already slightly open for you: a conversation that ended with "let's stay in touch", a skill you are halfway through learning, an offer someone made that you never took up. Don't judge them yet; just list them.

Then pick the smallest one and take one step through it before the week ends: send the follow-up, book the class, ask the question. Inky did not wait for a bigger drain. A small opening, used, beats a big one you are still waiting for.

lesson: Look for the gap. The way forward is often smaller than you think, and it may already be half open.
check: What is one door in your life that is already half open, and what is the first small step through it this week?

When did Inky the octopus escape?
Early in 2016. The National Aquarium of New Zealand made it public in April 2016, about three months after the escape.
Where is the aquarium Inky escaped from?

Was Inky ever found?
No. Staff found only his trail. According to reports at the time, he was not seen again after he went down the drain.

title: Business Deals That Were Turned Down: 10 "No"s That Cost Billions
seo_title: Business Deals Turned Down: 10 Nos That Cost Billions
summary: Excite passed on Google, Yahoo refused $44.6 billion, Sony skipped the Avengers. 10 famous turned-down deals, with sources, and what each one teaches.
intro: In 1999, two Stanford graduates were ready to sell their search engine for less than a million dollars. The buyer they approached, Excite, said no. The search engine was Google.

Stories like this get passed around as jokes about foolish executives. The real versions are more useful. Most of these people had sensible reasons at the time, and that is exactly why the lessons matter: the same reasons will sound sensible to you one day too. Here are 10 famous business deals that were turned down, checked against reputable sources, plus two refusals that turned out to be right.

sections.h: 1. Excite: the chance to buy Google for under $1 million (1999)
paras: Larry Page and Sergey Brin were keen to get back to their studies and were willing to sell. Investor Vinod Khosla, who told the story on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt in 2010, said the founders agreed to a price of $1 million and that he talked them down to $750,000. Excite's chief executive, George Bell, still said no.

Bell has given his own side. He told CNBC in 2015 that money was not the real obstacle: Page insisted that Excite rip out its own search technology and replace it with Google's, and Bell says he chose his company's culture over the opportunity. Excite was later sold on and faded. Google became one of the most valuable companies in the world.

sections.h: 2. Blockbuster: Netflix for $50 million (2000)
paras: In 2000, Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph flew to Dallas and offered their small, loss-making DVD-by-mail company to Blockbuster for $50 million. Blockbuster, then the giant of video rental, declined. Randolph later said they were laughed out of the room.

Blockbuster did eventually build its own online service, and for a while it gave Netflix a real fight. But it filed for bankruptcy in 2010, while Netflix moved into streaming. The full story is here: https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/blockbuster-netflix-50-million-offer-2000/

sections.h: 3. Yahoo: Microsoft's $44.6 billion offer (2008)
paras: On 1 February 2008, Microsoft offered to buy Yahoo for $31 a share, about $44.6 billion. Yahoo's stock had been trading below $20, so it was a large premium. Ten days later, Yahoo's board rejected it, saying the offer "substantially undervalues" the company.

Nine years later, in June 2017, Verizon completed its purchase of Yahoo's core business for about $4.48 billion, roughly a tenth of what Microsoft had offered. Yahoo's board believed in its own future, and that belief was not unreasonable in 2008; the internet simply moved faster than anyone inside expected.

sections.h: 4. Friendster: Google's $30 million offer (2003)
paras: Before Facebook and MySpace, there was Friendster, one of the first popular social networks. In 2003, Google offered about $30 million for it, according to TechCrunch and Mental Floss. Founder Jonathan Abrams turned the offer down; Mental Floss reports that investors told him the long-term prize was too big to give up, and he took venture funding instead.
Within a few years, its users had moved on to MySpace and then Facebook. A $30 million offer in Google stock in 2003, before Google went public, is one of the most painful "what ifs" in tech.

sections.h: 5. Groupon: Google's offer of about $6 billion (2010)
paras: In December 2010, Groupon, the daily-deals company, turned down a reported takeover offer from Google of about $6 billion, according to the Chicago Tribune as reported by The Next Web, and eWeek. Groupon reportedly believed it was strong enough to stay independent.

It went public instead, in November 2011, at $20 a share. Within three weeks the shares had already slipped below that price. Whether Groupon should have sold is still debated, but it remains the classic example of an offer that looked too small at the time.

sections.h: 6. Sony: almost every Marvel hero for $25 million (1998)
paras: In 1998, Marvel was just out of bankruptcy and needed cash. According to Ben Fritz's book The Big Picture, excerpted in The Wall Street Journal and reported by Quartz and /Film, Marvel offered Sony the film rights to nearly all its characters, including Iron Man, Thor and Black Panther, for $25 million. Sony wanted only Spider-Man.

Marvel went on to make those films itself and was bought by Disney for about $4 billion in 2009. How Marvel climbed back is told here: https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/marvel-bankruptcy-1996-to-disney-4-billion-comeback/

sections.h: 7. Decca: the Beatles audition (1962)
paras: On New Year's Day 1962, a young band from Liverpool played 15 songs at Decca's London studio. Decca passed and signed another group instead. Months later, the Beatles signed with EMI's Parlophone label.

The famous line "guitar groups are on their way out" is often pinned on Decca's Dick Rowe, but he denied saying it all his life. Decca's consolation: on a tip from George Harrison, it later signed the Rolling Stones. Read the full story: https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/decca-rejected-beatles-1962-audition/

sections.h: 8. Hewlett-Packard: Steve Wozniak's computer, five times
paras: Steve Wozniak designed the computer that became the Apple I while he was working at HP. He felt he owed his employer the first chance at it. He has said, including at the Computer History Museum, that HP turned him down five times.

Wozniak has also said that by the end he was hoping they would say no, because he wanted to build Apple. HP stayed a successful company, but it let a personal computer built by one of its own engineers walk out of the door.

sections.h: 9. IBM, GE and RCA: the photocopier nobody wanted
paras: On 22 October 1938, in a makeshift lab in Astoria, New York, inventor Chester Carlson made the first dry copy of an image using static electricity, a process later called xerography. Over the next years he showed it to major companies, including IBM, General Electric and RCA. They turned him down. It took him years, through the Second World War, to find anyone willing to back it.

The non-profit Battelle Memorial Institute backed the research in 1944, and a small Rochester company called Haloid bought into it. Haloid later renamed itself Xerox, and its Xerox 914 copier went into production in 1959. The idea that big companies passed on became the word people used for copying itself.

sections.h: 10. Hollywood studios: Star Wars
paras: In the early 1970s, George Lucas went looking for a studio to fund his space film. United Artists passed. Universal, which had backed his hit American Graffiti, also let the project go, deciding it would cost too much, according to the American Film Institute's catalog.

Alan Ladd Jr., then a creative executive at 20th Century Fox, had loved American Graffiti and agreed to take a chance on Lucas. Star Wars opened in 1977 and became one of the most successful film series of all time.

sections.h: The other side: two "no"s that were exactly right
paras: Not every refusal is a mistake. In 2006, Yahoo offered about $1 billion for Facebook. Mark Zuckerberg, then 22, said no, according to the books Becoming Facebook and An Ugly Truth. He has said the painful part was not the refusal itself, but that many of his staff left afterwards because they did not believe in it.

In India, around 1990, Infosys was offered $1 million, and some of its founders were tempted to sell. Narayana Murthy has said he argued against it and was even ready to buy out his colleagues, though he had no money to do it. They stayed. How Infosys began: https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/how-infosys-started-with-10000-rupees-sudha-murty-1981/

sections.h: What these turned-down deals have in common
paras: Almost every "no" on this list was judged against the business as it stood that day: Blockbuster's stores, Excite's search, Sony's need for one hit, Hollywood's budgets. The people saying yes were judging what the thing could become.

None of this means you should say yes to everything. Zuckerberg and Murthy said no too. The difference is what they were refusing: a price, not a future they believed in. The executives on this list were often refusing a future they could not yet see.
That is the borrowed hindsight. Before you turn something down, ask two questions: would I still say no if this grew ten times bigger, and am I refusing the idea or just the way it looks today?

lesson: Most famous bad "no"s judged the idea as it looked that day, not what it could become. Before you refuse, picture it ten times bigger.
check: What is one offer, idea or person you turned down because of how it looked today?
Would you still say no if it became ten times bigger?
faq: Did Excite really turn down buying Google?

Yes. Investor Vinod Khosla said in 2010 that Google's founders agreed to sell to Excite in 1999 and that he negotiated the price down to $750,000, but Excite's CEO George Bell declined. Bell told CNBC in 2015 that his main objection was Larry Page's demand to replace Excite's search technology with Google's.
How much did Microsoft offer for Yahoo?
In February 2008 Microsoft offered $31 a share, about $44.6 billion. Yahoo's board rejected it as too low. In 2017 Verizon bought Yahoo's core business for about $4.48 billion.
Did Sony really turn down the Marvel characters?

According to Ben Fritz's book The Big Picture, excerpted in The Wall Street Journal, Marvel offered Sony the film rights to almost all its characters in 1998 for $25 million. Sony only wanted Spider-Man.
How much did Netflix ask Blockbuster for?
In 2000, Netflix's founders offered to sell the company to Blockbuster for $50 million. Blockbuster declined, and filed for bankruptcy in 2010.
Which companies turned down the photocopier?
Chester Carlson, who made the first xerographic copy in 1938, was turned down by large companies including IBM, General Electric and RCA. Haloid, later renamed Xerox, took the idea to market.
