title: Seven Investors Said No to Airbnb: The $150,000 Offer Nobody Took, and What Happened Next
seo_title: Airbnb Rejected by 7 Investors: The $150,000 Offer
summary: In 2008 Airbnb's founders offered 10% of the company for $150,000. Of seven investors, five said no and two never replied. The true story and the lesson.
intro: In the summer of 2008, three young founders in San Francisco tried to sell 10% of their company for $150,000. They were introduced to seven investors. Five wrote back to say no. The other two never replied.
The company was Airbnb. Twelve years later, on its first day as a public company, it was worth more than $80 billion. This is what happened in between, and what the rejections really tell us.

sections.h: How did Airbnb start?
paras: In 2007 Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia, two designers who had studied together at the Rhode Island School of Design, were sharing an apartment in San Francisco and struggling to pay the rent. A big design conference was coming to town and the city's hotels were full.

So they laid air mattresses on their floor and offered visitors a place to sleep plus breakfast in the morning. Their first guests each paid $80. A third former roommate, the engineer Nathan Blecharczyk, joined to build the website, and the idea got a name: Air Bed and Breakfast.
It was a tiny, scrappy start. The founders did not have a grand plan for a global company. They had a rent problem and an empty floor.

sections.h: Who rejected Airbnb, and what did they say?
paras: In June 2008 the founders were trying to raise $150,000 at a valuation of $1.5 million, which means the money would have bought 10% of the company. They were introduced to seven well-known investors in Silicon Valley.

In 2015 Brian Chesky published the rejection emails on Medium under the title "7 Rejections", with the investors' names removed. Five investors replied and said no. The reasons were polite and short: the idea was outside the firm's focus, the firm was not keen on travel businesses, or the market opportunity did not seem large enough. Two investors did not reply at all.

Chesky counted all seven as rejections, and that is how the story is usually told. The more precise version is five written noes and two silences, which, to a founder waiting for an answer, feel much the same.

sections.h: Why did investors doubt Airbnb?
paras: Today it sounds obvious that people will rent a room or a whole home from a stranger. In 2008 it sounded odd, even risky. Many investors simply did not believe that strangers would want to sleep in each other's homes, or that enough people would do it to build a large business.

That doubt is worth remembering. An idea that is new often looks wrong at first, because there is nothing to compare it with. The investors were not foolish. They were judging an unusual idea, with little data, on one day.
It also helps to remember what a rejection email usually is: a short, polite answer from a busy person who sees many pitches every week. It is rarely a careful verdict on whether your idea can work.

sections.h: How did cereal boxes keep Airbnb alive?
paras: By late 2008 the founders were broke and in debt. During a big convention in Denver, when visitors again needed places to stay, they designed their own limited-edition cereal boxes and sold them for $40 each. According to the founders, the boxes brought in about $30,000.

The money mattered, but the boxes did something more. When the founders interviewed for the start-up programme Y Combinator, its co-founder Paul Graham was struck by how hard they had worked to keep going. Airbnb joined the programme in early 2009, renamed itself Airbnb in March 2009, and in April 2009 received a $600,000 seed investment from Sequoia Capital.

sections.h: How big did Airbnb become?
paras: Airbnb listed its shares on the stock market on 10 December 2020. The shares were priced at $68 and closed their first day at $144.71, more than double. At that closing price the company was valued at about $86.5 billion, according to CNBC.

Put next to the 2008 offer, the gap is huge. Ten percent of the company for $150,000 would have been worth billions on paper at that moment, before any later dilution. That is why the rejection emails became famous: they are a rare, written record of a "no" that turned out to be wrong.

sections.h: Myth vs fact: what the Airbnb rejections really teach
paras: Myth: the investors who said no were bad at their jobs. Fact: experienced investors say no to most pitches, and most of those noes are right. The lesson is not that experts are always wrong, but that a single no is one person's view of your idea on one day, with the information they had then.

Myth: Airbnb succeeded because someone finally believed in it. Fact: the founders kept going before anyone believed in it. They kept hosting, kept improving the site and found money in unusual ways, so that when the next person looked, there was more to see.
If you have had a no recently, the useful question is not "were they right?" but "what would make the next person say yes?" Then send it to someone new.

title: Oldest Olympic Medal Winners: Athletes Who Won Medals After 40
seo_title: Oldest Olympic Medal Winners: Medals After 40
summary: Oscar Swahn won Olympic silver at 72. Meet 9 athletes who won Olympic medals after 40, from 1908 to Paris 2024, with sources for every age.
intro: In the summer of 1920, a 72-year-old Swede stood at the shooting range in Antwerp, took aim at a moving target 100 metres away and helped his team win an Olympic silver medal. More than a hundred years later, no man has won an Olympic medal at an older age.

Most of us quietly assume the Olympics belong to the young. The record books say something more interesting. In sports that reward patience, judgement and calm hands, people have stood on the podium in their forties, fifties and sixties, and a few of them had already retired, become parents, or spent decades trying before their medal came. Here are 9 of them, oldest first, with every age checked against two reputable sources.

sections.h: 1. Oscar Swahn: Olympic silver at 72 (shooting, Antwerp 1920)
paras: Oscar Swahn did not even start at the Olympics until he was 60. At London 1908 he won two golds and a bronze in the running deer event, where shooters fire at a deer-shaped target that slides across an opening 100 metres away. Four years later in Stockholm, at 64 years and 258 days, he won team gold and became the oldest Olympic champion in history, a record Olympics.com says still stands.

In 1920 he came back once more and won team silver at 72 years and 281 days. Guinness World Records lists him as the oldest male Olympic medallist ever. Every one of his team medals was won alongside his son Alfred. His career total: six medals at three Games.

sections.h: 2. Andrew Hoy: silver and bronze at 62 (eventing, Tokyo 2020)
paras: Andrew Hoy won his first Olympic medal in 1992. At the Tokyo Games, held in 2021, he rode for Australia at his eighth Olympics, aged 62, and won team silver and then individual bronze. His individual bronze came 21 years after his last individual medal, a silver at Sydney 2000.

The Australian Olympic Committee called him Australia's oldest Olympic medallist, and reports at the time noted he was the oldest Olympic medallist of any nation since 1968. He told reporters he was grateful people could still talk about his age, because when he started he was proud of being the youngest in the team.

sections.h: 3. Ian Millar: first medal at his ninth Olympics, aged 61 (show jumping, Beijing 2008)
paras: Canada's Ian Millar made his Olympic debut at Munich 1972. Then he kept coming back. He was named to the 1980 team, which Canada did not send to Moscow, and rode at Games after Games without a medal. He even competed at Sydney 2000 with a broken hand.

At Beijing 2008, his ninth Olympic Games, he finally won one: team jumping silver, at 61. Four years later at London 2012 he became the first athlete in any sport, from any nation, to compete at 10 Olympic Games, and finished ninth individually. Fans called him Captain Canada. Two of his children also became show jumpers.

sections.h: 4. Mark Todd: team bronze at 56 (eventing, London 2012)
paras: New Zealand's Mark Todd won back-to-back individual eventing golds in 1984 and 1988. Twenty-eight years after his first Olympic podium, he was back at London 2012 at 56, riding a young horse called Campino who, his team said, had done his first advanced competition less than a year earlier.

The horse was tired after the cross-country day and Todd missed an individual medal, but New Zealand took team bronze. It was Todd's fifth Olympic medal, drawing him level with New Zealand's most successful Olympians at the time.

sections.h: 5. Isabell Werth: gold in her fifties, at a seventh Olympic Games (dressage, Paris 2024)
paras: Germany's Isabell Werth won her first Olympic gold at Barcelona 1992. At Paris 2024, in her mid-fifties, she helped Germany win team dressage gold at Versailles in what she called the closest finish she had ever seen. It was Germany's third straight Olympic team dressage title, edging Denmark.

Olympics.com reported it was her 13th Olympic medal and that she became the first athlete to win a medal at seven different Olympic Games. The Associated Press called it an equestrian record. She has won gold at every Games she has entered.

sections.h: 6. Queenie Newall: the oldest woman to win Olympic gold, at 53 (archery, London 1908)
paras: Sybil 'Queenie' Newall, the eldest of seven daughters, only joined her local archery club in Cheltenham in 1905. Three years later, at the 1908 London Games, she won the women's Double National Round gold at 53 years and 275 days.

Guinness World Records and the Olympic historians at Olympedia both list her as the oldest woman ever to win an Olympic gold medal. She was not done after the Games either: she went on to become British national champion in 1911 and 1912.

sections.h: 7. Yusuf Dikeç: silver at 51 with earplugs and ordinary glasses (shooting, Paris 2024)
paras: At the Paris 2024 Olympics most pistol shooters wore large ear protectors and special lenses. Türkiye's Yusuf Dikeç, 51, wore small yellow earplugs and what looked like a regular pair of glasses, and shot with his free hand in his pocket. Photos of his calm stance went around the world.

He and partner Şevval İlayda Tarhan won silver in the 10m air pistol mixed team event. NBC News and Olympics.com both reported it was Türkiye's first ever Olympic medal in shooting, and Olympics.com said it made him his country's oldest Olympic medallist. "I did not need special equipment. I'm a natural, a natural shooter," he told reporters.

sections.h: 8. Kristin Armstrong: gold the day before her 43rd birthday (cycling, Rio 2016)
paras: Kristin Armstrong had already won the Olympic road time trial in 2008 and 2012, and famously held her young son Lucas on the podium in London. She stepped away to work in community health at a hospital in Boise, Idaho, but, as she put it, something kept driving her back.

In Rio, a day before her 43rd birthday, she won the time trial again. Team USA and The Christian Science Monitor both noted that she became the first cyclist to win the same road event at three Olympic Games, and the oldest female Olympic cycling champion.

sections.h: 9. Dara Torres: three silvers at 41, and beaten by one hundredth of a second (swimming, Beijing 2008)
paras: Dara Torres first swam at the Olympics in 1984. She retired after Sydney 2000 and had a daughter in 2006. Then she came back, and at 41 she swam at her fifth Olympics in Beijing.

She won three silver medals, in the 50m freestyle and two relays. Sports Illustrated reported that in the 50m final she lost to Britta Steffen by one hundredth of a second, and that it was the first Olympic swimming medal of its kind won by a woman over 33. Her reaction, reported by VOA, was a joke: maybe she should not have filed her nails the night before.

sections.h: What do older Olympic medallists have in common?
paras: Look at the list and three patterns stand out. First, most of these medals come in sports where experience can make up for raw speed: shooting, archery and equestrian events, where calm nerves, reading the course and partnership with a horse matter as much as fitness. If you want to compete into later life, pick the version of your sport that rewards judgement.

A note on how we checked: each age above is the athlete's age on the day of the medal, as given by Guinness World Records, an Olympic committee or a major news organisation, and we only kept ages that a second reputable source agreed with. Where sources gave no exact age, we left it out.

Second, almost all of them kept turning up. Ian Millar waited nine Games for his first medal and Yusuf Dikeç competed for years without a top-ten finish before Paris. Third, several came back after stepping away completely, like Dara Torres and Kristin Armstrong. Their ages are not the miracle; staying in the game long enough for the chance to arrive is.

If you like stories like these, read our list of late bloomers who found success after 50 at https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/late-bloomers-people-who-found-success-after-50/ and the story of Harbhajan Kaur, who started a business in her nineties, at https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/harbhajan-kaur-besan-barfi-chandigarh-started-business-in-her-nineties/. For an athlete who came back from a painful Olympic failure, read Mirabai Chanu's story at https://www.borrowedhindsight.org/stories/mirabai-chanu-rio-2016-did-not-finish-tokyo-silver/.

lesson: Age rarely closes the door. Quitting does. The oldest medallists kept turning up, and picked the arena where their experience counted.
check: What have you stopped doing only because you think you are too old for it?
Which version of it would reward your experience instead of your speed?
faq: Who is the oldest Olympic medal winner ever?
Sweden's Oscar Swahn. He won a team silver in running deer shooting at the 1920 Antwerp Olympics aged 72 years and 281 days, according to Guinness World Records and Olympics.com.
Who is the oldest Olympic gold medallist?
Also Oscar Swahn, who won team gold at Stockholm 1912 aged 64 years and 258 days. Olympics.com says that record still stands.
Who is the oldest woman to win an Olympic gold medal?
Britain's Sybil 'Queenie' Newall, who won archery gold at the 1908 London Olympics aged 53 years and 275 days, according to Guinness World Records and Olympedia.
Who is the oldest Olympic medallist in recent Games?
At Tokyo 2020 (held in 2021), Australia's Andrew Hoy won team silver and individual bronze in eventing at 62. Reports at the time said he was the oldest Olympic medallist since 1968.
Can you win an Olympic medal after 40?

Yes. Athletes have done it in swimming, cycling, shooting, archery and equestrian events. Dara Torres won three swimming silvers at 41, and Kristin Armstrong won cycling gold the day before turning 43.

title: Sent to the Gym to Lose Weight: How Neeraj Chopra Found the Javelin and Won Olympic Gold
seo_title: Neeraj Chopra: From Gym to Lose Weight to Olympic Gold
summary: Neeraj Chopra's family sent him to a gym to get fit. It shut down, he found the javelin at Panipat's stadium, and in Tokyo he threw 87.58 m for gold.
intro: The first gym Neeraj Chopra was sent to did not even last. His family in Khandra, a village in Haryana's Panipat district, wanted the boy to get fit because he had put on weight as a child. They found him a local gym. It soon shut down.

So they tried the stadium in Panipat instead. That second choice, made for fitness and nothing more, is where a farming family's son first held a javelin. On 7 August 2021 in Tokyo, the same boy threw 87.58 metres and won India's first Olympic gold medal in athletics.

sections.h: Where did Neeraj Chopra grow up?
paras: Neeraj grew up in Khandra village near Panipat in a large joint family of farmers. His father, Satish Kumar, and his uncles worked the land, and nobody in the family had a sporting background. "We do not have a sporting background, we are farmers," a family member told The Week in 2022.

Like many children in a big, loving household, he was well fed, and by his early teens he was carrying extra weight. Nobody at home was thinking about medals. The family's goal was simple: help him get fitter.

sections.h: Why was Neeraj Chopra sent to the gym?
paras: According to the accounts his uncles have given (to The Week, and in Norris Pritam's 2023 biography The Man Who Made History, excerpted by ThePrint), the family arranged for him to go to a nearby gym to lose weight and get active. One uncle took him there. Then the gym closed.

It is the kind of small setback that ends most fitness plans. Instead, the family looked for another place he could train, and settled on the stadium in Panipat (ThePrint names it Shivaji Stadium). The idea, his uncle Bhim told The Week, "was to focus on his fitness."

sections.h: How did Neeraj Chopra start javelin?
paras: At the stadium, Neeraj watched older athletes throwing the javelin and, by his own account in the biography, was fascinated by how it flew. He made friends with a local thrower and coach, Jaiveer, who one day asked him to try a throw.

The first attempt was good enough that Jaiveer told him to keep going. ThePrint's excerpt puts it plainly: his journey began that day. The Week's family interview says the same thing in fewer words: it was there that he met Jaiveer, who introduced him to the javelin. The family still describes Jaiveer as both a coach and a brother to Neeraj.

sections.h: What did Neeraj Chopra achieve at the Tokyo Olympics, and after?
paras: Years of training later, after a world junior record in 2016 and an Asian Games gold in 2018, Neeraj reached the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, held in 2021. In the men's javelin final on 7 August 2021 his best throw measured 87.58 metres, enough for gold ahead of the Czech pair Jakub Vadlejch and Vitezslav Vesely.

Olympics.com called it India's first-ever Olympic gold in track and field, and noted that he became only the second Indian to win an individual Olympic title, after shooter Abhinav Bindra. Scroll and the Free Press Journal reported the same milestone the same day.

The gold was not the end of the climb. At the 2023 World Athletics Championships in Budapest he won gold with 88.17 metres, becoming India's first world champion in athletics (reported by India TV and Onmanorama). At the Paris 2024 Olympics he won silver with 89.45 metres, his second Olympic medal, as the Free Press Journal's year-end review recorded.
For a boy whose first sporting goal was simply to get fitter, that is two Olympic medals and a world title.

sections.h: What can you borrow from how Neeraj Chopra started?
paras: Most people wait for a big enough reason before they begin: a clear goal, a perfect plan, a sign that they are talented. Neeraj's start had none of that. The reason was ordinary (get fitter), the first plan fell through (the gym closed), and the sport he became famous for was something he simply happened to see other people doing.

Two small choices did the heavy lifting. His family did not give up when the gym shut; they found another place. And when a coach offered him a javelin, he said yes to one throw. Neither choice needed courage on a grand scale. Each needed only a willingness to try the next small thing.

That is the useful part of his story for the rest of us. You do not need to know where something will lead to start it. You need a place to show up and a first attempt. If you have been putting something off because the reason feels too small, give it ten minutes this week and see what it turns into.

sections.h: Myth vs fact: was he a 'natural athlete' from the start?
paras: It is tempting to read his story backwards and assume he was always destined for the javelin. The sources say otherwise. He came from a family with no sports background, started for fitness, and his first plan (the gym) failed. The talent showed only once he was in the right place, with someone who handed him a javelin.

You will also see exact childhood weights quoted online. We have not repeated them here because we could find only one source for each figure. What both family accounts agree on is the shape of the story: weight, a gym that closed, a stadium, a coach, and a first throw.

title: The Five-Month-Old Bird That Flew 13,560 km Without Landing: The Bar-Tailed Godwit's Record Flight
seo_title: Bar-Tailed Godwit Record: 13,560 km Non-Stop in 11 Days
summary: A five-month-old bar-tailed godwit flew from Alaska to Tasmania without landing once: at least 13,560 km in 11 days. The true story of the record.
intro: On 13 October 2022, a young bird about five months old took off from the mudflats of south-west Alaska. It did not land again for eleven days. When it finally touched down on a beach in north-eastern Tasmania, it had flown at least 13,560 kilometres without a single stop, and had lost about half of its body weight on the way.

The bird was a bar-tailed godwit, known only by the number on its satellite tag: 234684. Guinness World Records now lists its flight as the longest non-stop migration by a bird. It was the first big migration of its life.

sections.h: Who was godwit 234684?
paras: Bar-tailed godwits are wading birds with long legs and a long, slightly upturned bill. They breed in Alaska in the northern summer and spend the rest of the year on the coasts of Australia and New Zealand, which means a crossing of the whole Pacific Ocean every autumn.

Godwit 234684 hatched in Alaska in 2022. Researchers fitted it with a small solar-powered satellite tag on its lower back, so its position could be followed in near real time. It was so young that the team did not even know whether it was male or female, CBC reported.

Young godwits make that first journey later than the adults. The grown birds leave Alaska first; Live Science reported that juveniles set off up to six weeks after their parents, which gives them more time to fatten up. BirdLife Tasmania's Eric Woehler, who was part of the research project, told the AP that this bird was therefore unlikely to have followed experienced adults south.

sections.h: How far did the godwit fly, and how long did it take?
paras: The bird left the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta in south-west Alaska on 13 October 2022, according to tracking data from Germany's Max Planck Institute for Ornithology, reported by the AP and CBC. It landed at Ansons Bay, on the north-eastern tip of Tasmania, eleven days later.

Guinness World Records gives the distance as 13,560 kilometres (8,435 miles) and the time as 11 days and 1 hour, "without the bird landing once". Live Science, quoting New Zealand's Pukorokoro Miranda Shorebird Centre, put it at 13,575 km and 265 continuous hours. Either way, it is roughly a third of the way around the planet in one go.

Guinness also noted something remarkable: on the way, the bird appears to have passed up chances to stop and refuel at islands such as New Caledonia and Vanuatu. It simply kept flying, day and night, over open ocean.

sections.h: How can a small bird fly for 11 days without food or rest?
paras: The secret is preparation. Before migrating, bar-tailed godwits build up some of the largest fat loads of any migratory bird ever studied, and they shrink parts of their digestive system to save weight. Guinness describes godwits absorbing part of the tissue of their digestive tract, liver and kidneys before the journey, because those organs are not needed in the air.

Then they burn that fuel, hour after hour. The AP and CBC reported that godwit 234684 lost about half its body weight on the journey; Woehler, quoted by Guinness, said it probably lost "half or more" of its weight during continuous day and night flight.
On arrival, the job is simple: rest and eat. The young bird would fatten up again on the Tasmanian shore, Woehler said.

sections.h: What record did it break?
paras: Godwits already held the records. In 2020 an adult male tagged 4BBRW flew from Alaska to New Zealand, a flight Guinness listed at about 12,200 km. The following year the same bird flew about 13,000 km to New South Wales in Australia, CBC and Live Science reported.

Godwit 234684 beat both, on its first try. When the flight was first reported in October 2022, the research had not yet been published or peer reviewed, so outlets called it a likely record. In January 2023 Guinness World Records published it as the longest non-stop migration by a bird.

Even the researchers were surprised. Tasmania is not where most godwits end up, and Woehler told CBC the team did not know whether the bird got lost, had an accident of navigation, or was following a normal pattern for the species.

sections.h: Myth vs fact: did the godwit really never stop?
paras: Fact: every source that reported the tracking data (Guinness World Records, the AP, CBC and Live Science) describes the flight as non-stop. The tag showed the bird in continuous flight from Alaska to Tasmania.

Myth to avoid: some posts say the bird "flew alone" or "followed no one". The researchers said they did not know whether it flew alone or with a flock. What is known is that adults leave Alaska earlier than juveniles, so it was not simply following its parents.
Myth to avoid: exact numbers vary slightly between reports (13,560 km or 13,575 km; landing on 24 or 25 October). The safe figure is "at least 13,560 km in about 11 days".

sections.h: What the godwit teaches us about finishing what we start
paras: It is tempting to read this as a story about toughness. But the godwit's flight was won long before take-off: in weeks of feeding, in fat stored up, in a body made lighter for one purpose. When the moment came, it did not need to stop halfway, because it had prepared for the whole distance.

Most of our unfinished projects fail the other way round. We start before we are ready, then stop at the first island that offers a rest. The borrowed hindsight from a five-month-old bird is to do the preparing first, then commit to the full distance.

How old was the godwit that set the record?
About five months old. It was a juvenile on its first southward migration, which is why researchers did not yet know its sex.
How do bar-tailed godwits fly so far without stopping?

Before migrating they store very large amounts of fat and shrink some digestive organs to save weight. They then burn that fuel in continuous flight; the record-setting bird lost about half its body weight.
Where did the godwit land?
At Ansons Bay on the north-eastern tip of Tasmania, Australia. Researchers said they were not sure whether it meant to land there or drifted off its usual route.
Did the godwit fly alone?
Nobody knows. The researchers said it was unclear whether it flew alone or with other birds, but adult godwits leave Alaska earlier than juveniles, so it was not following its parents.

title: The Job Ad Said "No Women". Sudha Murty Wrote to J.R.D. Tata (1974)
seo_title: Sudha Murty's Postcard to JRD Tata: "Lady Candidates Need Not Apply" (1974)
summary: In 1974 a TELCO job ad said lady candidates need not apply. Sudha Murty, the only girl in her class, wrote a postcard to J.R.D. Tata. What would you have done? The true story, with sources.
intro: Imagine you are 23, in the final year of a master's degree, and the only girl in your department. One day a notice goes up for engineers at one of India's biggest companies. You read to the last line: "Lady candidates need not apply."

In April 1974 that happened to Sudha Murty at the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore. She was not even planning to take the job. What she did next changed her life, and opened a door for many women after her. Before you read on, ask yourself: what would you have done?

sections.h: The notice: "Lady candidates need not apply"
paras: TELCO, the Tata company that made trucks (today Tata Motors), wanted young, bright engineers with excellent academic records. The notice ended with one line that stopped her: women need not apply.

In her own account, "Appro JRD", published by Tata, she describes being upset and angry, not because she needed the job, but because a company she admired was shutting out women before even looking at their marks.

sections.h: Choice 1: stay quiet, or write to the man at the top?
paras: Option A was to let it go. Nothing would happen to her. She had other plans, and in 1974 most people would have stayed quiet.

Option B was to complain, and not to a clerk. She decided to write to J.R.D. Tata, the chairman of the Tata group and one of the most powerful men in Indian business. He might laugh, or simply never reply.

When we asked this question on Instagram, every single person who answered chose B. One reader put it best: she would rather be laughed at than keep the door closed for herself and the girls after her.

sections.h: What she wrote on the postcard
paras: She wrote that the Tatas had always been pioneers, in basic industries like iron and steel and in higher education, and asked how a company such as TELCO could discriminate on the basis of gender.
Then she posted it, and waited. She did not expect a reply.

sections.h: The telegram: "Come to Pune"
paras: Less than ten days later a telegram arrived. TELCO asked her to come for an interview at its Pune works, with the company paying her fare.
When she walked in, a panel of six people was waiting.

sections.h: Choice 2: the research lab, or the factory floor?
paras: The panel was polite and frank. They could see she was a top student. But this was a factory, they said, not a co-educational college. TELCO had never employed a woman on its shop floor. People like her belonged in research laboratories.
Here was a second choice, and a harder one. A research job was safe, respected and fitted her degree. The factory floor was where no woman had ever worked. What would you have done?

sections.h: What she actually said
paras: She told them that someone had to make a start. If no one did, no woman would ever be able to work in their factories.
She was hired as an engineer. In her account, she became the first woman to work on the TELCO shop floor in Pune.

sections.h: Why choice 1 was harder than it looks
paras: Looking back, B feels obvious. In 1974 it was not. She was a student writing, uninvited, to the head of one of the country's largest business groups, about a rule his own company had published. There was no social media to make the complaint go viral, no law she could quote, and no guarantee anyone would even read a postcard from Bangalore.

The cost of A was invisible: nothing would happen, and the line would stay on the next notice, and the one after that. The cost of B was personal and immediate: embarrassment, or silence. Most of us weigh the visible cost more heavily. That is exactly why so many unfair rules survive.

sections.h: Why choice 2 was the real test
paras: Being invited to the interview was a small victory. The bigger test came inside the room. The panel was not hostile; it offered her a respectable way out. A research job would have let everyone feel they had been fair, and changed nothing about who could work on the factory floor.

Her answer, that someone has to make a start, turned a personal opportunity into a precedent. That is the difference between winning an argument and changing a rule: the second one usually means accepting the harder, less comfortable option.

sections.h: What you can borrow from it
paras: You do not need a famous chairman to write to. The pattern is simpler. Notice the rule everyone accepts. Ask about it respectfully, in writing, to the person who can actually change it. Then, if the door opens, walk through the harder one, not the easier one offered as a compromise.
Most of the time the reply will be smaller than hers. But the question costs very little, and the silence can cost a great deal more than it seems on the day you choose it.

sections.h: Why this story still matters
paras: The postcard cost her a few paise and one evening of courage. Staying quiet would have cost nothing that day, and much more over time, for her and for every woman who applied after her.
Sudha Murty later became one of India's best-loved authors and philanthropists. But the turning point was small and private: a young woman deciding that an unfair line deserved one honest question.

She joins TELCO as an engineer, the first woman on its shop floor
lesson: An unfair rule often survives only because nobody asks about it. One honest, respectful question can open a door for everyone after you.
check: Is there a rule around you that everyone accepts but nobody has questioned out loud?

title: He Was Packed to Leave Anand. A Farmer Asked Him to Stay a Few More Days. That Became Amul
seo_title: Verghese Kurien's Choice in 1949: How "Stay a Few More Days" Became Amul
summary: In 1949 Verghese Kurien had his release letter and his bags packed for Bombay. A farmers' leader asked him to stay a few more days. What would you have done? The true story behind Amul, with sources.
intro: Imagine you are 27, with a master's degree from America, posted to a small town you never wanted to live in. You count the days until you can leave. Finally your release letter arrives, and your bags are packed for Bombay.

Then a farmers' leader knocks and asks for one small favour: stay a few more days and help us set up our dairy machines. That was Verghese Kurien's choice at the end of 1949. Before you read on, ask yourself: what would you have done?

sections.h: A posting he never wanted
paras: Kurien had gone to the United States on a government scholarship and earned a master's degree at Michigan State University. The scholarship came with a condition: he had to serve the government when he returned.

On 13 May 1949 he arrived in Anand, in what is now Gujarat, to work at the Government Research Creamery. By Amul's own account, he wanted only one thing: to finish his bond and leave as soon as he could.

sections.h: The release letter, and a ticket to Bombay
paras: Towards the end of 1949 his relieving order came through. He was free. His plan was to go to Bombay, the big city where a young engineer with an American degree could build a real career.
Most people in his place would have caught the next train. The small creamery had been a duty, not a dream.

sections.h: Choice: the big city, or a few more days?
paras: Option A was obvious: go to Bombay. A bigger salary, a bigger city, a career that matched his degree.

Option B was to agree to a small request. Tribhuvandas Patel, the chairman of the Kaira District Co-operative Milk Producers' Union, a small group of local dairy farmers, asked him to stay a few more days and help assemble the cooperative's dairy equipment.
It did not look like a life decision. It looked like a favour. That is exactly what makes it interesting.

sections.h: What he actually did
paras: He agreed to stay a few days. He never left. In 1950 he became the head of the Kaira union, the farmers' cooperative that later took the name Amul.
Through cooperatives like it and the national programme Operation Flood, India went from importing dairy products to becoming the world's largest milk producer, passing the United States in 1998.

sections.h: Why option A was the sensible choice
paras: It is easy to admire B in hindsight. At the time, A was the rational move. Kurien had a release letter, a qualification few people in India had, and no obligation to stay. Nobody would have blamed him for leaving.

The cost of B was invisible: a few days of his time. The cost of A was also invisible: a future he could not see. Most big turning points look like this. They arrive disguised as small, slightly inconvenient requests.

sections.h: Why a few days mattered so much
paras: Those few days put him next to people with a real problem and the will to solve it: farmers who were being underpaid by middlemen and wanted to own what they produced. Working on their machines, he saw what their cooperative could become.

His career did not come from a plan. It came from saying yes to something small, paying attention, and then choosing to stay when he saw the opportunity was bigger than the city he had been waiting for.

sections.h: What you can borrow from it
paras: When someone asks you for a little of your time on something real, it can be worth saying yes before you know where it leads. The detour is cheap. The view from it is sometimes priceless.
And if you feel stuck where you never wanted to be, look around once more before you leave. The thing worth staying for is not always obvious on the first day.

lesson: Big turning points often arrive disguised as small favours. Saying yes to a few more days can be how you find your life's work.
check: Is someone asking you for a little time on something real that you have been brushing off?
